en: (B1) Now begins the second quarter.
(Section 1: "When there is a different word, there is a difference of action, because of the connection with a specific [auxiliary] element. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.2.1)

Having concluded the introductory discussion (*upodghāta*) concerning the section on the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha-adhikaraṇa*), which relates to the distinctions among meditations (*bhāvanā*) and the resulting distinctions among the unseen potencies (*apūrva*), as well as the various incidental topics (*prasaṅgānupraṣaṅga*), the distinction based on "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*) is now being stated.
Regarding those [passages] situated within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, such as:
"One should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*).

In the deliberation as to whether sentences such as “he gives gold to the Ātreya” and “he offers the sacrificial fees” possess the capacity to indicate a difference in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)— despite having different verbal root meanings—
it is established by parsimony that the injunction “one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma” prescribes merely the productive operation having heaven as its object.

Since the sentences concerning Soma and the rest enjoin sacrifices qualified by Soma and so forth by way of restating that [sacrifice], and since all of them are taught as already established (utpannaśiṣṭa), the logic of a subordinate quality (guṇanyāya) does not apply; therefore, there is no difference in the efficient force (bhāvanā). Nor is it impossible for multiple meanings of verbal roots to be produced by a single type of effort.
Because there is no sublation [of the injunction].

Nor is it the case that, since suffixes denote their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), it would be impossible for the verb situated in the fruit-statement (*phalavākya*) to enjoin a pure efficient force (*bhāvanā*) unqualified by the meaning of the verbal root; for even though the verb denotes an efficient force qualified by the meaning of the verbal root, the operation of the injunction does not apply to that specific aspect.

Therefore, in cases where there is a connection between a quality (*guṇa*) and a result (*phala*), even when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is merely restated (*anuvāda*), it is the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) alone that is enjoined.
For this very reason, in the sentence stating the result, the term "sacrifice" (*yajati*) serves as an indicator for all the meanings of the verbal roots under discussion.

Furthermore, the word *jyotiṣṭoma* is a name for all [the sacrifices] according to the maxim of the "man with the umbrella" (*chatrinyāya*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the author states]: "Of a property that exists only in what is to be accomplished..."

Since it is necessary for the distinctness of sacrifices (*vijātīya-yāgatva*) and the like to serve as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the status of being an effect (*kāryatā*) with respect to something,

and since effort (*yatna*) is already present [in the agent] toward that which is delimited by such distinctness, causality belongs to effort itself precisely by virtue of its own distinctness (*vaijātya*).
Consequently, due to the distinctness of each verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), the distinctness of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is established.
And the state of being a different word consists precisely in having distinct root-meanings (*dhātvartha*).

Therefore, in the case of the injunction “He offers three oblations,” once a difference between the oblations is established by the number, the resulting difference in the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) must be understood as arising from the aforementioned type of difference in words, and not from the [difference in roots] mentioned in the original text; this is how it should be considered.

Furthermore, since enjoining multiple items such as the *soma* sacrifice by way of restating an already established productive urge would result in the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), one must accept that in each respective sentence, there is an injunction of a productive urge qualified by both its specific accessory (*guṇa*) and its root-meaning.

In this regard, according to the logic of the *cāturthika* [the fourth book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras], only the Soma sacrifice denoted by the term *jyotiṣṭoma* has its connection with the fruit established by the sentence concerning heaven (*svarga-vākya*), while all others are merely its subsidiaries.

Nor should it be argued that the connection with the fruit occurs in the *svarga-vākya* itself through the prior origination of the sacrificial bhāvanā, and that the sentence concerning Soma (*soma-vākya*) merely enjoins the Soma substance alone;

for, according to the logic of the *rājasūya*, this would result in the connection with the fruit belonging only to the *iṣṭi*s, animal sacrifices, and [other] *yāga*s mentioned in that context, leaving no evidence for the injunction of any other sacrifice.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to enjoin the Soma sacrifice when animals and other substances have already been restricted, there must necessarily be an injunction for a distinct ritual act in the Soma passage.
The purpose [of this analysis] is that the Soma sacrifice alone possesses primacy. // 1 //
Thus ends the first section, concerning the difference of words (*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*).

(B2) [The connection of this section is that it provides the occasion for determining the distinctions in the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the subject matter of the chapter; the reason for examining the means of proof known as "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*) first; and the summary of the meaning of the section.]

[The author] shows that a different word occurring within the same section (*ekaprakaraṇagataśabdāntara*) serves as the example here, and demonstrates the "contextual connection" (*avasarasangati*)—the necessity of this point—for the task to be performed in this quarter (*pāda*), which is the determination of the difference in productive activity (*bhāvanābhedanirūpaṇa*) that constitutes the subject matter of the chapter. [This is indicated by the phrase: "of the difference in productive activity."

The introductory section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) and its locus (*adhikaraṇa*), ending with the section on praise and injunction (*stutaśāstra*), includes as a necessary consequence the determination that the verbal suffixes in mantras are not injunctive; further following from that, the refutation of the threefold or fourfold classification of mantras; and included under the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the determination of the extent of the *yajus* formulas and so forth. Once that is completed, having found the appropriate occasion, the primary subject matter of the chapter—the distinction between various types of efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—is now determined.

In this regard, since it is clear that a difference in verbal roots—being a distinct form not synonymous with other roots and cognizable through other means of knowledge—differentiates the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) by way of differentiating the root-meanings, the authority of "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*) serves to resolve the objection raised in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*. That objection was that even when there is a difference in root-meanings, there is no differentiation of the *bhāvanā* which is the cause of the *apūrva* (transcendental result), and thus the differentiation of the *apūrva* produced in accordance with the difference of root-meanings [cannot be established]. Therefore, the authority of "difference of words" is intended to provide a solution to this.
First, there is the determination [of difference].

Therefore, the sense is that the subject matter of this chapter (*pādārtha*) is the determination of difference based on means of proof such as "difference in words" (*śabdāntara*), which is distinct from "difference in context" (*prakaraṇāntara*).

This is because the difference in the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is established solely through the substitution [of one word for another] by means of "difference in words" occurring within a different context. Regarding "difference in words":

Since an operation [of the injunction] is impossible there, he expresses a doubt by first providing an example, indicating that operation among those things subsumed under a single performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*): "In the Jyotiṣṭoma..."—by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *stauti*, *śaṃsati*, and so forth is intended.
(Through the practice of the suffix *ti*, there is the removal of the doubt regarding a distinction in the cultivation [of the action],
and the justification for multiple verbal root meanings being produced by a single effort;
this is because there is no application of the principle of subordinate elements [*guṇanyāya*].)

Although a distinction might be suspected due to the repetition of the suffix *ti*, which denotes the act of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), nevertheless, because that suffix is accepted as being a restatement (*anuvādaka*) for the purpose of enjoining the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it lacks independence; thus, this [argument] also serves as an indication that [the suffix] is ineffective.
This is because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).

The meaning is that, just as there is no obstacle to accepting multiple objects for a single cognition that takes a collection as its objective support (*samūhālambana*), so too there is no obstacle to accepting that [the effect] is produced by a single effort through multiple delimiters (*avacchedaka*).

(The beginning of the Siddhānta: "The object of the *bhāvanā* enjoined by each respective sentence of result is precisely the meaning of the respective verbal root; thus, due to the difference between the meanings of the roots such as 'sacrifice' (*yaji*) and 'give' (*dā*), there is a difference in the *bhāvanā*.
First of all, it is beyond dispute that *bhāvanā* consists in volitional activity (*kṛti*) and possesses an object.
Furthermore, its being an object is not like the objecthood of knowledge and so forth, which resides in an already established entity.

Moreover, because it subsists solely in that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is synonymous with "being produced" (*janya*). Consequently, when the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) enjoined by the sentence concerning the fruit requires an object, the sacrifice (*yajati*) alone— introduced by the verbal root— is the object, and not giving (*dāna*) or other acts, because they are not introduced by the verbal root.
Furthermore, there is no evidence for [the view that the term ‘sacrifice’] is merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*).

In that case, since the subject matter is restricted to sacrifices as expressed by the word-hearings (*pada-śruti*), it is impossible for giving (*dāna*) and offering (*homa*) mentioned in other sentences to be connected as the subject matter; thus, the sacrifice alone constitutes the essence.

Consequently, because the delimiters of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), such as "sacrificeness" (*yāgatva*) and so forth, differ, it is necessary to postulate a distinct generic property (*vaijātya*) even in the effort (*kṛti*) which serves as the cause.

Since there is a difference between the performance of giving (*dāna*) and the like and the performance of sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like, it is necessary that in their respective sentences, distinct *bhāvanās* colored by the meanings of those respective verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) be denoted.

Even so, if a single common property (*dharmasāmānya*), which pervades the functions of all the verbal roots occurring in the context, were conveyed by some word as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the effect (*kāryatā*),
then— due to the unity of the delimiting factor of the effect— the unity of the *bhāvanā* serving as its cause would follow.
This is not the case here;
for by means of sentences concerning *soma* and so forth, the respective meanings of the verbal roots are presented precisely as sacrifices (*yāga*) and the like.

Consequently, when there is a difference between the meanings of the verbal roots conveyed by those respective verbal root-words—which denote the delimiters of the objecthood (*kāryatā*) of each [action]—there arises the postulation of multiple *apūrva*s based on that difference.
Intending to show that it is not faulty because it is based on authoritative means of knowledge, he states the established conclusion: "only the effect" (kāryamātra).
(Justification of sacrifice and the like as causes by way of being a heterogeneous effort):
Nor is it the case that causality belongs solely to the state of being a result delimited by its respective specific effect-ness,
and not to the state of being a heterogeneous effort.

It must be stated that the contingency of the sacrifice arising at the time of the origin of the *homa* is due to the absence of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of a heterogeneous unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). This dispels the objection that—rather than postulating a heterogeneity in the unseen merit—it is more reasonable to postulate a heterogeneity in the effort (*yatna*) already present; this is indicated by the phrase "of the present" (*upasthitasya*).
(An establishment of the truth that non-synonymous verbal roots have distinct meanings by refuting the claim that they are merely different words):
In this regard, the ancients have stated that a difference in *bhāvanā* arises from "different words" (*śabdāntara*) in the form of a difference between non-synonymous verbal roots;
demonstrating the untenability of such a status as "different words," he states the definition of "different words" as follows: "it is simply the state of having distinct root-meanings."

The meaning is that there is a distinction in the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) by means of another word whose verbal root meaning is different, through the communication of a difference in the delimitors of the status of being an effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*).
However, it will be stated that this is indeed conflated with the principle regarding subordinate elements (*guṇanyāya*). "But not... [end of quote].

The meaning is that because all three oblations are grasped by a single *juhoti* [suffix], there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of that [distinction], since there is no difference between the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the nominal stem (*pada*).
[This applies] to the various acts such as *homa* and *yāga*.

(Somādivākye guṇādapi bhedasiddherabhedapūrvapakṣānupayuktatvāddākṣiṇānītyasyaivaitadudāharaṇatvamiti nirūpaṇam): By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the injunction of multiple qualities—such as gold, Ātreya, and the gift—in the passage concerning gold is included.

By this, it is indicated that in such examples, since difference is established precisely on account of the qualities that cause syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) of non-difference is irrelevant.

As for the statement, “He offers the dakṣiṇā-oblations,” it should also be understood that this indeed serves as an example, because the word *dakṣiṇa* functions as a name (*nāmadheya*), and thus only the meaning of the verbal root *hu* (to sacrifice) is enjoined.

(The definition of the nature of the principle from the fourth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra]: that by virtue of being a restrictor of the sacrifice, the Jyotiṣṭoma does not refer to the Iṣṭi and other sacrifices).
This refers to "by the principle of the fourth book."
For in the fourth [book], just as in the case of the term *rājasūya*, since the term *jyotiṣṭoma* has an unestablished meaning, it cannot logically serve to restrict the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).

Thus, having proposed as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that all the *iṣṭi*s and animal sacrifices within the context are connected with the fruit, [the sūtra] establishes that it refers only to the Soma sacrifices, by virtue of their connection with the possession of *stomas* in the form of light (*jyotis*), as understood from the supplementary passage: "These indeed are those lights which are its *stomas*."

The meaning is: by that same principle, it has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that because the name [of the sacrifice] is well-known, it is capable of restricting the general sense of the root *yaji* (to sacrifice)— just like the terms *darśapūrṇamāsa*— and therefore, since that [name] alone is connected with the fruit, it possesses primacy while the others are subordinate (*aṅga*).
He dispels a related doubt with the words "And not... (na ca).
(Refutation of the view that the fruit-statement "one desiring heaven [should sacrifice] with the Jyotiṣṭoma" is intended as an originative injunction:
It follows that there must necessarily be an injunction for a distinct ritual act.
And thus, since the animal and other substances are already prescribed for sacrifices such as the Agniṣomīya, it is necessary that the Soma-sentence refers to a distinct ritual action;

and since the connection with the fruit is established by the fact that this very action bears the name Jyotiṣṭoma, one need not assume—under the burden of unnecessary complexity—that the fruit-sentence also intends to originate that ritual action. This is the meaning.
He connects the very purpose mentioned in the fourth [sūtra] with the word "purpose" (prayojana).
(An explanation of the necessity of establishing "another word" as a distinct means of proof, based on the dual application of the principle that "difference arises from a quality"):

In this context, since the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) in the fruit-statement is already occupied by the sacrifice as its instrument, it is indeed possible for a difference [of action] to arise from a quality due to the introduction of other verbal roots as instruments;
nevertheless, it should be understood that the presentation of that [quality-based distinction] serves solely to refute the opponent's position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

For a quality (guṇa), since it is impossible for there to be a restatement of a mental impression (bhāvanā) in a form not colored by preceding qualities, does not differentiate [the action] when it makes that [action] known in a form colored by the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha); this much alone is to be established here.
Furthermore, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that all verbal root-meanings (*dhātvartha*) qualify the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) enjoined by the *jyotiṣṭoma* injunction,

although it must be stated that there is a conjunction of instruments (*karaṇa-samuccaya*) because the sacrifice mentioned in the fruit-injunction (*phala-vākya*) is taken as a representative term (*upalakṣaṇa*) due to being expressed in a single word, nevertheless,
since a difference in instruments is necessarily pervaded by a difference in the agent's activity (*kartṛvyāpāra*), a distinction in the productive urge (*bhāvanā-bheda*) would inevitably follow.
That [distinction] does not arise from the logic of qualities (*guṇanyāya*);
for there is no determining factor as to which [action] would achieve self-sufficiency through the simultaneous connection with those various instruments (*karaṇa*).

Therefore, since in that case the distinction between the productive operations (*bhāvanā*)—which depends on the distinction between the respective instruments—is established by the authority of "different words" (*śabdāntara*), its investigation is not purposeless.
(An investigation into the fact that it is only when there is no mental substitution [of the original word] that another word functions as a differentiator):
And this other word is a differentiator only when there is no mental substitution, but not even when there is mental substitution.

Therefore, it should be understood that in the case of "he offers the fourfold portion" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*), even though there is a different word, there is no distinction because the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of the sacrifice—which constitutes a part of the act of offering—is already present; rather, the distinction lies only in the productive urge of the act of throwing [the oblation] into the fire.
Thus ends the first section, concerning "another word" (śabdāntara).
(B1) (Section 2) (A.2 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 2):
[Concerning] that which is situated within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

In such passages as “He sacrifices the fuel-sticks,” “He sacrifices Tanūnapāt,” “He sacrifices the Iḍā,” “He sacrifices the sacrificial grass,” and “He sacrifices with the utterance of Svāhā,” there is no difference in the productive activity (bhāvanā) because there is no difference in the sacrifice itself, as it is recognized as being the same;
nor does the repetition (abhyāsa) cause a difference.
Because repetition (*abhyāsa*), by virtue of establishing unity, is contradictory [to the claim of plurality].
Nor does repetition, in the form of the repeated hearing of an injunction, serve to differentiate the sacrifices that are the objects of the injunction;

for, as in the case of "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), the power of the injunction is transferred to a subordinate quality in the form of the deity, and thus it lacks the capacity to have the sacrifice itself as its objective domain.

Nor can it be argued that because the injunction of the quality (guṇavidhi) by the subsequent sentence is precluded by the presence of a quality in the original sentence enjoining the production of the sacrifice,
the word *samit* in the first sentence must be accepted as a name (*nāmadheya*) according to the *tatprakhyanyāya*, since there would otherwise be no other recourse.
In reality, however, if the substance *samit* were obtained from the wording of the *yājyā* mantra, [the objection would not hold].
In that case, it would be no different for Tanūnapāt and the others as well.
Therefore, by way of a restatement of the Upāṃśuyāja or a restatement of the action enjoined by the *vidvadvākya*, there is an injunction of the five deities.
Nor is there a lack of possibility for its application.

Since it is possible for the deities such as Vasanta to be obtained optionally even from the *anumantraṇa* mantras—just as they are from the wording of the *yājyā* mantras—it is logical that these [latter] function as restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*). Therefore, since there is no repetition of the text with a purpose other than this, there is no differentiation of the ritual action (*karmabheda*). This being the position reached: [we reply that] because the capacity to determine the deity belongs primarily to the *yājyā* mantras—which are established by the force of the mutual requirement (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*)—they take precedence over the *anumantraṇa* mantras, which are established only by the force of a one-sided requirement (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*).

Since the postulation of a deity is untenable, words such as *samit* do not function to restrict a deity. Consequently, because the meaning of the accompanying word (*upapada*) possesses a possibility of being already established, and because it is understood through direct verbal expression (*pada-śruti*) and other means that the injunction has the root-meaning and the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as its object, it is impossible to enjoin what has already been enjoined. Thus, by virtue of being the delimiting factor of the thing to be enjoined, the status of these words as names is established through the principle of "being known from that" (*tat-prakhyanyāya*), and the distinction [between the acts] is accomplished by the name itself.

Even if the status of these as qualifiers (*guṇavidhi*) is refuted by the principle of "being known from that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*), the determination that they are names (*nāmadheya*) does not yet follow; for since the function of a name is accomplished by even a single one in relation to a single action, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the redundancy of multiple names, and thus it would be more appropriate to regard terms such as *samit* and so forth as mere restatements of qualities (*guṇānuvādaka*).
However, once the difference between actions is established through repetition (*abhyāsa*), each individual action possesses a meaningful name, and thus their status as names is determined.
The "purpose" (prayojana) refers to the purpose of the subsequent section (adhikaraṇa).
Other purposes are clearly explained in the Kaustubha. // 2 //
Thus ends the second section concerning practice.

(B2) (The demonstration that the section on repetition (*abhyāsādhikaraṇa*) proceeds immediately after the section on different words [*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*] because of the desire for a parallel counter-example, despite the lack of similarity due to the commonality of being a differentiator of the productive urge [*bhāvanā*]:

Although it follows that the name [*saṃjñā*] should be considered immediately after [the section on] different words— because, being of the nature of a word, it shares a similarity with "different words"— nevertheless, since a name pertains only to the meaning of the verbal root and thus differentiates only that, whereas "different words" denote verbal roots whose distinctness is clearly established by other means of knowledge, [the two are not similar].

Because there is no difference in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and because [the name] differentiates the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) by means of that [root], it is distinguished from the name (*saṃjñā*). However, since repetition (*abhyāsa*) consists in the act of re-enjoining, and since an injunction has as its object the efficient force colored by the meaning of the verbal root—thereby differentiating both—the two are similar insofar as they differentiate the efficient force. Thus, when there is a difference in the verbal root, the efficient force is differentiated due to the difference in the meaning of the root; whereas when there is no difference in the meaning of the root...

The ancient commentators have shown the immediate connection of this [topic] by means of an introductory prima facie argument (*pratyudāharaṇapūrvapakṣa*), based on the ease of the position that "since there is no difference in the object, there is also no difference in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). However, in reality, even in the case of repetition (*abhyāsa*), since the operation is possible as a mere differentiation of the root-meaning— just like [the differentiation caused by] technical names (*saṃjñā*) and numbers— it follows that the productive activity is differentiated by another word consisting of the utterance of a different root which expresses a different meaning.

Since there is no purpose in postulating that [the action] is distinct even in those cases, there is neither a similarity in terms of being a differentiator of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), nor a distinction based on names and the like;
rather, when there is a difference in the verbal root (*dhātu*), a difference in the efficient force is logically established due to the difference in its meaning.

In the present case, however, since there is no difference in meaning because the verbal root (*dhātu*) is also one, and since there is no evidence for a difference in the *bhāvanā* that has become the result, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises.

Without explicitly stating the connection as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for the sake of establishing a difference in *bhāvanā*—which would be obvious—the author first shows the subject matter and then states the prima facie argument itself: "In the Darśapūrṇamāsa... and so forth.

(The prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] is that sentences such as "he sacrifices to Tanūnapāt" function to provide accessory details for the sacrifice enjoined by the sentence "he sacrifices to the Samidhs," just as in the case of "he offers with curd").

Because the prima facie view is established on the grounds that sentences such as "he sacrifices to Tanūnapāt" enjoin deities such as Tanūnapāt, the phrase "situated in the context" (*prakaraṇastha*) is stated in order to demonstrate the possibility of their inclusion within the sacrifice under discussion.
And it is not [the case that they are] injunctions (*vidhi*).

The operation of an injunction (*vidhi*), which consists in setting in motion what has not yet been set in motion, is understood through the direct hearing of the word (*padaśruti*) to have as its object the *bhāvanā* colored by the meaning of the verbal root.
Since that [action] would already have been enjoined if there were only one action, it would be rendered redundant; therefore, it would result in a sublation (*bādha*).
Consequently, the sense of the doubt is that this will necessarily lead to the establishment of a distinct action (*karmāntara*).

"According to the principle that 'the verbal suffix first enjoins the action according to its capacity, but when its capacity is projected by another [word], it then expects that which is restated,' where a word denoting a quality (guṇapada) is heard, since multiple injunctions are impossible, one accepts that the restatement applies to that which is already established, and the injunction transfers to the other [element]. This is the case in the passage "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*).

Having considered that the attainment of the root-meaning [is required], he provides the following rebuttal—that it is possible here as well, just like a prescription for a mere quality after the verbal root has been uttered: "by means of curd" (*dadhnā*).

(Regarding Pārthasārathi’s view that the four sentences serve as injunctions of deities because they pertain to a sacrifice already obtained through the sentence concerning the first fuel-stick (*prathamasamit*), and his own presentation of his position—that, due to the lack of conviction in that view, these are injunctions restricting the deity by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the *upāṃśuyāja* or a reference to the rite enjoined by the two "knowledgeable" (*vidvat*) sentences:
Now, one might object: just as in the case of "he sacrifices to Viṣṇu," if we accept that the words *tanūnapāt* and so forth ending in the accusative case denote deities...

Even if one accepts that the injunction refers back to the sacrifice (*yāga-anuvāda*), since the sacrifice is already established in that sentence, another deity is also enjoined therein; therefore, one raises the objection: "In that case, being excluded by that [other deity], how can these [deities] find a place?"—this is expressed by the words "And not... (*na ca*).

Since it is observed elsewhere that the prescription of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) occurs subsequent to the prescription of the ritual action (*karmavidhāna*), here too, when some prescription of an action must be accepted, there would arise a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) because priority alone cannot serve as a regulator. Therefore, following the reasoning of Pārthasārathi, it is appropriate to accept that the word *samit* found in the *samid* sentence itself is a name (*nāmadheya*), thereby establishing its status as an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*); thus, there is no obstruction by another deity (*devatāntarāvarodha*) therein.
He avoids it, [thinking] "it has not come."
Refuting this, he states another position with the words "But in reality":
therefore, [it is] the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Regarding the prescription of deities such as Tanūnapāt for the Upāṃśuyāja, [the author], being dissatisfied because the pairs of *yājyā* verses dedicated to deities like Viṣṇu—though recited in sequence there—would have to be displaced from their position by the force of the *liṅga* (indicative power) assisted by the *samākhyā* (name), states another alternative view: "In the case of the *vidvadvākya*..."

The meaning is: "in all five sentences. Since the *yājyā* mantras beginning with "May the *samidhs* enjoy the clarified butter at the front; may *Tanūnapāt* enjoy the clarified butter, O Agni," etc., are not recited in the context of the *upāṃśuyāja* and other rites, there is no evidence for their being subordinate (*aṅga*) elements therein. Consequently, it is impossible for them to contain injunctions regarding deities that would have to be inferred; rather, they function solely as illuminators (*prakāśaka*) of the deities—such as *Samit* and others—who are already established by direct injunctions.

Since it is determined to be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to those respective sacrifices, it does not have the status of something already established; thus, even though the latter [explanation] exists, he provides another solution by way of its applicability, stating:
"like the wording of the *yājyā* mantra."

He concludes that there is no difference in the ritual action because there is no repetition of hearing an injunction for something else, as in the case of "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and so forth; thus he says: "And therefore... (*ataśca*).

(The established conclusion is that because the meaning of the *upapada* already possesses the possibility of occurrence, it is impossible to enjoin what has already been enjoined; therefore, difference [of acts] is established through repetition. Regarding the phrase "because it possesses the possibility of occurrence": [The opponent asks: Why is it said that there is no injunction of what is already enjoined? [The author replies: Because the meaning of the *upapada* already possesses the possibility of occurrence (*saṃbhavatprāptikatva*). That is to say, since the act of giving (*dāna*) is already established by the general rule of giving, it is not possible to enjoin that same act again. Therefore, the word "gives" (*dadāti*) must be understood as signifying a different act from the previously established one. Thus, the difference between the acts is established through repetition (*abhyāsa*). This is the established conclusion.

The meaning is as follows: since it is possible for [the term] to be a name (*nāmadheya*) by virtue of its having a corresponding attainment (*saṃbhavat-prāptikatva*), it is not appropriate to rely on the force of a weaker recognition (*durbala-pratyabhijñā*) to hold that the object of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is colored by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) understood through direct word-hearing (*pada-śruti*). Rather, when possible, one should resort to the first type of injunction (*vidhi-prakāra*). Consequently, even the complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the postulation of multiple distinct transcendental potencies (*apūrva-bheda*) is not a fault, because it is based on valid authority (*prāmāṇikatva*). [This applies] to cases where repetition (*abhyāsa*) establishes itself depending on a name; although the name acts as a differentiator (*bhedaka*) there, in the present case, [repetition is not the differentiator] because multiple names would otherwise be rendered useless.
(The determination that repetition does not depend on its establishment through a name, because sentences such as "tanūnapāt" would otherwise result in being mere restatements [anuvādaka], etc.)—
this is by means of the *tatprakhyanyāya*.

In cases such as "atha eṣa jyotiḥ" and so forth, where there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a verb, and consequently no specific sacrifice is understood, the assumption of a verb in the injunctive sense occurs only through the connection of the word *atha* with the meaning of entitlement (*adhikāra*), resulting in the determination that it is the name of an unspecified action.
Since the establishment of a repetition depends upon a name, the distinction [between sacrifices] is made by the name itself.

In cases such as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," where there is no [previously established] name, it is possible for the connection of the very sacrifice under discussion with the fruit to be established by the sentence; however, since that [connection] can then be enjoined again by the injunction, repetition cannot function as a differentiator because it lacks independence from other factors. In such instances, the name itself is the differentiator. But where the nature of the repetition does not depend on a name for its establishment, [repetition alone serves as the differentiator].

Just as in the present case, since the name is established by the principle of "being recognized as such" (*tatprakhya-nyāya*), it does not depend on the injunction of a sacrifice understood through repetition;

rather, were it not for its status as a name, there would be the contingency of it being subordinate to a quality or having another purpose, whereby the repetition itself would depend upon that [injunction]. Thus, it is precisely by means of the name that the distinction [of the rites] can be established.
Nevertheless, since it is possible for a single rite to be delimited by a single name, the names such as *tanūnapāt* and so forth would otherwise be rendered redundant.

The sense is as follows: since it would follow that [the terms] are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of those respective deities, it would be impossible for the name (*saṃjñā*) to effect a distinction by way of determining the deity; rather, because the name is determined to be such through its utility in establishing a distinction between rituals via repetition (*abhyāsa*), it is the repetition itself that effects the distinction.

Furthermore, just as there is a distinction between individual instances, when there is a distinction in what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), a distinction in the delimitors of the property to be enjoined (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*) is necessary; thus, there must also be distinct universals (*jāti*) subsumed under "being the *samidh* sacrifice" and so forth.

Having indicated through the verbal root *yaj* (to sacrifice) present in each respective sentence those classes—such as *samidyāgatva* (the nature of the *samidh*-sacrifice) and *tanūnapādyāgatva* (the nature of the *tanūnapāt*-sacrifice)—which are pervaded by the universal *yāgatva* (the nature of sacrifice), the individual instances of sacrifice delimited by those classes are enjoined by those respective sentences; this and more should be seen in the Kaustubha.
(The determination that the purpose of this section is indeed the purpose of the subsequent section):
"Regarding the subsequent section."

In the view that the *upāṃśuyāja* involves a prescription of deities, since passages such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to silently" (*viṣṇurupāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ*) would be mere restatements (*anuvāda*), they could not function as explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Consequently, the status of each of those as an injunction (*vidhi*), which was asserted by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) in the upcoming section stating "the *upāṃśuyāja* should be like the *paurṇamāsī*," is established.
However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), that is not the case.

Thus, in the case where an action is enjoined by the words of a learned person (*vidvadvākya*) under the view that it is an injunction regarding a deity (*devatāvidhipakṣa*), since the character of an injunction is established there through the attainment of a form (*rūpalābha*), a restatement of a collective whole (*samudāyānuvāda*) is impossible; consequently, the purpose stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) in that section is achieved.
However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the purpose of the final conclusion in that same section is achieved—this is the meaning of the purpose of the subsequent section.
(An examination of other purposes mentioned by Kaustubha:
"Other purposes," it is said.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, since the deities mentioned as being connected with the act of drawing [the soma] (grahaṇa) are connected to the sacrifice through that very act of drawing by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa), and since the context grasps all subsidiary elements simultaneously— thereby indicating their combination (samuccaya)— and because each deity is individually connected to the act of drawing,

it is impossible for them to be connected to the sacrifice as a combined whole; thus, even though combination is understood through the repetition of the sacrifice, there is no evidence for such repetition.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the deities are the purpose, since they serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), there is performance only once due to the optionality of the alternatives.

However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because the five *prayāja* offerings have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), they must be performed [separately]; this further purpose is to be seen in the *Kaustubha*. This is the meaning.

As for the other [objections], although they have been stated here according to the various types of prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*), I do not set them forth because they were not mentioned in this context and are therefore not relevant.
Thus ends the second section concerning practice.
(B1) (Section 3 / A.2 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 3) But the context belongs to the Full Moon [sacrifice], because there is no mention of its specific form.

In that very context, in such passages as, "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the Full Moon day, attains as much as is attained by the Ukthya; he who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the New Moon day, attains as much as is attained by the Atirātra," etc., [the context applies].
Even so, there is a distinction of actions due to repetition;
nor is this the *laṭ* (present tense),
for even if it were the *leṭ* (subjunctive), because the injunction is obstructed by the word *yat*, there is an absence of a repeated hearing of the injunction.

Because, as in the case of the injunction "He offers the *samidhs*," the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is understood [as expressing an injunction], and because the word *yat*—as in "he who is initiated" (*yo dīkṣitaḥ*)—prevents the injunction from being restricted to the act of knowing alone;
for this very reason, the terms *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* are also names [of sacrifices];

for by the two sentences "one should sacrifice with the *paurṇamāsī*" and "one should sacrifice with the *paurṇamāsī* on the full moon day," the time is prescribed specifically for the two rites enjoined by that [original] sentence.

Nor is there an absence of form (*rūpa*), because by the statement, "The *vārtraghnī* verses are recited at the full moon sacrifice, and the *vṛdhanvatī* verses at the new moon sacrifice," these verses— though obtained through their position in the sequence of the *ājyabhāga* offerings— are enjoined as constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the rites prescribed by this specific sentence, thereby overriding that sequence; thus, there exists a deity consisting of Agni and Soma based on the wording of the mantras (*māntravarṇika*).

Furthermore, because the substance is already obtained through the statement, "Indeed, that which is the clarified butter in the *dhruvā* vessel is taken for the sake of this entire sacrifice," or alternatively—

because the form [of the rites] is established by the injunctions of the substances and deities through the sentences concerning the *āgneya* and other offerings, which refer back (*anuvāda*) to the rites enjoined by the present sentence as presented by the terms "Full Moon" (*paurṇamāsī*) and "New Moon" (*amāvāsyā*). Nor does the injunction of multiple elements result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Since it is grammatically established (*vyutpanna*) that there is a mutual connection between a substance qualified by a deity expressed by a *taddhita* suffix and [the verb], the prescription of a qualified [action] is justified.
As for the acquisition of the form [of the injunction] through another method, that should be seen in the *Kaustubha*.
In any case, in the "Vidvad-vākya," there is the injunction of a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

And thus, by the fruit-bearing sentence, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," in the first view, there is a connection with the fruit for all the Āgneya and other offerings as well as for the two rites enjoined by this sentence, through their commonality with the Prayāja and other subsidiaries; but in the second view, it applies to those two alone through that commonality.
Although the nominal stem *darśapūrṇamāsa* is well-known in its application to times [of performance], the dual suffix is not so known;
and although that [dual] is well-known in the case of the *ājyabhāga* offerings and others, the nominal stem is not.

Therefore, according to the principle of the *rājasūya*, it is untenable for the name to act as a restrictor; thus, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), all sacrifices indeed have a connection with the fruit.

Although the dual number is not well-established by the *pāśādhikaraṇa* principle, since the nominal stem itself is established, the duality can somehow be justified as referring either to those connected with time or to these two [mantras] themselves; however, it does not refer to the six [deities] beginning with Āgneya. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: since the *vārtraghnī* and *vṛdhanvatī* mantras—having been established as subsidiaries to the *ājyabhāga* offerings by virtue of their indicative mark (*liṅga*) and sequence (*krama*)—require a rule for their specific application, the sentence regarding the *vārtraghnī* mantras is appropriately explained as providing that required regulation. Therefore, it cannot be taken as signifying that they are subsidiaries to the rites enjoined by the *vidvadvākya*, which would entail an unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
And for this very reason, it will be stated later that this [passage] is intended solely to establish the restriction by way of time or by way of ritual action;
therefore, neither does the attainment of a deity result from this, nor from the sentence concerning the Āgneya sacrifice and others.
Because there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if multiple qualities were enjoined by restating an already established action;

for it is everywhere established that the fruit of an injunction— the making known of what was previously unknown— has only a single object, and if it were to have multiple objects, there would be the consequence of contradiction.

Nor can it be argued that there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-vidhāna*), because such a qualified entity is not already established through linguistic usage (*avyutpannatvāt*).

For this has been stated: where a derivative formation (*taddhita*) or the like occurs through the relation of being a *kāraka* (case-role), there is no mutual coreferential connection (*parasparānvaya*); rather, it is only where [a compound] such as *aśvābhidhānīm* occurs through a relation other than that [of *kāraka*] that such a connection is possible.
The function resides in that very [deity] alone.

Consequently, since the deity-hood in the present case constitutes the factor of the recipient (*saṃpradāna-kāraka*), a mutual relationship [between the two deities] is untenable; therefore, it is necessary to enjoin a distinct ritual action qualified by both [deities].
And thus, the absence of a [defining] form remains exactly as it was.
Or, even if the status of being a *rūpa* (verbal form) were somehow established,
nevertheless, there is no injunction regarding ritual action (*karmavidhi*) in the statement of the learned [sages];
for, due to the obstruction of the injunctive power by the word *yat*, there is simply no further hearing of an injunction.

Nor does it serve merely to prohibit the act of experiencing that [pleasure], because it is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that a word such as *yat* functions as a correlative restrictor for a word such as *tat*.
Furthermore, even on account of its being subservient to another purpose, there is no establishment of the actual nature of repetition (*abhyāsa*).

For instance: in that context, by means of the root *yaj* ending in *laṭ* found in the statement of the learned (the Veda), only the three [sacrifices] beginning with the Āgneya—which are the subject at hand—are restated (anūdyante) as being connected to their respective times by virtue of their respective names.
And the purpose of that is the establishment of two groups, because multiple [sacrifices] are taken up by the single root *yaj* through *tantra*.
The purpose of that, in turn, is the establishment of the connection of all six [sacrifices] with the fruit in the sentence stating the result.
Because the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is well-known to denote the six [cases] through connection with time,
and because the dual number denotes the meaning of plurality by means of the relation of "subsisting in a member of the aggregate that constitutes the aggregate which is its own denoted substratum";

and it is precisely the two sentences concerning the learned (*vidvat*) that serve to capture the intended meaning of this indication (*lakṣaṇā*), by way of establishing the aggregate that constitutes the relation between the denoted and the indicated.

Otherwise, in the absence of the *vidvadvākya* (the two sentences concerning the "knowers"), there would result a connection with the fruit for only two *Āgneya* offerings—those which, by virtue of being included in a single sentence, possess duality and are associated with two points in time.
How two *Āgneya* offerings are established from the passage "that which is dedicated to Agni, on eight potsherds" has been explained in detail in the *Kaustubha*.

Therefore, the purpose of the *vidvadvākya* is precisely to establish the connection of all six offerings with the fruit in the manner described; and since its intent lies elsewhere, the nature of repetition cannot be established here as it is in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva."

Nor does this lead to the redundancy of the two sentences, "At the full moon [one performs] the Paurṇamāsī," for their meaningfulness as injunctions for the performance of the triad of sacrifices taken together will be explained in the eleventh [book].

Otherwise, because each [sacrifice] would be connected to its own time in the originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*), there would result a separate performance of each primary sacrifice accompanied by its own preceding and following subsidiaries.
And thus, even the mention of time in the originative injunction is solely for the purpose of restricting the word *yajati* found in the qualification-injunction and the knowledge-injunction;

therefore, these two are merely restatements (*anuvādaka*) of the constituent parts for the sake of establishing the whole, and not an injunction of a separate ritual action—this is established. // 3 //
Thus ends the third section concerning the full moon sacrifice.

(B2) (The determination of the connection as an exception based on the preceding section) By means of demonstrating the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) which has as its cause the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the preceding section, [the author] indicates the connection as an exception (*apavāda-saṅgati*). Having first presented an illustrative example, he states the prima facie argument itself:
"tatratya eva" (it is indeed that very one).
From repetition there is a distinction of action,
the attainment of form,
and the injunctive nature of the passage "he who knows thus."

The determination that [the word] *samit* is a fuel-stick (*iḍ*), like the statement regarding the fuel-sticks, is established through its utility for the accomplishment of the nature of repetition (*abhyāsa*) consisting in the repeated hearing of an injunction; it is for this reason that the word "therein" (*tatra*) was used.
Consequently, its status as a repeated hearing is indicated in comparison with the injunction of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) found in the sentences concerning the Āgneya and other offerings.

By means of the word *eva*, the ease with which the form [of the injunction] will be established is indicated; this is done by suggesting that the refutation of the opponent's position—which holds that the absence of a visible form (*rūpābhāva*) is the reason for the non-establishment of the form—is common to cases such as the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Although the phrase "as long as" (*sa yāvat*) is not useful for the present investigation, it is introduced here to reinforce its status as an injunction by indicating that such an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would otherwise be untenable in the absence of an injunction.
This is illustrated by the example: "He offers the *samidh* oblation" (*samidho yajati*).
Just as in that case there is a determination of the *leṭ* [subjunctive] mood because its meaning has not yet been attained, so it is here as well.
Thus, the meaning is that even the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) beginning with "as far as" (*sa yāvad*) becomes purposeful by way of praising what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*).
Therefore, it is said: "for this very reason."

(The demonstration that "one who knows thus" (*ya evaṃ vidvān*) is an injunction for a sacrifice, based on the fact that otherwise the sentence "on the full moon day, [one should sacrifice] on the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsyāṃ paurṇamāsyā*) would be rendered purposeless and so forth:

The meaning is that it is precisely because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *yajati*—which presents the object to be enjoined—that there is no obstruction to the injunction of the sacrificial productive operation (*yāga-bhāvanā*).
This is because [otherwise] the time [of performance] would have to be enjoined [separately].

And it should not be argued that there is a fallacy of mutual dependence— namely, that if it is a prescription of time, it cannot be a name, and if it is a name, it cannot be a prescription of time by way of restating that [name]—

because, according to the logic of the *agnihotra*, once its status as a name is determined through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) at first, it is subsequently possible to determine the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) by connecting it with the time prescribed by restating that very name.

In the Siddhānta, however, since the Āgneya and other sacrifices have their times prescribed by their original injunctions (*utpattivihita*), and the Prayājas and others have their times determined solely by the time of the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*), the attainment of those respective times would follow automatically; consequently, these two sentences would become redundant.

Furthermore, because those sacrifices are many, the use of the singular forms "the Full Moon" (*paurṇamāsīm*) and "the New Moon" (*amāvāsyām*) would be untenable, resulting in the undesirable consequence that one must resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sense of plurality.

Therefore, since the prescription of these two [times] alone constitutes the prescription of two distinct rites designated as the Full Moon and the New Moon sacrifices, it is logical that they are separate rites;

for the accusative case in "he offers the Agnihotra" (agnihotraṃ juhoti) functions as an indicator of the instrumentality [of the substance], while here it merely restates the status of being an end to be accomplished as implied by the context. This is the meaning.
(An investigation into the two mantras, the *vārtraghnī* and the *vṛdhanvatī*):
"The *vārtraghnī*," [it is said]. // //
For in the sequence of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, four sections (*anuvākas*) are recited:
one dedicated to Agni, one to Soma, one to Agni, and one to Soma.

Among these, the pair of mantras beginning with “Agni shall strike down the Vṛtras” and “O Soma, you are the lord of the virtuous, you are the king and the slayer of Vṛtra” is called *vārtraghnī* because they contain words that manifest the slaying of Vṛtra.
“Agni, adorning his own body with an ancient hymn, the seer has been magnified by the inspired singer.”

The two mantras, “*somagīrbhistvā vayam vardhayāmo vaco vidaḥ*” and so forth, are called *vṛdhanvatī* because they contain words that manifest growth (*vṛddhi*). While it might be assumed that these [mantras] belong to the *ājyabhāga* offerings according to their sequence, this is set aside by the injunction of the sentence “*vārtraghnī-pūrṇamāsyām, vṛdhanvatī amāvāsyāyām*,” which assigns them as belonging to these rites known by the names *Paurṇamāsī* and *Amāvāsyā*. Thus, because they belong to these rites through the sublation of sequence, [the deities are determined] from the indicative power of the mantras (*māntravarṇika*) as Agni and Soma—

It should not be argued that "the acquisition of each deity in its respective place is easily obtained; and since there is no contradiction when a non-contradictory application is possible, it is illogical to assume a contradiction—because it will be stated in the third [book] that the mantras, which have already attained their sequence in the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, merely serve to establish a restriction where none was previously established, and thus they do not function here as indicators of the deities. [This is because... (The rest of the sentence is missing from the source text).

Since there is no injunction regarding the full-moon and new-moon times for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, and because they are performed on the first day (*pratipad*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), they would not apply to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) performed on other lunar days; thus, a restriction based on time is untenable. Furthermore, because the two terms "full moon" (*paurṇamāsī*) and "new moon" (*amāvāsyā*) occurring in this sentence immediately bring to mind the two rites enjoined by the *vidvadvākya* as names, it is logical that [the *ājyabhāgas*] are indeed subordinate to those very rites.
Otherwise, there would be the fault of *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) regarding the two *ājyabhāga* offerings which are subsidiary to the full-moon and new-moon sacrifices.

Therefore, rather than resorting to *lakṣaṇā* for the nominal stem occurring in the opening statement, one should accept *lakṣaṇā* for the locative case itself—just as in the case of the injunction "one should offer the *jaya* oblations"—and thus enjoin the mantra with reference to that [locus] alone; consequently, [the mantra] reveals Agni and Soma as the deities.

Since the two *vārtraghnī* verses constitute an auxiliary part of the Full Moon sacrifice, and likewise the two *vṛdhanvatī* verses constitute an auxiliary part of the New Moon sacrifice, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the two pairs of mantras for each respective rite because they serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Consequently, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the two deities as well; thus, each single rite prescribed by the "Informed" injunctions (*vidvadvākya*) must be repeated, just like the Agnihotra.
Based on the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) that "the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* have the deity as their defining characteristic," one should simply assume a pair of combined *yājyās*.

Alternatively, following the method stated in the *Vārttika*—namely, that between those two very same mantras, one serves as the *anuvākyā* and the other as the *yājyā*—one may accept, by way of the principle of the *manotā*, that both are indicative of the deity; thus, the *yājyā* is easily obtained.
Furthermore, in this view, there is no sublation of the designation (*samākhyā*) of "anuvākyā."
Since the word *anu* is justified by the mere fact of following the *praiṣa* (direction), there is no contradiction.

As for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, because the deities Agni and Soma are prescribed by the very injunction, "One sacrifices the two *ājyabhāgas* to Agni and Soma," one merely postulates an *anuvākyā* (invitatory verse) corresponding to them.
Since the *yājyā* (offering verse) is already established by the order of sequence, there is no defect whatsoever.
And thus, the sense is that for these two, the attainment of a deity is not difficult to obtain.

(Refutation of the view that the sentence "sarvasmai vai" merely prescribes the status of *ājya* as *dhruva*; its fulfillment through the exclusion of the *ājya* used for decoration; and the resulting acquisition of the substance.)
"To everyone indeed."

By this statement, since the *dhruvājya* substance is prescribed with reference to all sacrifices by means of the dative case in the sense of purpose (*yajñāya*), the substance is obtained here just as it is in the *upāṃśuyāja*. Nor should it be argued that—wherever *ājya* is already obtained by this [text]—there is only the prescription of its being *dhruva*, and thus a prescription of the substance is impossible for those sacrifices where *ājya* has not been obtained previously; for, if one were to refer back (*anuvāda*) to *ājya* as a constituent part of the sacrifice, there would be the fault of referring to a qualified object (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*); whereas if one were to refer back to *ājya* in general, that same fault would apply even to the *ājya* used for decoration. Therefore, it is necessary that the *dhruvājya* itself be prescribed with reference to the sacrifice.

And it should not be argued that—since one thus takes [the butter] from the four-fold *dhruvā* vessel—the injunction would be redundant because the status of being an auxiliary to the sacrifice is established through mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) alone: namely, the expectation of a purpose on the part of the *ājya* (clarified butter) which arises without being specifically connected [to a rite], and the expectation for a substance on the part of sacrifices for which no substance has been specified.
This is because the injunction serves a purpose by excluding *ājya* intended for purposes such as decoration.
For this very reason, in the case of consecration and other rites, only the clarified butter (ājya) from the cooking pot is taken;
therefore, by that scriptural statement, the clarified butter itself is established as the substance—this is the meaning.
"But the accessory [is enjoined] because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement" (Jaimini 2.2.5).

According to the method stated in this *guṇasūtra*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that—since there is no syntactical split (*avākyabheda*) due to the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) by means of the *Āgneya* passage—the accessory is thereby established.

Thus, having established the attainment of the form [of the rite] independently of the *sūtra*, the present *sūtra*, "But the accessory [is enjoined] because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement," is intended for the proponent's renewed rebuttal.
In order to support that point, he establishes the attainment of form [as follows]: "Or rather... (athavā).

Furthermore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the *āgneya* injunction caused by two distinct objects of reference (*uddeśya*); for, in order to avoid the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) that would otherwise require the postulation of an unmentioned sacrifice, one may—just as in the case of the phrase "half within the altar" (*ardham antarvedi*)—employ figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) on two words [namely, *āgneya* and *paurṇamāsyām*] to take the contextually relevant primary sacrifice as the object of reference. Thus, the objection does not arise. (This explains an alternative method: that the deities are assigned by the *samit* and other injunctions, made possible by the interpretation of the phrase *juhvām aupabhṛtam*).
In another way.

Alternatively, in the five sentences concerning the *samit* and other offerings, there is an injunction regarding the deities by way of restating the rites already prescribed in the words of the learned;
and their combination is established by the force of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the text: "Having passed over the *iḍā*, the *barhis* is brought back.

For here, unlike the case of the *upāṃśuyāja* where the injunction of a deity would be contradicted by the impossibility of restating [the deity] in such passages as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice," there is no such contradicting factor present.

Nor should it be argued that, if the words *barhis* and so forth in this context refer to the deities of the rites enjoined by the *vidvadvākya*, there would be an inconsistency regarding the *dhruva* vessel being the substance for the *aupabhṛtha* [offering] in the passage "the *aupabhṛtha* [is taken] with the *juhū*";

for even under this view, such [an inconsistency] does not arise due to the force of the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) in passages such as, "Five *prayāja*s are offered; what one takes in the *juhū* is for the *prayāja*s."

Since there are five *prayāja* offerings, at the time of the repetition of the ritual action dedicated to *barhis* as ordained by the "vidvat" injunctions, the act of pouring [the butter] from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū* at the beginning of the *prayājas* is logically established; thus, there is no room for the objection that such a procedure would otherwise be untenable.

[Objection: Even if the performance were to take place over five days by subverting the time of the *Paurṇamāsī* sacrifice according to the principle of "sublation of the primary by the subordinate" (*aṅgaguṇanyāya*)—since that would involve a fault due to the subversion of the time belonging to those [rites] occurring at other times—the form [of the sacrifice] would still be obtained through the extended application (*atideśa*) of the *Saumika* (Soma-related) characteristics; thus, one might follow this alternative method. Or rather: because it is unmanifest (*avyakta*), the form is obtained through the extended application of the *Saumika* characteristics. And even if that [Saumika] application were to occur, there would be no contingency of subverting the time prescribed by the two sentences, "One should sacrifice with the *Paurṇamāsī* on the full moon day," since that would result in the [sacrifice] being a five-day rite. [Response: No, because the *Paurṇamāsī* sacrifice is not unmanifest. Since it is manifest, the *Saumika* characteristics cannot be extended to it. Furthermore, the *Paurṇamāsī* sacrifice is indeed manifest, for its form is established by the sentence "One should sacrifice with the *Paurṇamāsī* on the full moon day. Moreover, the *Paurṇamāsī* sacrifice is not unmanifest simply because it is performed over five days; for the *Paurṇamāsī* sacrifice is established as having a single-day duration by the sentence "One should sacrifice with the *Paurṇamāsī* on the full moon day. Therefore, the *Saumika* characteristics are not extended to it. Consequently, the form is not obtained through extension, and thus the *Iṣṭi* sacrifice must be performed with its own specific materials. Therefore, the view that the *Iṣṭi* sacrifice is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* is untenable. Hence, the *Iṣṭi* sacrifice is an independent (*svatantra*) rite. This is the conclusion. [Note: The term *avyakta* here refers to a sacrifice whose specific ritual form is not clearly defined by its own constituent parts, such as the *Soma* sacrifice, which serves as the archetype for the *Saumika* rites.]

In accordance with that, even if there is a sublation of those [rites] occurring at times other than the Soma-pressing, there is no reason for sublation regarding the non-extension of those occurring at the time of the Soma-pressing itself.

In reality, however, even though the Soma sacrifice with its constituent parts (sāṅga-somayāga) is prescribed for a single full moon or new moon day, it is impossible to perform it because it cannot be accomplished within that timeframe.
Just as in the case of the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other constituent rites, where the timing of the Soma sacrifice takes precedence over them, here too—

since it is improper to abandon the primary rite (pradhāna) merely to conform to a subordinate factor such as time— there is no obstacle to performing the sacrifice over five days, even if this involves overriding the scripturally prescribed (vācanika) time of the full moon and so forth.

The meaning is that even for the subsidiaries belonging to times other than the *sutyā*, there is no omission at all; thus, the acquisition of form is indeed possible through the extension (*atideśa*) of the characteristics of the Soma sacrifice, and this alternative method of acquiring form should be examined in the *Kaustubha*.
He concludes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*).
(An examination of the purpose of the prima facie position regarding both the first and second positions:
He states the purpose of the prima facie position with the words "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*),
referring to the first position.

In the first view—that the deities are to be inferred from the wording of the *vārtraghnī* and *vṛdhanvatī* mantras and that the sacrificial substance is the clarified butter (*ājya*) in the *dhruva* vessel—the sentences concerning the *āgneya* and other offerings also enjoin sacrifices; therefore, the connection with the fruit applies to these two [mantras] by virtue of their commonality with those sacrifices.

In the second view—that the sentences concerning the *āgneya* and others enjoin the substances and deities—since those sacrifices do not exist [as independent acts], the connection with the fruit for these two [mantras] occurs by virtue of their commonality with the auxiliaries such as the *prayājas*. He explains this very point: "The Darśapūrṇamāsa... and so forth.
For a name whose meaning is well-established acts as a restrictor of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), such as the name "Jyotiṣṭoma.

However, this [name] has an unestablished meaning; therefore, it functions in accordance with the verb (*ākhyāta*) where that occurs. Since the verb refers to all sacrifices, he says that there is a connection with the fruit for all of them—therefore...
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is "by the logic of the Rājasūya sacrifice" and "by the logic of the fourth section (adhikaraṇa) of the fourth quarter.

Alternatively, he states another position—that it applies to the eight [offerings] alone and not to the prayājas and others alike—on the grounds that since the primary nominal sense is established for the eight [offerings] connected with the time, the dual number can be justified through the indication (lakṣaṇā) of plurality according to the logic of the *pāśādhikaraṇa*. This is expressed by the word "pāśa."

Alternatively, since there is no purpose for resorting to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) even in the case of the dual number, he states another position—that the connection with the fruit is possible for these two alone—by saying: "of these two alone."

(Justification for the restatement of the rites enjoined by the *vidvadvākya* through the terms *darśa-pūrṇamāsa*, by establishing the synonymy between the terms *paurṇamāsī-amāvāsyā* and *darśa-pūrṇamāsa*):

Although the dual number in the sentence concerning the result (*phalavākya*) must refer to the duality residing in the meanings of the terms *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*, and cannot possibly refer to the duality residing in the rites designated as *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā*; nevertheless, [the scripture states]:
"Of these two, the *darśa* is the first and the *pūrṇamāsa* is the latter. Now, if one were to begin with the *pūrṇamāsa* first, it would be performed out of its proper sequence."

Therefore, for one beginning with the Full Moon sacrifice first, the injunction states: "One should offer a *caru* to Sarasvatī and a cake on twelve potsherds to Sarasvant; for Sarasvatī is indeed the New Moon (*darśa-amāvāsyā*) and Sarasvant is the Full Moon (*pūrṇamāsa*). From this remainder of the *anvārambhaṇīyā* passage, it is understood that the terms *darśa* and *amāvāsyā* are synonyms. Consequently, by using the word *pūrṇamāsa*—which is a part of the name [of the Full Moon sacrifice]—there is a reference to the whole name by means of a part of the name.

Since their synonymy is established by logical reasoning, they possess a single meaning; thus, the application of the dual number—expressing duality—referring to those [meanings] is justified, as indicated in some way by the word "kathañcit" (in some manner).

(The introduction to the final conclusion: since the four mantras obtained without restriction from the two sentences containing *vārtaghna* and *vṛdhanvat* cannot provide the required form for the rite enjoined by the *vidvadvākya*, those sentences do not possess injunctive force.
Explaining the reason for the final conclusion found in the Sūtra—"on account of the non-mention of the form"—he states the conclusion itself: "By the indicative mark... because it is required."

Since there is no contradiction when [the meaning] is established without sublation, sublation is improper; furthermore, because the two Brāhmaṇa statements contain the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā*, which refer to time, if they were taken as referring to the ritual acts (*karman*), it would result in the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Moreover, the locative case-ending itself would then have to indicate the primary status [of the acts]. If one accepts that this is an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), then one must assume the injunction of unmentioned deities, the assumption of unmentioned alternative *yājyā* verses, and the assumption of unmentioned *anuvākyā* verses for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.

Furthermore, because it would entail prolixity (*gaurava*), and because it is simpler to enjoin a mere restriction (*niyamamātra*) regarding the four mantras—which are already established as subsidiary to the *ājyabhāga* offerings—rather than enjoining their status as subsidiaries to the *ājyabhāga*, it is improper to resort to an injunction for what is not required. Therefore, those four mantras are indeed subsidiary to the *ājyabhāga*. Consequently, even when the materials for the two rites enjoined by the *vidvadvākya* are obtained, they lack a form (*arūpa*) due to the absence of a deity.
The meaning is that there is the possibility of its being an injunction.

[This section contains] an investigation establishing that, since the failure to perform the *vārtraghnī* mantras on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and at the *vikṛti* sacrifices would follow if one were to accept that the term *paurṇamāsī* indirectly indicates the *ājyabhāga* offerings when respect is paid to a division based on time, it is more appropriate to maintain a division based on the ritual action itself;
[it also includes] the refutation of the aforementioned prima facie view and the demonstration of the utility of the division based on time as well.
Since there is simplicity (*lāghava*) in the rule of restriction (*niyamavidhi*), for that very reason the determination is made in both ways;

thus he restates the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the third section (*adhikaraṇa*) regarding "mutual connection with no purpose" (*mithaścānarthasaṃbandha*) by saying "for that very reason" (*ata eva*).

Although, by the direct denotation (*śakti*) of the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā*, which signify time as their meaning, and by the denotation of either occasion (*nimitta*) or locus (*adhikaraṇa*) through the locative case,

it is possible for a temporal restriction (*kālakṛtavyavasthā*) to exist— since the *vārtraghni* and *vṛdhanvatī* verses, having been established as subordinate to those [offerings], would be subordinate to the full-moon and new-moon times as parts of the *ājyabhāga* offerings due to occurring at those times; yet...

Nevertheless, since the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are performed on the first day (*pratipad*), it is impossible for them to have that [full-moon or new-moon] time as their occasion; and even if they were possible at times when the lunar phase is incomplete, they would be impossible at a full phase. Consequently, this would result in a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of the principal acts—namely, the cessation of the mantras. Therefore, in accordance with the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) regarding a restriction of the subsidiaries, one must accept that the terms "Full Moon" (*paurṇamāsī*) and "New Moon" (*amāvāsyā*) indirectly indicate (*lakṣaka*) the *ājyabhāga* offerings which are themselves subsidiary to the principal acts occurring at those times.
Since it is possible for that [time] to belong to the primary [act] by way of the commencement of its performance, it is logical here that it is produced by the ritual action (*karma*) itself.

For this very reason—in the archetype (*prakṛti*), because of the conformity with other scriptural statements such as "one should sacrifice around the junction" (*sandhim abhito yajeta*)—the injunctions regarding the time of the full moon and so forth have precisely the nature of being mediated by the commencement of the performance.
Furthermore, the locative case ending refers solely to predominance (*prādhānya*).

And therefore, just as the fixed determination [of the mantras] is established in the archetype (*prakṛti*) due to the prescription of specific mantras for those two *ājyabhāga* offerings, so too— even if they are performed on any day whatsoever during a modification (*vikāra*) of the Full Moon sacrifice or a modification of the New Moon sacrifice— the fixed determination of those two is established. With this in mind— namely,
that it is possible to refute the attainment of form even by means of a determination based on the ritual action— the author has made that statement out of a lack of serious concern.

Although, as in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the necessity of resorting to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) for both the nominal stem and the suffix is equal; nevertheless, the sense is that even if one accepts such figurative indication, since a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) is possible, it is not proper to accept it as an original injunction (apūrvavidhi).

(Regarding the objection that, just as in the case of enjoining multiple qualified single factors when the bhāvanā is already established, the word *aṣṭākapāla* functions as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*), and since both fire (*agni*) and the substance (*dravya*) are intended by the term *āgneya* itself,
the sentence *āgneya* possesses a well-established syntactic unity (*viśiṣṭavyutpanna*) and thus cannot be suspected of merely providing the form [of the sacrifice]:
For in those cases where an unestablished *bhāvanā* is enjoined as qualified by multiple factors, [the situation is different].

Since the operation of the scriptural injunction (*śrautavidhi*) consists solely in enjoining a qualified productive urge (*viśiṣṭabhāvanā*), and since the enjoining of the qualifiers is accomplished by an injunction itself—postulated through the principle of "presumption based on the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) of the qualified injunction—the scriptural injunction has no further operation there.
