Consequently, there is no breach of the single-subjectivity of the injunction’s fruit, which is the making known of what was previously unknown; thus, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Just as in cases such as "sauryaṃ carum" (the sacrificial pap for Sūrya),
so too, even before the connection with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)— which has not yet been established— the mutual qualification of the various qualifiers is understood.

In that case, since only a single qualified object, though itself qualified by multiple qualifiers, is the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by repetition.

Just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), where the genus denoted by the nominal stem *paśu* is connected—by virtue of the word-hearing (*padaśruti*) and the hearing of co-referential designation (*samānābhidhānaśruti*)—with the number, and that [number] is connected with the instrumentality expressed by the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), resulting in the prescription of a single qualified *kāraka*;

however, as for the fact that this sentence is cited in the *Śāstradīpikā* and the *Kaustubha* as an example of prescribing a qualified [object] by way of restating a [previously] established action (*prāptakarmānuvādena viśiṣṭavidhāne*), [it is as follows].

For such a statement—namely, "one should sacrifice with the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma"—is established solely through what is heard and what is inferred, according to the *Nyāyasudhā*; thus, because it is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) for the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma, it is impossible for it to be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of a rite already obtained elsewhere. This [claim] is therefore merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhimātra*).

For this very reason, the sentence "he buys [the Soma] with a goat" (*ajayā krīṇāti*) alone has been cited as an example to demonstrate a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) based on a restatement of a rite already obtained.

Regarding the passage "In the south," according to the view of the ancients, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) already established by the rule "he gives the fee to the officiating priests" (*ṛtvigbhyo dakṣiṇāṃ dadāti*). By means of the word "that" (*tasya*), there is an injunction of the number one hundred and twelve, qualified by its connection to the cows denoted by that pronoun.
This is because, in their system, the grammatical competency (*vyutpatti*) for the genitive case-meaning to be construed with the number is well-established.
By this very logic, even when a word ending in the genitive functions as a qualifier of the subject (*uddeśya*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Just as in the case of "one should take [the draught] for a Brāhmaṇa at the Atirātra sacrifice" and so forth,

so too here, according to the principle to be stated under the section on Qualities (Guṇādhikaraṇa), the word *aṣṭākapāla*— like the word *āmikṣā*— functions as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*).

Since there is no lack of being expressed by separate words, the single compound ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) denotes the substance consisting of eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) qualified by the deity Agni and others.

He raises an objection regarding the absence of sentence-split (*vākya-bheda*) and refutes it with the words "And not" (*na ca*): because [the agent] is already distinguished by proficiency even prior to the cultivation [of the knowledge], the injunction is justified even when the cultivation of the sacrifice prescribed by the words of the learned is already established;

on the contrary, if that were not admitted, the *taddhita* suffix denoting a deity (*devatā-taddhita*)—as in the case of *sāsyadevatā*—which is prescribed in the section concerning the connection with the substance, would be untenable. Thus, having raised the doubt, he provides the rebuttal.

(The presentation of a specific grammatical rule [vyutpatti] regarding compounds and the like, even in the absence of a connection with a *kāraka* [participant in an action], as in the case of "aśvābhidhānīm" and so forth. // .//

By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the injunction regarding the redness residing in the priests (*ṛtvij*)—as found in the passage "The priests with red turbans perform [the ritual]" (*lohitoṣṇīṣā ṛtvijaḥ pracaranti*)—is included by way of restating the performance already established there.

For this very reason, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) stated in the eighth [book] that even the compound *śatāgniṣṭoma* denotes a group (*gaṇa*) qualified by both attributes; thus, it is said that just as in the case of "red-turbaned," a single unified object is what is enjoined.

(An exposition, including the refutation of other views with their roots, establishing that in cases such as "there are fifteen *ājya* [chants] in the separate places" and "one hundred and twelve of that," there is a connection of all [the words] with the action):

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* under the *Citrā* section that even though there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) in compound formations (*samāsa*) and the like due to a relation other than that of a *kāraka*, where there is no compound— as in "there are fifteen *ājya*s"— there indeed occurs that [syntactical split].

In the present case, however, since the status of being a deity (devatātva) constitutes the factor of the recipient (*saṃpradāna-kāraka*), if it were to connect with another [word] first, there would arise the consequence of a contradiction regarding its status as a *kāraka*. Therefore, its connection with the action must be accepted first, and only afterwards its connection with the substance.

It is precisely with this intention that the formation of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) and the like occurs; for since a qualified relation (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is not established [by the word itself], a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) is unavoidable.
Nor is this assumption groundless.

“Even though multiple factors (*kāraka*) are conveyed by a single word, because there is no mutual syntactic connection (*parasparānvaya*) between them, it is impossible to enjoin one as qualified by the other; therefore, in the case of ‘[the offering] for Agni’ (*āgneya*), an injunction [of the deity] as a singular entity is not possible,” and so forth; likewise, “even in the case of enjoining one factor as qualified by another, since the substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*) are distinct factors (*kāraka*), and since two factors cannot serve as mutual qualifiers, it is impossible to enjoin one factor as qualified by another factor.”
Because this has been indicated in the *Nyāyasudhā* during the detailed discussion on the "splitting of sentences" (*vākyabheda*) by the phrase beginning with "tyādinā," it is well-founded.

Such being the case, those things which— though expressed by separate words— attain a mutual connection through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or through the genitive case prior to their connection with the verb, do so both verbally and in fact, even while disregarding the injunction (*vidhi*)— as, for example, in the *Abhyuditeṣṭi*.

Even by the two words "Viṣṇave" and "Śipiviṣṭāya," a single referent is established as being qualified by the form of Viṣṇu pervaded by rays—denoted by the word *śipi*—based on the meaning of the mantra and its explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "O Viṣṇu, what was that which was to be hidden from you, when you said, 'I am Śipiviṣṭa'? That which is the abundance and the nourishment of the animal—that is Viṣṇu; Śipiviṣṭa is the surplus; indeed, he bestows the surplus."
Pārthasārathi has stated that there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the understanding of a qualified connection (*viśiṣṭānvaya*);
the refutation of that position, as set forth in the *Kaustubha*, will be clarified in the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭha-adhyāya*), in the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement "its [the hundred] consists of twelve hundred," the ancients proposed that even in the case of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), a mutual connection (*parasparānvaya*) should be assumed in order to avoid the contingency of a syntactical split that would arise from enjoining both the cow and the number.

Even if one were to somehow avoid the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) by enjoining a number qualified by "cow," that would still lead to the unavoidable consequence of enjoining horses and other items as well;
since it is necessary to enjoin the giving of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) qualified by both [the cow and the number], and since that very injunction avoids the fault, one must—
conforming to that— invent a different etymological derivation to postulate the connection of even the genitive case-meaning.
It should be understood from the Kaustubha that [the objection] is futile because there is no purpose [served by it].
(Conclusion regarding the rejection of the acquisition of form by means of the *āgneya* passage:

Therefore, because it is necessary that the passages concerning the *āgneya* sacrifice and others enjoin distinct sacrifices qualified by specific materials and deities, he concludes that "the form of these two is not obtained" with the words "therefore" (*ataśca*).
(Refutation of the acquisition of form through a different method by rejecting the application [atideśa] and others due to the resulting mutual dependence of the *saumika* rituals):
Having somehow kept in mind the acquisition of form according to the alternative method stated in the Kaustubha, he states the refutation up to its conclusion with the words: "Or let it be so."

Since the extension (*atideśa*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* ritual properties to the Soma sacrifice depends on the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* injunctions through the mediation of subsidiaries such as the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*, and since those two [the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*] would likewise depend on it, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Consequently, because it is impossible to perform the sacrificial realization (*iṣṭibhāvanā*)—qualified by the subsidiaries obtained through extension—at the morning time, the performance of the sacrifice on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad-iṣṭi*) becomes untenable; this impossibility is indicated by the word "somehow" (*kathañcit*) in the text.

(The demonstration that there is no injunction of an object [karma-vidhi] because the word *yat* merely indicates the attainment of an object limited by the word *tat*, and because another interpretation is possible in the present context:
"limited by the word *tat*" (*tacchabdāvadhika*).

Since it is necessary to supply the word "sa" (he) before the phrase "yāvad ukthyena," there is an obstruction to its being an injunction by virtue of indicating that the object [of the injunction] has already been established. Even so, because the presence of the word "yat" (which) functions merely to indicate what is already established, if that qualified object has not been established by any other means of knowledge, one must—out of necessity—accept that it indicates the establishment of the qualifier alone; and thus, out of necessity, even a qualified injunction [is accepted].
The meaning is: [the objection] is accepted as being like the case of "he who is initiated" (*yo dīkṣita*);
however, that is not the case here, because there is no possibility of the [objection] arising, since—as will be explained later—meaninglessness is impossible.
(The collective reference [samudāyānuvāda] by means of the statement of the learned;
likewise, the determination that the connection with the fruit belongs to the six alone, etc.)—
because of the mention of many [elements].

The meaning is as follows: just as when many trees situated in one place are designated by the single word "forest" (*vana*), they are established as a collective because they become the object of a single cognition, so it is here. In this context, based on the literal commentary stating that "the two words expressing the collection are the restaters of the collection," there arises the misconception that the two words *paurṇamāsī* and so forth denote the two collections [of rites] themselves and are thus connected to the fruit. To ward off this error, he says: "of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikasya*). This indicates that the nominal stems refer to the individual constituent acts.

Since the aggregate lacks connection with time, it does not fall within the scope of the *tatprakhyanyāya* (the principle of being named after its constituent parts), and thus it is impossible for it to be the name [of the sacrifice]. Furthermore, because the aggregate is not established by any other means of knowledge (*māna*), it is impossible for the two *vidvadvākya* sentences to function as restatements (*anuvāda*) of it. If the root *yaj* were to restate it, there would be the fault of *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication). Since the nominal stem denotes only those who constitute the aggregate of the six sacrifices, it is precisely those constituents that are restated for the purpose of the injunction; therefore, [the result] belongs to the constituents alone.
The meaning is "connection with the fruit.
He resolves the objection regarding the impossibility of the dual number in the sentence concerning the fruit, when there is a restatement of the constituent parts, by stating: "of the dual number."
The term *svapada* refers to the dual number.

Therefore, the meaning is that the two sentences containing the word "learned" (*vidvat*) serve to indicate the intention toward the duality of the two groups that constitute the relation for the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of plurality—specifically, the relation of residing in the individuals that form the aggregate which is the substratum of duality;
this is as expressed by the phrase "and just as."

(An exposition of Pārthasārathi’s view that the Āgneya sacrifice is a single unit: since it is prescribed as an auxiliary by means of practice at both morning and evening— thereby establishing its connection with two times— and because there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by multiple objects of reference (*uddeśya*), and because the principle of "another context" (*prakaraṇāntara*) does not apply due to the presence of the [sacrifice's] immediate proximity (*upasthiti*) and its inclusion within a single sentence.)

Furthermore, although in the sentence concerning the Āgneya sacrifice a distinction [of rites] based on a quality characterized by two simultaneous times is not possible— since it is impossible to enjoin two times for a single rite, as that can be accounted for even through repetition just as in the case of the evening and morning times of the Agnihotra—

nor is such a distinction possible based on a quality that would cause a syntactical split (vākyabheda) due to the plurality of times, because time is not something to be enjoined (anupādeya) but rather something to be referred to (uddeśya).

Even though time is not something to be adopted [as a primary object], its prescription as a subordinate factor (aṅga) is possible—just as in the case of "in the afternoon on the new moon day"—and thus there is no contingency of syntactical split (vākyabheda) caused by multiple things to be enjoined as objects. Nor does it arise from a different context (prakaraṇāntara) consisting of the connection with non-adoptable qualities; for that [different context] does not apply when there is proximity (sannidhi).

Furthermore, since there is a rule that the means of knowledge for a difference distinct from number must differentiate [an action] with respect to an action enjoined by another sentence, it is impossible for them to convey a difference with respect to an action mentioned within its own sentence; therefore, that [distinction] does not apply here.
Consequently, what was stated by Pārthasārathi—that the Āgneya sacrifice is one—is indeed correct.

(An investigation into the fact that, just as number is a factor that differentiates actions, the times of the full moon and new moon—due to the disparity between evening and morning—are likewise differentiators of action;

and thus, even so, for the sake of making the *vidvadvākya* meaningful as a restatement of a collective whole, there is the application of the term "plurality" [as a metaphorical indication] in the phrase "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," etc., despite the duality of the Āgneya sacrifice.
Nevertheless, there are certain ritual elements (*padārtha*) which, without differentiation or repetition, would not be fit for connection with the ritual action.

Since it is established in the case of number and other factors that a quality residing in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) serves to differentiate the action, whereas a quality residing in a non-originative injunction (*anutpannavākya*) serves to indicate a repetition, so too here, because the quality resides in the originative injunction, it is logical that the quality alone differentiates the action. For this very reason, since the qualities [of "evening" and "morning"] reside in non-originative injunctions regarding the times of evening and morning, it is logical that the quality alone differentiates the action.

For this very reason, because [the terms] "evening" and "morning" occur within the sentence expressing non-origination (*anutpatti*), they necessarily bring about repetition (*abhyāsa*). Furthermore, the distinction (*bheda*) here is established solely by way of indicating multiplicity, like a number, and not as having some counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).
Because, as with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is impossible to convey a difference determined by that [counter-correlate] prior to the counter-correlate itself being established;

this being the case, there is no harm even if, by the force of the means of valid cognition, a quality—just like a number—conveys a difference having as its counter-correlate the ritual action enjoined by its own sentence.
Therefore, the meaning is that this is clearly stated in the *Kaustubha* as "the difference from the Āgneya."

By the inclusion of the term *prapañcita* (elaborated), it is indicated that the refutation of other modes [of interpretation] as proposed by the author of the *Prakāśikā* should also be understood therein.

Nor should it be argued: "In that case, since the dual number is appropriate in that very context regarding the division of the *Āgneya*, and the connection with the fruit is thus established for those two alone, why resort to the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of plurality?

The sense is that this [resort to plurality] is necessary because one desires to know the purpose, in order to avoid the futility of the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the aggregate found in the *vidvadvākya*.
[The utility of the collective restatement in the Vaiśvadeva sentence] is as in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva."

The meaning is that, just as this sentence—by means of establishing a collection consisting of a sacrifice whose deity is the Viśvedevas—serves the purpose of securing the connection of the eight sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya to a location sloping toward the east and so forth, and thus, being intent on something else, does not enjoin a separate ritual action; so it is here.

(An analysis showing that the two groups of three [offerings] are restated as a collective pair for the purpose of establishing a single performance of each triad, because otherwise there would be the consequence of subverting the time of two days and the morning time obtained from other scriptural statements): "Otherwise, indeed... [etc.]
Nor is there an impossibility of achieving a single result when individual performances are postulated;

for even though the Āgneya and other rites are performed individually, their coexistence toward a single result is established through their existence at one and the same moment in the form of an *apūrva*, just as in the case of the Anīkavatī and other such rites.
For this very reason, just as the injunction "One should perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices on level ground" prescribes spatial coexistence, so too is the coexistence of moments understood.

Furthermore, there is no fault even if, on a single identical day, one performs the ritual application of each principal sacrifice— characterized by the auxiliary rites beginning with the *agnyanvādhāna* and ending with the *brāhmaṇatarpaṇa*— during three full-moon or new-moon days;
for it is not logical to perform three applications of the principal sacrifice on one and the same full-moon or new-moon day.

Since there would otherwise be the contingency of subverting the two properties of "occurring on the second day" and "occurring at the morning time," which are already established by other scriptural statements, these two sentences are necessary to establish that each triad of elements constitutes a single performance, thereby excluding them from being performed separately. Thus, they are not redundant.

(An exposition on how there is no separate performance [of the Āgneya sacrifice], even though the time is heard in its very originative injunction, because of its difference from the sentence "He who [desiring offspring]..."):

For this very reason, although the time is heard in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), the formulation of a performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*) occurs only in accordance with the subsequent syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of that [time]; since the performance has already been enjoined by these two preceding sentences, no further formulation of a performance injunction is required for that [originative injunction] either.
Just as in the sentence "ya iṣṭyā," there is no room for the suspicion of a separate performance here, because it merely prescribes the time by way of restating a performance already established;

whereas in the case of "ya iṣṭyā," through the co-occurrence with the word *yat*, there is a restatement of the performance of the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) followed by the prescription of the time alone.

Because the assumption of separate performances is permitted, and because it is impossible for those means that accomplish distinct results to be the objects of a single performance-rule due to the impossibility of a fixed necessity of desire, there is indeed a difference in performance for those whose conjunction is not intended as something to be expressed, since such conjunction resides in the subject matter of the restatement (*anuvāda*). However, in the present case, even though the principal acts are already established, they are enjoined as being the objects of performance; therefore, by virtue of being the objects of performances qualified by their respective times—

The meaning is that because both the concomitance pertaining to the enjoined sacrifices and the concomitance pertaining to their constituent parts are intended to be expressed, a difference in performance is not appropriate.

(The determination that the mention of time in the originative injunction is for the purpose of restricting the root *yaj* [to sacrifice] as it occurs in the injunctions concerning qualification and so forth.
He dispels the doubt—"For what purpose, then, is the time mentioned in the originative injunction?"—with the words "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).
"For the sake of establishing the whole."
(Justification for the authority of the statements of the learned:

By this, the objection that if everything were merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*), it would fail to possess the essential nature of authority—which consists in making known an object not already apprehended—is refuted; for even in the case of a restatement of a possible meaning, authority is established by virtue of its capacity to convey a collective sense (*samudāya*) not yet apprehended.
(An examination of the purpose of the preceding and subsequent sections:
It is established.

And thus, the scriptural indication (*liṅga*)—"fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day, thirteen on the new moon day"—which concerns the counting of the *vaṣaṭ*-offerings made in the *āhavanīya* fire, also becomes consistent.

Otherwise, in the first position, there would result fifteen [offerings] on the full moon day and fourteen on the new moon day; and in the second position, there would result twelve on both occasions, which is untenable. According to my view, however, there are five *prayāja*s, two *ājyabhāga*s, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, three *anūyāja*s, and three principal offerings on the full moon day—thus totaling fourteen; whereas on the new moon day, there are fifteen because the two *sānnāyya* offerings are performed together, as they share a common deity.
And the fact that the number thirteen is thus established is made clear by the very presentation of the prima facie and final positions.
Thus ends the third section concerning the full-moon sacrifice.
(B1) (Section 4 / [A.2 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 4]) The Upāṃśuyāja should be like the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice.
In that very same context, the scripture states: "Indeed, a redundancy is created in the sacrifice when two *puroḍāśa* cakes are offered consecutively;

one should sacrifice to Viṣṇu in a whisper for the sake of non-redundancy; one should sacrifice to Prajāpati in a whisper for the sake of non-redundancy; one should sacrifice to Agni and Soma in a whisper for the sake of non-redundancy.
Just as in the previous case, this intermediate sentence (*antarāvākya*) does not enjoin a separate ritual action.

Moreover, it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of establishing the collection of sacrifices enjoined by sentences ending in the suffix *tavya*, which are characterized by deities and low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*).
And its purpose is the injunction of the intermediate time (*antarāla-kāla*) for these three.

The two [deities] said, "O Agni and Soma, one should sacrifice for us two with clarified butter alone, silently, at the full moon. Since this is connected to a specific time, the connection with the fruit is established through the apprehension of the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

Otherwise, because the connection with the time would belong only to that which has Agni and Soma as its deities, there would be a connection with the fruit [only for them]. Such being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: because the beginning and the conclusion refer to the same subject, they are perceived as a single syntactical unit; therefore, there is no injunction of a ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) by means of those sentences ending in the suffix *tavya*.
However, it is precisely within the intermediate sentence that there is an injunction for a single action qualified by [the attributes of] time and low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*).
And this entire preceding and subsequent portion constitutes its explanatory praise (*arthavāda*);
otherwise, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result.
Therefore, the view that the injunctions ending in the suffix *tavya* enjoin only the deities for the rites mentioned in the intermediate passage (*antarālavākya*) is also refuted.
Furthermore, there is no obtaining of a deity there;

for it is possible that the pairs of *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses dedicated to Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, and Agni-Soma—which are recited in the sequence of this sacrifice according to different Vedic branches—serve to determine those respective deities through option (*vikalpa*).
And for that [action], there is a connection with the fruit because of its connection with time, as expressed by the words "Then they two said."

Nor should it be argued that— because the Āgneya and other offerings, which have a connection with the time prescribed at their very origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), are immediately present and thus attain a connection with the fruit, while the Upāṃśuyāja, which has a connection with the time prescribed after its origin (*utpannaśiṣṭa*), would otherwise obtain the times such as the Full Moon (*paurṇamāsī*) only through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for its connection with the interval between the sacrificial cakes, and consequently the Upāṃśuyāja itself would attain a connection with the fruit, making it impossible for the sentence "tāv abrūtām" (those two spoke) to have that same fruit. This is not to be said.

They both said: "Immediately after this [statement], it is recited that 'one performs the Upāṃśuyāja sacrifice in between'. According to the observation in the Vārtika, since this time is also enjoined by its own originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is no lack of syntactic unity (*bhinnavākyatva*) due to the absence of separate sentences; thus, because they possess equal force, the connection with the result is established.
Therefore, it is proven that this is not a collective restatement (*samudāyānuvāda*).
The purpose is clear. // 4 //
Thus ends the fourth section concerning the Upāṃśuyāja.
(B2) (Establishing the connection of these first three sections with the preceding section by way of an exception):

Hereafter, since the repetition [of mantras] is determined through three sections by means of an exception to the status of being a collective restatement (*samudāyānuvāda*), the connection with the present topic is not explicitly stated— given that it is obvious because there is a difference of ritual acts (*karmabheda*) in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and unity of the ritual act (*karmaikya*) in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)— but rather [the connection is presented] preceded by a demonstration of the subject matter (*viṣaya*).
He states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "As with a sister" (jāmivat).

In the tenth [book], in the sūtra beginning with "jāmikaraṇācca," the author of the Bhāṣya explains that *jāmitā* means similarity (*sādṛśya*). Furthermore, since it is stated in the Nyāyasudhā that even though the word *jāmi* denotes beauty, it has the sense of similarity as its secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*), it follows that this laziness, which is similar to *jāmi*, is being performed for the sacrifice— namely,
that two cakes (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Agni and to Agni-Soma are made consecutively without an interval.
Therefore, the meaning is that in order to avoid that [fault], another sacrifice must be performed in between.

Since the performance of three *upāṃśuyāja*s would result from enjoining sacrifices by means of the sentences concerning Viṣṇu and others—and since this would lead to sixteen oblations on the full moon day—this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises by challenging the previously mentioned observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Thus, the phrase "in that very place" (*tatraiva*) is used to indicate that the consideration of the *upāṃśuyāja* is appropriately first, due to its specific connection with what follows immediately.
(The prima facie view regarding the intermediate sentence:

Because the *laṭ* and *leṭ* suffixes are ambiguous in an intermediate sentence, whereas in passages such as "one's own Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*), the suffix *-tavya* is seen to be undoubtedly injunctive; therefore, wherever there is a form that characterizes a sacrifice by means of its substance, deity, and so forth, there alone do both [the *laṭ* and *leṭ*] function as injunctions due to their predominance.

Intending to establish the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by considering that, according to logical principle (nyāya), the injunction of a sacrifice is understood [in the first sentence], whereas in the intervening sentences there is no such injunction of a sacrifice, but rather they are injunctions of sacrifices only in those sentences containing the suffix *tavya*, he explains the prima facie position with the words: "just as before."

Nor should it be argued that— because there is a perception of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) through a single subject matter, as seen here in the *jāteṣṭi* passage where the opening with "jāmi" and the conclusion with the mention of "jāmitva" (the defect of repetition) serve to praise the rite that removes it—

there would be the consequence of violating that unity if those sentences were taken as enjoining three separate sacrifices, which would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This is because [the structure here is different].

Since the conclusion regarding the absence of redundancy (*ajāmitva*) is applied to each [deity] individually, it is understood—by virtue of following that—that the opening statement must also be connected to each one individually; therefore, it is more appropriate to regard them as distinct sentences.
Otherwise, as in the case of the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice, if that [conclusion] were to apply only once at the end, its application to each [individual deity] would be untenable.
Consequently, although the suffix *-tavya* indicates that Viṣṇu and the others are the primary objects, [the sentence structure remains distinct].

Nevertheless, since those [offerings] are not possible because they lack utility for what has already occurred or will occur, it is logical that they function as subordinate elements (guṇa) characterized by the preparation of the *saktu* and so forth; thus, the injunction of sacrifices qualified by specific deities and the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is not untenable.
Furthermore, the word *yaji* (to sacrifice) found in the intermediate sentence (*antarāvākya*) is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of those very same sacrifices.

The term *upāṃśuyāja* is also an unanalyzed name (*nāmadheya*) for those very [offerings] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and not an etymological derivative (*yaugika*). For if it were the latter, the form would result as *upāṃśuyāga*, because by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇyatoḥ*, the substitution of *k* (known as *kutva*) is prescribed for a verbal root ending in *j* when followed by the suffixes *ghin* or *yat*.
For this very reason, in the intermediate sentence (*antarāvākya*), there is no injunction regarding the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*);

rather, only the time "in between" (*antarākāla*) is enjoined with reference to the three sacrifices mentioned by the term *yajati*. Nor is it proper to argue that syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*) is impossible because the commencement concerning the defect of redundancy (*jāmitā*) is interrupted by the injunction regarding the interval; [for the connection is established through the context].
This is for the purpose of praising the entire collection (samudāya), since here too the positive concomitance (anvaya) is established without interruption.

In reality, however, because the phrase "for the sake of non-weariness" (*ajāmitvāya*) is recited even in the intermediate passage of the Taittirīya branch, the introduction regarding weariness refers exclusively to that [intermediate] matter alone.

In the passages concerning Viṣṇu and the others, the mere mention of "for the sake of non-weariness" is a restatement (*anuvāda*)—since non-weariness is already obtained through the injunction of the intermediate time which effects non-weariness—and serves solely to praise the sacrifice.

And thus, since the pairs of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, and Agni-Soma—which are recited in sequence according to different Vedic branches (*śākhā*)—can be established as subsidiaries to those respective sacrifices by the force of their indicative power (*liṅga*) alone, there is no need to assume an injunction for a deity;
this is parsimony (*lāghava*).
Nor should it be suspected that even in the intermediate sentence (*antarāvākya*) there is an injunction for a separate sacrifice.
Because there is an absence of any means of proof for a distinction [between them],

and because it is impossible to postulate deities based on the wording of the mantras here— since those respective *yājyā* verses function as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to those respective sacrifices— their form is not established, and thus that [distinction] does not arise. Therefore,

the sense is that it is logical that the sentences concerning Viṣṇu and the others enjoin three sacrifices, while the sentence concerning the "whispered" (*upāṃśu*) sacrifice is a collective restatement (*samudāyānuvāda*) of the term "he sacrifices."

(An exposition of the two purposes: [1] the prescription of the intermediate time for the restatement of the aggregate, and [2] the connection of the three with the fruit when that [intermediate time] is not otherwise obtained. He states the purpose of the restatement of the aggregate: "That is its purpose. // .//

And since it is not appropriate for this [avoidance of *jāmitā*] to be the purpose—given that the performance in the interval is established by the force of the restatement (*anuvāda*) which removes the *jāmitā* produced by the immediate succession of the *puroḍāśa* offerings—the author states another purpose out of this underlying dissatisfaction:
"Of the three," etc.

For in the absence of this [principle], since the words "Agni" and "Soma" are mentioned in the sentence "They two said," Agni and Soma—whether as qualifiers or as indicators (upalakṣaṇa)—would be construed with that sentence; consequently, only a sacrifice of a different class (vijātīya-yāga) dedicated to the deities Agni and Soma would be prescribed for the time of the full moon. Thus, because only that [sacrifice] would be grasped by the two "knowledge-vidhi" sentences (*vidvadvākya*) and the "result-vidhi" sentence (*phalavākya*), the connection with the result would be established for it alone, while the other two [sacrifices] would necessarily result in being merely subsidiary (*aṅga*).

Since that [mention] exists as a restatement of a collective group (*samudāyānuvāda*), it is understood that the three [offerings] possess the designation *upāṃśuyāja*; thus, in the passage "silently on the full moon day" (*upāṃśu paurṇamāsyām*), because of the connection with time through a part of the name, the status of those three is established.
For in that case, the term *āgnīṣomīya* cannot function either as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) or as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*);
rather, like the term *vaiśvadeva*, it serves as an indicator for the deities Viṣṇu and the others, lest the restatement of the collective group be rendered purposeless.
Therefore, the meaning is that the purpose is the establishment of the connection between the three [factors] and the fruit.

(The commencement of the Siddhānta: Since the concluding statements regarding "non-repetition" (*ajāmitva*) with respect to each of the deities, Viṣṇu and the others, are justified as demonstrating the capacity for non-repetition in each case, they form a single syntactical unit; thus, the injunction for the sacrifice resides solely in the *upāṃśu* passage, while the passages concerning Viṣṇu and the others are merely explanatory (*arthavāda*).

[This is established] by way of demonstrating the capacity for effecting non-repetition in each of the deities, Viṣṇu and the others, through the concluding statements regarding non-repetition made with respect to each.

Since it is appropriate to accept a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) by taking the passage as being intent upon praising the sacrifice produced by that [preceding injunction], it is improper to abandon the unity of syntactical meaning—perceived through the principle of the *Vaiśvānara* passage by virtue of the correspondence between the opening and the conclusion—and instead assume a separate syntactical unity (*bhinnavākyatā*) through ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*). Furthermore, this is because it would entail a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the injunctive suffix *tavya*. Just as in the case of the passage "He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in the interval," where, since the matter is not already established, one assumes the suffix to be *leṭ* (the Vedic subjunctive).

Intending to show that while the injunction of a sacrifice is logical, it is not so in those sentences containing the suffix *tavya*—because in such cases a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) would result, making it more appropriate to regard them as mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "upakrama... (beginning with...).

And thus, since the monotony (jāmitā) produced by the immediate succession of the two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) is understood to be removed by the enjoined [act] connected with the intervening time, there is an attachment to the quality consisting of the interval; and because the injunction of the ritual act is perceived right there, the meaning is that the injunction of the ritual act resides in the sentence concerning the interval itself.

(An objection is raised on the grounds that [the Upāṃśuyāja] refers to Viṣṇu and other deities mentioned in mantras as optional alternatives, thus being merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the meaning of sentences concerning Viṣṇu and others; furthermore, it is argued that because the previous section has already functioned, the intermediate time is already prescribed, and since the word *upāṃśuyāja* is etymological (*yaugika*), it prescribes an offering qualified by "inaudibility" (*upāṃśu*) at that intermediate point, and so forth.

For this very reason, he states that there is no lack of form (*arūpatva*) there, because a deity is postulated based on the wording of the mantra itself: "by way of different recensional branches" (*śākhābhedena*).
In the *Aitareyaka*, between the two pairs of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to Agni and Indra-Agni, both "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and "pratadviṣṇuḥ" are recited;
or alternatively, "trirdevaḥ pṛthivīm" is recited in place of "pratadviṣṇuḥ.
In the *Taittirīya*, between those [verses], "prajāpate na tvat" is recited.
The pair "sa vedasā" is thus handed down;

likewise, in the Aitareyaka itself, in the midst of that [section], the pair "anyaṃ divo agnīṣomau yo aghāyi" is handed down according to the division of the recensional branches (śākhā)—this is the meaning. [This applies] even by way of option (vikalpa).
Since the purpose of the three deities is directly perceived, there is an option (vikalpa) between them.

And thus, given the difference in deities suggested by the wording of the mantras, it is not logical to accept a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhi) based on the assumption of a qualification by a deity provided by an explanatory passage (arthavāda);
for that [deity] is established as being merely an arthavāda.

Nor is the injunction regarding the intermediate time redundant on the grounds that the performance at that time is already established by the force of the result itself for the purpose of removing the defect of *jāmitā* (monotony); for, since the injunction of the intermediate time is implied by that [result], it is logical to accept that injunction for the sake of making the sacrifice "elevated" (*abhyudayaśiraska*) through its prior commencement, thereby justifying the injunction of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of the sacrifice characterized by low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) during the intermediate time—
even though the term *upāṃśuyāja* does not possess an etymological meaning (*yaugikatva*).

Although there is the possibility of the *kutva* substitution [of *t* for *d*], nevertheless, according to the rule "in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), one follows what is observed," one may somehow avoid the *kutva*. Since there is no evidence for postulating a distinct power (*śakti*) by abandoning the perceived meaning of the constituent parts, the term is etymological (*yaugika*)—just like the word *prokṣaṇī*—and thus there is no fault; this is the meaning.

(Tāvabrūtām... [The explanation of] *tasya ca*: Since the substances, deities, and sacrifices are already established, it is impossible to enjoin them; therefore, even though the sentence has the form of an injunction, like the passage "ya iṣṭyā," its purpose is solely to establish a connection with time.
The connection of that [time] with the fruit is explained by the words "the fruit" (*phalam*) and so forth.
The meaning is: "of the sacrifice enjoined by the intermediate sentence.

Furthermore, although this statement takes the form of an *arthavāda* in the style of a *purākalpa*, even if an injunction is postulated because the restatement as an established fact would otherwise be inexplicable, it is not an enjoiner of the sacrifice;
for that has already been obtained through the intermediate sentence itself.
Nor does it enjoin the deities Agni and Soma according to the method stated in the Bhāṣya;
for since both [deities] are equally to be assumed, they are already obtained from the wording of the *yājyā* mantra itself. For this very reason, it does not enjoin the *ājya* offering either.
Therefore, this [text] is an injunction prescribing a time that has not yet been established.

Consequently, under the view that there is a single sacrifice (*yāga-ekatva*), since the time is enjoined by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the sacrifice, the qualification of that [time]—namely, its being dedicated to the deities Agni and Soma—is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*) because it resides in that which is being referred to. Thus, the connection with the fruit is established even for that which is dedicated to a triad of deities.

For in this case, since the rite is enjoined as something to be performed (*prayoga-viṣaya*) at the time that has already been obtained as something to be adopted (*upādeya*), there is no possibility of intending the significance of its qualifications.

Since the performance (*prayoga*) is already established by the hearing of the intermediate time within the very originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), it is impossible to enjoin it as an object of that injunction;
therefore, the meaning is that its establishment occurs through the attainment of the name "Darśapūrṇamāsa" by merely establishing a connection with time, just as in the case of the term "iṣṭi."

(The explanation that [the statement] "They two said" is also an *arthavāda* because, as part of a single syntactical unit with an injunction, it conveys through that qualified injunction the *bhāvanā* of a sacrifice characterized by the time of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the interval between the *upāṃśu* and other offerings;

and because the absence of independent injunctive status has been established even in the *Vidhirasāyana*; and thus, since it possesses the time of the full moon as taught in its originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), the connection of the *upāṃśuyāja* with the fruit is established;
for this very reason, the inclusion of the *āgneya* and others in the sequence beginning with "This is indeed the head of the sacrifice" is also justified—such is the detailed analysis. And not so.
Nor can it be argued that the connection of the *upāṃśuyāja* with the fruit is established simply because the injunction of the full-moon time (*paurṇamāsī*) would otherwise be rendered purposeless;

for since the intermediate time exists on the new-moon day (*amāvāsyā*) just as it does on the full-moon day, that injunction remains meaningful as a means of precluding its performance on the latter day as well.
Therefore, the sense of the objection is: "How can the purpose of the injunction be the connection with the fruit?"
This is because of the observation of the Vārttika.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement, "Moreover, this is indeed a repetition," and because it is understood from the context of the introductory injunction, "On the full moon day, they sacrifice for the two [deities] with the *ājya* in a low voice (*upāṃśu*)," that this [injunction] prescribes [the sacrifice] specifically on the full moon day; this is seen in the *Vārttika* on the final section of the tenth book.

Moreover, since there is no purpose in assuming that this [text] is an independent injunction, it is construed as a single syntactical unit with the injunction, "They sacrifice the *upāṃśuyāja* in between."

The meaning is that, because there is the cognition of an injunction for the *bhāvanā* of a sacrifice qualified by the time of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the intermediate time characterized by *upāṃśutva*, its connection with the fruit is established— just as in the case of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices— by virtue of having a time prescribed at its origin (*utpattiśiṣṭakālatva*), and its exclusion on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is likewise established. Furthermore, by the statement "because it is to be enjoined by the originative sentence itself," [it is shown that] the *paurṇamāsī* sentence lacks independent injunctive status.

In the *Vidhirasāyana*, having accepted that the sentence concerning the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) is an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), it was demonstrated that there is an over-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition of an original injunction;
this [objection] has been refuted, as indicated [here].

Furthermore, since [the author] himself demonstrated exactly the same thing in the *Vidhirasāyana* for the purpose of establishing the connection with the result, there is also a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

And on this view, although the status of the injunction as a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) is possible even with respect to the portion concerning Agni-Soma, its status as a restatement (*anuvāda*)—by means of the exclusion [of that possibility] through the force of the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) found in passages such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice" (*viṣṇurupāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ*)—should be understood.
Likewise, since the prescription of the low-voiced quality (*upāṃśutva*) is established by the word *upāṃśu* itself, the word *upāṃśu* does not function as a qualifier-injunction (*guṇavidhi*);
rather, it is either an unintelligible term or a name (*nāmadheya*) according to the principle of "being known from elsewhere" (*tatprakhyanyāya*). This is how it should be considered.

And thus, with the intention that even the mention of the principal [offerings] in the context of the *arthavāda*— namely, "The *āgneya* is indeed made the head of the sacrifice, the *upāṃśuyāja* is the heart, and the *agnīṣomīya* is the two feet"— is rendered appropriate by way of the delimitation of the *upāṃśuyāja* itself,
he concludes the refutation of the view that it is a collective restatement (samudāyānuvāda) with the words: "Therefore, this is not [the case]."
(The purpose of the prima facie and final positions) is clear.

The meaning is that in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), all three [deities] are performed because they are equally primary, whereas in the established conclusion (siddhānta), only one is performed through an option among the deities; this is clear.
Thus ends the fourth section concerning the Upāṃśuyāja.

(B1) (Section 5 on Adhikaraṇa) (a.2 pā.2 adhi.5): In that very context, regarding the scriptural injunction “he pours the libation” (*āghāram āghārayati*) and the statement “he offers the Agnihotra” (*agnihotram juhoti*),

since— as in the previous case— there is no defect of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), [the injunctions] such as “he pours straight” (*ṛjum āghārayati*) and “he pours continuously” (*santatam āghārayati*) [are taken as qualifying the act].

In the case of rites enjoined by such sentences as "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and "He offers with milk" (*payasā juhoti*), it is appropriate to regard them as collective restatements (*samudāyānuvādaka*) according to their respective contexts.

This is because the sentences concerning curd and other substances cannot be construed with the injunction if they refer merely to a quality devoid of an action; therefore, they necessarily enjoin a rite qualified by that quality.

Consequently, due to the absence of a defining characteristic (*rūpa*) and the absence of any means of proof for differentiation, there is no separate rite in the *agnihotra* sentence or the *āghāra* sentence.
Rather, this is a restatement for the purpose of establishing their collective formation;

its purpose is to ensure that all of them, by virtue of being designated as "agnihotra," are connected with the fruit [of the ritual]. Otherwise, the connection with the fruit would apply only to the oblation to the deity Agni.
The purpose of the collective restatement (*samudāyānuvāda*) in the *āghāra* passage should be examined in the *Kaustubha*.
Nor is there an absence of deities and so forth in the oblations of curd and the like;

for, by the force of the collective restatement, it is understood that they are subsumed under a single performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*), such that through a single performance, the deity who is a constituent part of the *āghāra* oblations [is satisfied].

Since it is possible for curd and the like to assist the oblation (*homa*) by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: because the third mode of injunction is applicable everywhere through the mere injunction of an accessory (*guṇamātra*), it is improper to accept a fifth mode of injunction; therefore, there is no injunction of a qualified action (*viśiṣṭakarma*) in the sentences concerning curd and the like.
Nor is there any inconsistency in the connection of the injunction with the accessory (guṇa);

for even when the connection of the injunction is with the productive urge (bhāvanā) which has the oblation as its object and the accessory as its instrument, the result of the injunction—consisting in the making known of what was previously unknown—is attained through the distinction between what is already established and what is not. This is because the bhāvanā itself is already established in its essential form.

Consequently, although in all cases there is an injunction of a qualified bhāvanā, the six types of injunctions are applied by taking into account only the result, and it has been stated previously that among these, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding.

And therefore, precisely because there is no possibility of obtaining [the materials], and thus no possibility of the sentences being mere restatements (*anuvāda*) of a collection, the two sentences concerning the *āghāra* and *agnihotra* are indeed injunctions of ritual acts (*karma-vidhi*) by way of original injunctions (*ādyavidhi*). Nor is there an impossibility of these being injunctions of acts due to a lack of knowledge of their form (*rūpa*); for while such knowledge is a cause for performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), it is not a cause for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

Therefore, once it is understood that the injunction pertains to what is delimited by being a sacrifice of a different class (*vijātīya-homa*), there is no defect even if the specific form [of the material] is obtained through another sentence.
The purpose is clear from the combination (*samuccaya*) or the option (*vikalpa*) regarding substances such as curd and the like. //5//
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the Āghāra and Agnihotra offerings.

(B2) [Demonstration of the connection by way of counter-example and the connection with the present context: In the preceding section, because the suffix *tavya* lacks injunctive force and because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), it was appropriate that it be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), since praise is perceived there. However, in the present case, since the qualities such as curd are not already established by the sentences concerning curd and so forth, they cannot function as explanatory passages through the mode of restatement (*anuvāda*). Consequently, a single syntactical unity is untenable; therefore, these must be distinct sentences.

Since even in the Siddhānta the status of being an injunction (vidhitva) is accepted, and since a pure injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) is impossible according to the method to be explained later—thereby necessitating an injunction of a qualified action (viśiṣṭakarmavidhi)—the restatement of the collective (samudāyānuvāda) is appropriate. Thus, indicating the immediate connection by way of a counter-example (pratyudāharaṇa) because it arises from the Pūrvapakṣa, and the connection with the present topic because it results in the distinction or non-distinction of actions, he states the Pūrvapakṣa preceded by the example: "In that very [case]... and so on.
Regarding the fact that the *āghāra* sentence is a collective restatement (*samudāyānuvāda*):

even though it is recited before the injunction for the wiping of the fire (*agnisaṃmārga*), which intervenes between it and the collective restatement of the sacrifices enjoined by the sentences concerning "upwards" (*ūrdhva*) and so forth that are read immediately after it—

[the author] says "in that very [context]" (*tatraiva*) to indicate its entry into the context (*prakaraṇa*), thereby suggesting that the *āghāra* enjoined by the *āghāra* sentence belongs to that same context as well.
By the phrase "as before," the connection with what was previously stated is indicated.

(An exposition demonstrating that since the object of the operation [vyāpāra] of the productive meditation (*bhāvanā*) must necessarily be an injunction of action even in sentences such as "curd" (*dadhi*), and since it is impossible to enjoin curd and the like— which are qualities connected to the origination [of an action]— as something already enjoined, a distinction of actions (*karmabheda*) is inevitable; therefore, in the *agnihotra* sentence, it can only be a restatement of a collective whole [*samudāyānuvāda*], etc.)— [the term used is] "devoid of operation" (*nirvyāpāra*).

Since an injunction (*vidhi*) consists in the impelling of a conscious agent, and since that impelling is an activity conducive to action, it is impossible to abandon its status as the object of the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) delimited by the meaning of the verbal root— given the proximity established by being expressed in a single word— and because an injunction cannot apply to a quality that is not itself an activity, a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is necessary; and since an injunction cannot apply again to what has already been enjoined, there is a distinction [between the acts] due to repetition (*abhyāsa*).

Nor can it be argued that, even though [the action] has already been enjoined, its status as a distinct injunction is not established because it can be enjoined again through a connection with curds and so forth—just as it is connected to results, causes, and the like;

for while an injunction is possible regarding the application (*viniyoga*) of something already produced by itself when it relates to results and so on, it is necessary that an origination (*utpatti*) occurs when there is a connection with a substance and the like, since that [substance] functions as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) inherent in the origination. Thus, because a re-enjoinment of what is already established is impossible, a distinction [between the injunctions] is necessary.

Therefore, in sentences such as those concerning curd and other materials—“That which [is offered] to Agni and Prajāpati”—and in sentences such as “Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā!”, there is a distinction between rituals everywhere because they possess specific forms, whether due to an accessory (*guṇa*) or repetition (*abhyāsa*).
For in the case of the *agnihotra* and similar sentences, there is no injunction of a ritual action when the form is not supplied;
moreover, the form is obtained through another sentence.

And furthermore— although in this way the substance is obtained in the case of oblations of curd and so forth from its own sentence, and in the case of oblations to Agni and so forth through implication—

even so, since there is no deity mentioned in its own sentence, and because it is not your position that there is an injunction for the deity alone as supplied by another sentence, the deity is not obtained through implication; how then can there be the possession of a form (rūpavattva)?

Thus it should not be said [that there is a separate performance for each]; for since these [rites] are means to a single fruit, their simultaneous performance is established by being subsumed under a single injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), just like the *sānnāyya* offerings. Furthermore, this is possible because even when other seasons (*hemāntara*) occur, the required materials, deities, and so forth can provide assistance through *prasaṅga* (extension of benefit).

Moreover, since Prajāpati is "unexpressed" (*anirukta*), and since no specific material is prescribed, the required material and deity are established by the general statements [of the texts], such as "clarified butter" (*ājya*).

Indeed, the cognition of possessing color (*rūpavattājñāna*) is not the cause for the cognition of being that which is to be enjoined (*vidheyatājñāna*); for even in the absence of a cognition of fitness (*yogyatā*), verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is experienced from a heard word solely through the absence of a certainty regarding unfitness (*ayogyatāniścayābhāva*). Therefore, since it is untenable for such a cognition [of color] to be the cause, the status of being that which is to be enjoined is established merely by the absence of a certainty regarding the lack of color. Consequently, since the distinction from other objects of action is established even by the mere connection with one form, when there is a need for it at the time of performance, it follows according to the previously stated method...
That is its justification.
As for the Agnihotra sentence, although it is possible [to derive the meaning] from Agni and Prajāpati,

nevertheless, since it is possible as a restatement of a collective whole (samudāyānuvāda), the idea is that it is improper to accept a separate ritual action (karmāntara) which would entail an unseen difference (adṛṣṭabheda).
(Regarding the purpose of the collective restatement in the *Agnihotra* injunction: And thus,

because the homas enjoined by the sentences concerning curd (*dadhi*) and so forth are obtained as a collection of efficient forces (*bhāvanā*)— just like the collection of the root-meanings— by means of an accumulation characterized by being read in a single portion of the same class, namely the form of offering (*havana*), the phrase "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*) in the *Agnihotra* sentence is a collective restatement (*samudāyānuvāda*) of that collection.

Then, just as with the term *vaiśvadeva*, for fear that the term *agnihotra* would be a redundant restatement of a collective whole (*samudāyānuvāda*), it is appropriate to interpret it as referring to all oblations—both those dedicated to Agni and those not dedicated to Agni; thus he states the purpose of the restatement of the collective whole, which consists in establishing the connection between the result and the occasion: "That is its purpose."

Similarly, in the case of the sentences regarding "the upward" (*ūrdhva*) and so forth, since the delimitation of the ritual act is possible through the qualities of "upwardness" and the rest—which take the form of substances and deities—just as in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja* by means of its low-voiced nature (*upāṃśutva*), the statement "he pours the *āghāra*" is a collective reference (*samudāyānuvāda*) to sacrifices qualified by those respective qualities and having fourfold-drawn clarified butter (*caturgṛhīta-ājya*) as their substance. As for its purpose, the Vārtika states: "With the mantra 'O Indra, upward [is] the sacrifice,' he pours the *āghāra*."
It has been stated that the unity of the *āghāra* (libation) is established through the injunction regarding the mantra.

In the case of the injunction "he pours the *āghāra* upwards," even within the injunction concerning the mantra, the status of the sacrifice is established—preceded by the establishment of its having Indra as its deity—by means of the simultaneous performance understood from the injunctive rule, which links the *āghāras* qualified by the mantra with the *āghāra* whose deity is Indra as determined by the wording of the mantra. This is accomplished through the *āghāra* having Indra as its deity.
The meaning is that the purpose [of this work] is merely to establish simultaneity, as should be seen in the Kaustubha.

(An exposition of the established conclusion [siddhānta] that, for the sake of ensuring the meaningfulness of the *agnihotra* injunction and for the sake of avoiding the excessive complexity [gaurava] of postulating multiple unseen potencies (*adṛṣṭa*) through various types of injunctions,

the injunction regarding the oblation resides in the *agnihotra* sentence alone, as the sentences such as "one offers with curd" have, by distinguishing between what is already obtained and what is not, a scope limited solely to the accessory [guṇa]).
The injunction regarding ritual action resides precisely in sentences such as "the Agnihotra," for otherwise they would fall into the error of being purposeless;
nor should it be argued that they possess purposefulness by way of being restatements of a collective whole.

Intending to show that—in sentences such as those concerning curd and other items—since there would be the consequence of resorting to multiple qualified injunctions (viśiṣṭavidhi) among many [sentences], which would entail a fifth type of injunction and the postulation of numerous unseen potencies (adṛṣṭa), an injunction of action is impossible and thus a restatement of a collective (samudāyānuvāda) is untenable, he states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "In all cases... [sarvatra].

Although a quality (guṇa) may be connected with an injunction either directly or indirectly, nevertheless, because the quality is connected to the productive urge (bhāvanā) as its qualifier (*prakāra*) by way of being a factor of action (*kāraka*), even an injunction that primarily prescribes a productive urge qualified by such a quality is,

through the principle of "distinguishing the obtained from the unobtained" (*prāptāprāptaviveka*), in effect directed toward the quality. This is because the productive urge qualified by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), even if already established [by another source], [is not independently enjoined].

Even when there is a re-enjoinment (punarvidhāna) by way of a specific quality (*guṇa*), although there is no result of making known what was previously unknown (*ajñātajñāpana*) regarding the substratum (*viśeṣya*), the injunction remains purposeful because it effects [the cognition] regarding the qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*).
With this in mind—that an injunction regarding the quality itself is indeed possible through the third mode of injunction—he says: "having the act of oblation as its object" (*homakarmaka*).

Although in the originative injunction the action is construed as an instrument (*karaṇa*), in the case of a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*), since that [action] is already established, it is restated within the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) which requires it; and with the intention that there be a connection through the objecthood (*karmatva*) itself—rather than through the "indication of possessive meaning" (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)—it is stated that [the action] has the oblation (*homa*) as its object.
(There is no contradiction in resorting to the sixfold manner [of injunction] even in every case of a qualified injunction, nor is there any conflict with the Vārttika.

Now, one might ask: since the injunction is uniform in nature because it always prescribes a qualified efficient force (*bhāvanā*), how is it that the sixfold nature was established in the *Udbhid* section? To this, he says: "For this very reason" and "and of those."

It has been stated that the former [injunctions] possess greater strength and the latter [injunctions] possess lesser strength due to the heaviness caused by the postulation of numerous specific qualifications and the lightness caused by the absence thereof. Furthermore,

the refutation of those who attempt to establish eight types of injunctions based on the mutual connection between the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), independent of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), has been carried out by Vārttikakāra.
The meaning is: "of the sixfold manner mentioned according to the method we have established."

(Although there might be a suspicion of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) regarding the action enjoined by the *vidvadvākya* even when it is established by the *āgneyavākya*, and although the refutation of that suspicion is incidental:

Even if, according to this method, it were possible for the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) enjoined by the *vidvadvākya*—though already obtained—to be enjoined again in the *āgneya* and other sentences as being qualified by the material and the deity;

nevertheless, although multiple qualifications are possible within a single efficient force, one does not accept such an injunction with respect to multiple qualities because that would entail repetition (*āvṛtti*) and thus result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, it is not accepted.

Although there is no repetition because the object understood from the word by means of the scriptural injunction is identical in its qualified form, nevertheless, due to the difference in the objects that constitute the intended meaning (*tātparya*), there is indeed a "splitting of the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) characterized by prolixity (*gaurava*).

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vārttika*: "Even though [the injunction] resides in the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), its subservience to that [purpose] is divided when it functions as an injunction."
And in this case, where [the injunction] has the qualification as its result, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*);
however, the intention is that in the present context, since the subject matter concerns a single quality such as curd and so forth, that [split] does not arise.

(Regarding the resolution of the doubt concerning whether the *agnihotra* sentence is an injunction or a restatement, given that even if the sentences concerning curd (*dadhi*) and so forth are merely injunctions of qualities, the sentences "to Agni" (*yad agnaye*) and so forth enjoin multiple qualities; thus, due to the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), it is necessary to treat them as injunctions of four distinct rites, just like the *āgneya* sentence.

Now, one might object: since the sentences concerning curd and so forth do not contain injunctions of a rite—by resorting to the third mode of injunction (*vidhi-prakāra*)—[how can they serve as the basis for the restatement?]

Even though it is impossible for [the sentence] to be a collective reference (*samudāyānuvāda*), since it is impossible to enjoin multiple subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) by way of a restatement of an already established action (*prāptakarmānuvāda*) within the two sentences beginning with "That which to Agni," and since the injunction of a distinct action (*karmāntara*) is necessary, one must understand— in accordance with the requirement to combine the deities prescribed in the originative injunctions— that two actions are enjoined within a single sentence, just as in the case of the *Āgneya*. Consequently, the statement "He offers the *Agnihotra*" will serve as a collective reference (*samudāyānuvāda*) for these four actions.
If it is argued thus—[we reply]: No;

because even in that case, since Agni and the others are obtained solely from the wording of the mantra, there is no contingency of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) by virtue of enjoining Prajāpati alone in conjunction with them. Since this was stated in the *Tatprakhyādhikaraṇa*, there is no possibility of it being an injunction for a separate ritual (*karmāntara*), and thus the third mode of injunction is established. With this intention, the passage concerning the *Agnihotra* and so forth concludes the refutation of its status as a restatement of a collective whole (*samudāyānuvāda*).
Thus he establishes the rule for ritual action with the words "therefore" (ataśca).
[The determination of the purpose of the prima facie and final positions regarding the sentences on the *agnihotra* and the *āghāra*:
"There is a combination of substances such as curd and so forth."

In the *agnihotra* passage, regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it is a restatement of a collective whole (*samudāyānuvāda*), the ten substances such as curd and the rest are taken together—just like the *sānnāyya* offering—and because they share a common deity, there is a single oblation; thus, the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of curd and the others.

The meaning is that within the single *agnihotra* rite itself, there is an option (*vikalpa*) among them. This also serves as an illustration for the purpose of the prima facie and final views regarding the *āghāra* passage.

And regarding this, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), among the qualities such as height and so forth, if by chance an obstacle occurs to any one of them, then that which is delimited by the universal (*jāti*) manifested by that single quality—such as height—is not accomplished; therefore, there must be a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of that ritual action.

However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because there is no difference in the ritual action itself, and because it is improper for the principal act to be repeated merely for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), there is no repetition. Rather, it should be understood that there is only the performance of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) necessitated by the omission of a subordinate element.
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the Āghāra and Agnihotra offerings.
(B1) (Section 6 / [A.2 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 6]) Because of the connection with a substance.
It is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," and likewise, "One should sacrifice with Soma.
In these cases, because the first type of injunction is impossible, it cannot be an injunction for a new ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) as in the previous instances.
Rather, it is merely a restatement of the aggregate.

As for the application of the action, in the case of the animal sacrifice, because of the injunctions such as "He first cuts off from the heart, then from the tongue," and so forth, it is impossible for the heart and other parts to serve as the means (*sādhana*) in a sacrifice for which the animal—prescribed by the original injunction—is already established as the means. Therefore, the injunction of the consecratory act called "cutting" (*avadyati*) is not with reference to those [parts].

Consequently, since the prescribed cuttings of the heart and other parts possess a similarity to the cuttings of the *sānnāyya* (curd and milk) in that they consist of cuttings from a substance originating from an animal, they are understood to have the *sānnāyya* cutting as their archetype (*prakṛti*).

Just as in the case of the *sānnāyya* offering, since the heart and other organs are established as means for the sacrifice through inference—similar to the *pūtīka* plants—the very sacrifices of the heart and so forth are enjoined; these are then referred to by the term *ālabheta* (he should immolate) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and Agni and Soma are enjoined as the deities.
Furthermore, the word "animal" (*paśu*) refers secondarily to the heart and other organs, because their being made from the goat—as established by the wording of the mantra—is already obtained.

Alternatively, the term *ālabhati* (to touch/sacrifice) can refer back to the very acts of touching implied by the portions (*avadāna*) prescribed in the sentences concerning the heart and so forth; then, once each of these portions— indicated by the word *paśu* (animal)— is connected with a deity, that many sacrifices, established through those deity-connections, are enjoined by that very injunction.
In every respect, the term *paśu* (animal) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a collective whole.

Similarly, in the case of the Soma sacrifice as well, through sentences such as "He draws the cup for Indra-Vāyu" and "He draws the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa," there is an injunction of a sacrifice inferred from the connection between the substance and the deity;
for it is impossible for a deity to be connected with the act of drawing [the liquid].

The substance is the liquid [Soma] obtained by means of a continuous stream, as established in the context of the phrase "he takes it with a fine stream," which is expressed through a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).

However, in the Soma-injunction, the Soma plant itself is enjoined as the material cause (*prakṛti*) of that substance, just as rice (*vrīhi*) is enjoined as the material cause for the sacrificial cake.

Alternatively, because the injunctions regarding the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as "he presses the soma," would otherwise be inexplicable, the word *soma* is a name (*nāmadheya*), since the substance is already obtained—just as in the case of "he chooses the Adhvaryu.
In any case, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the entire collection [of acts].
And the purpose of this position is that, by restating merely the sacrifice whose substance is soma, even those [acts] lacking stotras and śastras become connected with the fruit.
And the term *jyotiṣṭoma* is secondary (gauṇa), just like *vaiśvadeva*.

For, in the absence of a collective restatement (*samudāyānuvāda*), it would follow—by virtue of that term—that only those sacrifices associated with the *stotra*s and *śastra*s would be connected to the fruit, since they alone possess the connection with the *jyotis*-like *stoma*.

In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, because the sacrifice is one, there arises the necessity of indicating repetition (*abhyāsa*) through the root *yaj* occurring in the sentence regarding the fruit; thus, the connection with the fruit belongs only to that which is delimited by the nature of a distinct class of sacrifice (*vijātīyayāgatva*).

In the term *jyotiṣṭoma*, the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound consists in its being the locus of a collection constituted by the repetitions connected to itself. Therefore, since those two [terms] are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of the collection, such was the initial position (*pūrva-pakṣa*). However, because there is no evidence for the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the heart and other organs in the word "animal" (*paśu*), it is a prescription of a specific sacrifice (*viśiṣṭa-yāga-vidhi*) in that very context.
And by the sentences concerning the heart and so forth, there is merely a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) with reference to the heart and other organs.
Furthermore, the animal is not enjoined as the sacrificial offering (*havis*) directly;
