rather, it is so enjoined only by virtue of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the heart and other organs, in accordance with the indicators of the intended meaning found in the injunctions for slaughter and so forth.
This is because the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is possible both directly and indirectly, provided there is an indicator of the intended meaning.

For this very reason, even the connection of the heart and other organs with the portions (avadāna) obtained through extended application (atideśa) is for the purpose of establishing their status as sacrificial oblations (havis), and for the purpose of excluding other limbs from that status; this and more should be seen in the Kaustubha.
In the case of Soma as well, there is no injunction of a sacrifice by means of the sentences regarding the Aindravāyava and other cups due to the resulting complexity;
rather, there is an injunction of the act of drawing (grahaṇa) itself, qualified by the deity, with reference to the substance denoted by the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita).

Furthermore, although it is impossible for the deityhood to be qualified by the act of taking (*grahaṇa*) through the relation of being its qualifier (*nirūpakatā*), it is possible for the deity to be qualified by the act of taking through the relation of residing in that which is the object of the utterance at the time of taking.

Consequently, even though the deity is an auxiliary to the taking, when there is a requirement for a sacrifice, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) because one merely assumes that the sacrifice enjoined by the *Soma* sentence—which itself requires a deity—is what fulfills that requirement.

As for the word "Soma," although its acquisition is already possible due to the otherwise inexplicable nature of the purificatory injunction (*saṃskāra-vidhi*), it is not contradictory [to include it], as it serves the purpose of restricting the substance to Soma, thereby excluding barley flour (*saktu*).
And how, this being the case, there is a conjunction of the acts of taking and a repetition of the sacrifice, all of this has been explained in the Kaustubha.

As for the purpose: in the case of a modification of the animal sacrifice (*paśuvikāra*), according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the group of eleven portions (*ekādaśāvadānagaṇa*) is not obtained because [the modified sacrifice] has as its archetype (*prakṛti*) only one among the sacrifices of the heart and so forth; however, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is obtained—this is how it should be understood.
And for some, the very non-establishment of unmanifestness [is the case]. // 6 //
Thus ends the sixth section concerning the Animal and Soma Sacrifices.

(B2) (An examination of the connection by way of counter-example with the preceding section: Since it is possible for sentences concerning curd and so forth to enjoin only a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the rite already enjoined by the *agnihotra* sentence, there is no possibility here of those [sentences] being restatements of a composite whole (*samudāyānuvāda*), because the original rite does not exist; nevertheless, in this case, with reference to the sacrificial materials (*dravya*) enjoined by the sentences concerning the animal (*paśu*) and the soma, [the following applies].

Since the injunctions regarding the cutting out (*avadāna*) and other such acts directed toward the heart and other parts would be untenable as injunctions for the preparation (*saṃskāra*) of those parts, an injunction for a ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) necessarily follows;

thus, if the ritual action under discussion exists, let it be a restatement of a collective whole (*samudāyānuvāda*). Indicating this connection by way of a counter-example through the arising of such a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the example: "The animal dedicated to Agni-Soma" (*agnīṣomīyam*).

(An exposition of the grounds for the primacy of the *paśu* sentence, by means of raising and refuting the objection regarding the primacy of the *soma* sentence—just as with the *āghāra* sentence in the preceding section.

In the previous sūtra, because the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgin*) does not exist between the *āghāra* and the *agnihotra*, the rule "that which is more venerable comes first" is not applicable; thus, although the word *āghāra* was placed first simply because it has fewer syllables, here, even though the word *paśu* ends in the suffix *dhyat*, [it is placed first] according to the rule: "In the case of [words used in the sense of] a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or a cause (*hetu*)... [Pāṇini 3.2.126].

In the phrase "of the action" (*kriyāyāḥ*), since the suffix *dhi* is placed last, it is impossible for its being at the end of a compound to act as a restrictive factor; thus, although the word *soma* ought to be placed first in the sūtra due to its primacy and its status as the more venerable term, the word *paśu* is placed first with the intention that it is the more venerable because the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the animal sacrifice is difficult to establish within the systematic treatise that explains the underlying logic, and thus it is the object of greater attention in the exposition of that logic.
Because of the mention of "the first," with that intention in mind, the sentence concerning the animal sacrifice was itself cited prior to the sentence concerning Soma.

Since the first type of injunction is impossible in the *agnīṣomīya* passage—due to the principle that [the heart and other parts] are already occupied by qualities prescribed at their origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa-guṇa*)—they can in no way serve a purpose in the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*).

Although the first type of injunction, which consists of enjoining the pure verbal root-meaning, is possible in the *agnihotra* passage, here, because even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) one must resort to a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*) due to the mention of both substance and deity, it is untenable for this to be an injunction of a ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) since that [first type] cannot be obtained; therefore, it is merely a restatement of a collective whole (*samudāyānuvāda*).
He states the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) with the words: "In that regard" (tatra).

Although it might be argued that, just as in the case of the *Āgneya* injunction, the injunction of a sacrifice is established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the connection between substance and deity in the *Agnīṣomīya* sentence, nevertheless, because the animal prescribed by the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) would be destroyed by the act of cutting off portions (*avadāna*), its status as the means of the sacrifice—directly expressed by the scripture (*śruti*)—would be contradicted. Consequently, it is impossible for the sentences concerning the heart and other organs to enjoin the purification (*saṃskāra*) of the cutting-off by taking the substance of that [animal] as the object.
Furthermore, it is understood from the accusative case-endings that the heart and other organs themselves are what are to be purified.
Furthermore, there can be no possibility of an injunction for the heart and other organs when they are devoid of utility, either past or future;

for, since they are already secured by the animal itself, it is illogical to assume a separate utility for them, just as one does not assume a utility for the flour-meal (saktu) once the animal is secured. Even if such a utility were assumed, the injunction would be redundant, as that utility would already be obtained through extension (atideśa).

Therefore, intending that there is a cognition of an action (*karman*) therein—based on the inference that the portions (*avadāna*) prescribed with reference to the heart and other parts are *saṃskāra* (preparatory acts) and thus means for the sacrifice—the author establishes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words:
"For here... by inference, as in the case of the *pūtīka* [plants]."

(In the case of the *pūtīka* passage, just as in the case of the pressing of *soma*, the assumption of a sacrifice is justified here because of the recognition of the *sānnāyya* offering; the meaning is as follows:

Just as in the injunction "one should press the *pūtīkas," which prescribes the pressing as a refinement of the *pūtīkas," the inference that the *pūtīkas* serve as the means for a sacrifice is established—since this would otherwise be inexplicable without their being the means of a sacrifice—so it is here as well.

Although, in the case of the *pūtīka* plants, since the very act of pressing *soma* is recognized and enjoined as being connected with the *pūtīkas*, and since that [pressing] is observed to be a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the sacrificial substance, one might infer that the *pūtīkas* themselves are the sacrificial substance; nevertheless, here, because the portioning of the *sānnāyya*— which is already established as a purificatory rite for the sacrificial substance— is not recognized [as such], it is impossible to enjoin it with reference to the heart and other organs.
The inference that these [cuttings] are for the purpose of sacrifice is easy to establish;

nevertheless, because here—by the principle of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*)—there is the injunction of a distinct cutting, and because that [cutting], by virtue of its commonality as a cutting of a living being, is understood to have the *sānnāyya* cutting as its archetype (*prakṛti*), it follows by extension (*atideśa*) that they also function as sacrificial substances. Thus, for each individual cutting, regarding the substances to be cut...

In order to establish that a difference in sacrifice must be understood through the assumption of distinct means for accomplishing the sacrifice, the phrase beginning with "originating from animals" (*paśuprabhava*) and so forth was stated.

And on this view, since all [the sacrifices] are referred to by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) occurring in the Agni-Soma sentence as a restatement of a collective whole, the intention is that the deities are enjoined with reference to the sacrifice.
(An introduction to the view that the word *paśu* [animal] refers to the heart by means of secondary indication):

Now, one might object that if both the deity Agni-Soma and the fact of the animal being the material cause (*prakṛti*) were thus enjoined, there would result the fault of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), as well as the impossibility of the word *paśu* being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the patronymic suffix denoting the deity; to this he says: "And the word *paśu*... and so forth.

Because the mantra-verse "of the goat-offering" (*chāgasya haviṣaḥ*) is an auxiliary to the sacrifice of the heart and other parts, the status of the animal as the material substance (*prakṛti*) is obtained from that very source; thus, since the words "heart" and so on are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is no possibility [of a qualified injunction] because only the deity is being enjoined.
And in this way, since there is no qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) in the sentence concerning the animal, there is also simplicity (*lāghava*); such is the meaning.

(Conclusion of the prima facie view by establishing an alternative position: that the sentence concerning Agni-Soma has as its purport the sacrifice itself, which is inferred by means of making known the connection between the deities and the heart and other parts indicated by the word "animal").

Anticipating that it is impossible to infer a sacrifice because the property of residing in the sacrificial substance is not an auxiliary part of the Sānnāyya-offering and thus cannot be obtained through extension (*atideśa*), he states another position: "Or rather... (*athavā*).

Only the portions (avadāna) are enjoined with reference to the heart and other parts; and when there is a need for their application, since the sentence concerning the animal (paśu-vākya) enjoin deities with reference to the heart and other parts indicated by the word "animal" (paśu-pada), a substance and a deity are established.

Consequently, within that very sentence concerning the Agniṣomīya animal, sacrifices are enjoined by postulating a sacrifice—just as in the case of [the injunction] "he pours the libation" (āghārayati)—by postulating an application based on the possibility of a substance and a deity.
The meaning is that the root *ālabhati* (to sacrifice) signifies capability, and thus [the mention of the animal] is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

In this way, both the observation of sequence—namely, "one cuts from the heart first"—and the observation of conjunction—namely, "there are indeed eleven portions of the animal"—become logically consistent.

Otherwise, since there would be the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the heart and other organs within a single sacrifice, those two observations would be untenable; with this intention, he concludes that the word *paśu* (animal) is a restatement of the collection [of organs], stating: "in every respect."

(An examination of the purpose of the *samudāyānuvāda* status of the word *paśu*): And on this view, since the sacrifice is enjoined in the very sentence concerning Agni-Soma—just as in the case of the [text] "he pours the oblation" (*āghārayati*)—the word *ālabhati* lacks the status of a *samudāyānuvāda*. Therefore, it has been stated that the word *paśu* is the *samudāyānuvāda*. Its purpose is as follows: by means of establishing the connection with the deity through each of the heart and other organs individually, without intending their collective unity, a sacrifice is subsequently postulated for each one; thus, the term *ālabhati* functions by way of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
The intention is that there is the accomplishment of the ritual procedure for those sacrifices.

(An exposition of the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa]: that in sentences such as "for Indra and Vāyu," by assuming injunctions for sacrifices, all sacrifices are established; then, by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to all those sacrifices, the sentence "one should sacrifice with soma" enjoins *soma*—just like *vrīhi* rice—as the source material for the stream [of liquid], as in the case of the *graha* vessels.

In the sentences beginning with "for Indra and Vāyu," since the status of Indra, Vāyu, and others as deities is understood from the deity-designating secondary suffix (*taddhita*) in the term *aindravāyavam*, and since that status—which consists in being the intended recipient of the substance being relinquished—is impossible to connect with the act of taking up [the liquid] without a sacrifice, [the term] "for Indra and Vāyu" [refers to the sacrifice]. By means of the taking up, [the substance becomes] "for Indra and Vāyu."

Since the meaning [of "one should perform"] would otherwise be untenable, he states "likewise" (tathā), asserting that because of the connection between the substance and the deity, sacrifices themselves are enjoined by means of the verb "to take" (gṛhṇāti) through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

Now, one might object: even if the general category of substance (*dravyasāmānya*) is understood through the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), since its specific nature is not understood, how can there be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of sacrifice by virtue of its connection to that [substance]? To this, he says: "And the substance... (*dravyaṃ ca*).

Therefore, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*), since the *taddhita* suffix in the word "soma" denotes a liquid substance, it is impossible for the purificatory act called *grahaṇa* (taking up) to be enjoined with reference to that [liquid], while being simultaneously enjoined with reference to the creeper.

Furthermore, because a liquid substance cannot have either a past or a future utility, a displacement of the application (*viniyoga*) is necessary; thus, the injunction is made for a qualified sacrifice with respect to those very [liquids].
The meaning is that the sacrifices are indeed distinct from the forms and qualities of the respective deities being specified.
To the question, "What then is enjoined by the statement *somena yajeta*? he replies: "But in the Soma-sentence... [and so forth].

For this very reason, although in the phrase "he takes with a stream" (*dhārayā gṛhṇāti*) one might assume that by restating the act of taking— which is already implied by the sense— one is merely enjoining the "stream" itself, the stream pertains only to liquid substances; thus, since the qualification [of the sacrifice] is established therein, the view previously stated by the ancients— that Soma is enjoined as the substance for the sacrifices already delimited by the *taddhita* suffix in "Aindravāyava," which denotes the liquid substance used in the stream— is impossible.

The meaning is that, by means of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) in the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma," which serves as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the entire collection [of sacrifices], there is an injunction regarding Soma as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all sacrifices, and not an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
Now, one might object: how can the prescription of an archetype be appropriate there when the Soma juice itself has not yet been obtained?

The phrase "like the injunction regarding rice" (*vrīhividhivat*) is stated in order to dispel the following doubt: that here the *soma* juice is not obtained by virtue of being a substance capable of flowing (*dhārāsamarthadravyatva*), since it could also possibly refer to water and the like; and furthermore, if it were obtained as *soma* juice, the injunction of the archetype (*prakṛti*) would be rendered purposeless.

Therefore, in this case, by means of that illustration, since there is no injunction regarding the material cause (*prakṛti*) through a restatement of the modification (*vikāra*), there is no dependence on obtaining the modified form (*vikṛti*);

thus, when Soma is enjoined here—just like rice—with reference to the sacrifice, it is possible for it to serve as the instrument by way of being the material cause (*prakṛti*), even though the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) already occupies the place, because rice cannot be introduced there. This is the meaning.
(Another way of formulating the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] regarding the statement "one should sacrifice with soma" is as follows:

Alternatively, because the word *dhārā* (stream) is relational and because the verb *gṛhṇāti* (he takes) requires an object, it is connected by way of identity with the very substance of Soma juice— which is the subject under discussion, has been prepared by purificatory rites such as straining (*pavana*), and is contained in the *pūtabhṛt* and *āhavanīya* vessels— insofar as it stands in need of a correlative.

And then, since the injunction regarding the preparation (*saṃskāra*) of *soma* would otherwise be inexplicable—just as in the case of "one should choose the *adhvaryu*"—the status of *soma* as the material cause (*prakṛti*) is also obtained through its application (*viniyoga*).
Thus, he states another position: that the word *soma* here is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) and not a name (*nāmadheya*), by saying "soma."

In the *somavākya*, it is improper to assume the injunction of a distinct, qualified ritual (*karmāntara*) because that would result in excessive complexity (*gaurava*); furthermore, since the *ājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses can appropriately be assigned to the *aindravāyava* and other sacrifices through their indicative marks (*liṅga*), context (*prakaraṇa*), and sequence (*krama*), it is untenable to assume unmentioned optional deities based on context alone, as this would fail to provide the essential form (*rūpa*) of the rite.
Therefore, the word *soma* is the name of the very sacrifices enjoined by the *aindravāyava* and other sentences, according to the principle of "that which is already known" (*tatprakhya-nyāya*).

In this regard, even though there is another name, "Jyotiṣṭoma," that same sacrifice is fivefold; since we observe its usage under other names such as "Paśu" and "Soma," there is no pointlessness [in the designation].

Thus, regarding the two possible interpretations of the word "Soma," in the former view, because the word "Soma" serves as a designator for what is to be enjoined, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is not a collective restatement (*samudāyānuvāda*). In the latter view, however, it is a collective restatement. Therefore, both views are [valid].
Indicating by the word "sarvathā" that [the position] is beyond dispute, he says: "in every respect."
(Regarding the view that *soma* is a name: since the mention of the *saṃkalpa* [resolute intention] is clear, another purpose is investigated.
In both views, the word *yaji* is a restatement (*anuvāda*); because it refers to multiple sacrifices, its absence would mean it refers to only a single sacrifice.
Since this purpose is obvious, it may be set aside. However, when *soma* is a name, purposes such as the mention of the *saṃkalpa* do exist.
Furthermore, he states another purpose based on the absence [of other means]: "And the purpose," as in the case of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
The meaning is that it is like the word "vaiśvadeva" occurring in the sentence beginning with "prācīnapravaṇa."
"By virtue of that."

The meaning is: by virtue of the name "Jyotiṣṭoma," which signifies that which possesses the *stomas* (hymn-forms) consisting of light—such as the *trivṛt* and others—as established through its etymological derivation.
"Of those for whom the stotras and śastras have been recited."

And these [rites] are to be understood as follows: at the morning pressing (prātassavana), there are the offerings to Indra-Agni and the Viśvedevas; at the midday pressing (mādhyandinasavana), the offering to Mahendra; and at the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana), the Marutvatīya and the Āgrayaṇa, Āditya, Sāvitra, and Vaiśvadeva offerings, along with the repetition of a single cup (camasa).
How, then, is the status of the Jyotiṣṭoma established given that there is no repetition of stotras and śastras? To this, he says: "In the final conclusion (siddhānta), however..."

And thus, since sacrifices have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), they are to be combined; because those with different deities require a specific order, the observation of both sequence and combination— such as "the tenth cup is drawn for the Aśvins, he offers it third," and "the Adhvaryu draws these ten cups at the morning pressing"— is logically consistent.

Otherwise, because the sacrifice is a single unit, repetition would be untenable in accordance with the requirement of the subordinate acts of drawing [the cups] (grahaṇa); furthermore, since all the various drawings serve the same purpose—namely, the consecration of the substance used in the sacrifice—they would necessarily fall into an option regarding the deities as well. Anticipating this consequence, he concludes the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ).
(Description of how the sequence of drawing [the cups] and so forth is justified, even though sentences such as "he draws the cup for Indra and Vāyu" have the sacrifice as their primary referent):

Although, even if the sequence and combination of sacrifices were possible under the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)— because the root *grah* (to draw) would figuratively (lakṣaṇayā) enjoin the sacrifices themselves and there would be no separate injunction for the drawing, resulting in no distinction between them and thus making the observed sequence and combination of drawings inexplicable—

nevertheless, this applies to the soma-juice measured in ten handfuls (*muṣṭi*), which has been processed by such refinements as pressing, straining, and being placed in vessels such as the *pūtabhṛt* and *āhavanīya*.

Since the injunction "he offers a small amount" (alpaṃ juhoti) prescribes a purificatory rite called *homa* with reference to a small quantity— just as the injunction "he offers with four portions" (*caturavatta*) prescribes a *homa* with reference to the four-portioned oblation— and since, by way of restating the *homa*, other injunctions such as "he offers with *grahas*" and "he offers with *camasas*" prescribe the *grahas* and *camasas* as instruments (like the *juhū* ladle),

it is impossible for them to be the objects of purification through a *homa* performed with those vessels; therefore, a distinct act of drawing (*grahaṇa*) is necessarily required for each sacrifice, and thus there is no fault.

And here, the number ten regarding the *grahas* (libation cups) is to be understood in this manner: in the eighth section of the *Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa*, within the sub-context of the *bahiṣpavamāna* stotra, it is recorded that "the Adhvaryu draws nine *grahas* at the morning libation; he purifies those very [nine].
Regarding this, in the commentary by the venerable Guru Vidyāraṇya, it is stated: "The *upāṃśu*, the *antaryāma*, the *vāyavya*, and the *aindravāyava*... [and so forth].

Furthermore, the number nine is established by the summary verse composed by the ancient teachers: "Then the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Śukra, the Manthin, and the supreme Tapas; after that, the one named Āgrayaṇa, and the Dhruva is desired as the ninth. It is with reference to this very [set of nine] that the *Śruti* states, "The tenth cup is taken for the Aśvins," thereby declaring the tenth status of the Āśvina cup. Thus, there are ten cups ending with the Āśvina, and their tenth status is determined by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being performed during the morning extraction (*prātaḥsavana*).
It should be known.

By this [it is shown that]— having explained that the ten cups (daśagraha) consist of those ending with the Aindravāyava, Maitrāvaruṇa, Śukra, Manthin, the three Atigrāhyas, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Ukthya, and the Āśvina— the [view] that [the Āśvina cup] possesses the same single property as those others, namely being a "stream-cup" (dhārāgraha), must be disregarded; for it contradicts the statement of the Vedic commentator (*vedabhāṣyakāra*) that the demonstration of such an order of cups applies only to those [preceding ones], and because, even though the Āśvina cup is performed immediately after the Bahiṣpavamāna stotra, its extraction from a stream is nowhere recorded in scripture, and thus it is improper to call it a "stream-cup."

By this, even that which was stated by Somanātha—that there are ten cups (*daśagṛha*) consisting of those ending with the Āśvina cup, excluding the Vāyavya cup and including the Ukthya cup—is refuted.

For this very reason, among ritualists (*yājñika*), there is a well-known consensus that only the Upāṃśu, Antaryāma, Vāyavya, Aindravāyava, Maitrāvaruṇa, Śukra, Manthin, Atigrāhya, Tapa, Ukthya, Marutvatīya, and Dhruva cups constitute the "stream-cups" (*dhārāgraha*);
however, the distinction for Mīmāṃsakas is different. Enough of this elaboration.

(The final conclusion is established by the fact that all [objections] are resolved: in the sentence concerning Agni-Soma, because the word *paśu* would entail figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) if it were taken to mean the heart and other organs, and because prescribing the animal as the material cause (*prakṛti*) would entail a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), there is a prescription of the qualified whole; whereas in the sentence concerning the heart, since no sacrifice is present, there is merely a prescription of a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) with respect to the heart and other organs, while the animal is prescribed as the material cause.)
Demonstrating a common refutation for both modes established by the proponent (pūrvapakṣin), he states the final position (siddhānta): "In the word *paśu*... and so forth.

Since the application of the word "animal" (*paśu*) to the flesh of the heart and other parts does not manifest the state of being an animal, it would result in the word "animal" (*paśu*) being used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) for those parts;

furthermore, if the animal were enjoined as the material substance (*prakṛti*), the deity would also have to be enjoined, which would lead to a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, it is proper that the injunction of the qualified ritual act occurs in the *agnīṣomīya* sentence itself.

The meaning is that in the sentences concerning the cutting off (*avadāna*), since the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) is not heard and the deity is likewise not heard, it is impossible for a sacrifice to be brought to mind; therefore, it is untenable for the mere act of cutting off to imply a sacrifice, as in the case of the touching of the calf (*vatsālambha*). Thus, there is no injunction of a ritual action (*karma-vidhāna*).
What, then, is enjoined by the sentences concerning the heart and other parts?
In response to this inquiry, he says: "By means of the passages concerning the heart and so forth."

He resolves the contradiction with the injunctions for preparatory rites such as slaughter and cutting, which pertain to the animal established by the originative injunction as the means [of sacrifice], in the words: "And of the animal... (paśośca).
(An investigation into the connection with the animal-deity as being the material cause:
"Of the status of being an instrument."
The meaning is that [the animal] is characterized by the accusative case in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) as "the animal" (*paśum*).

For this very reason, the connection of the animal with the deities Agni and Soma occurs precisely through its being the material cause (*prakṛti*) for the heart and other parts; thus, there is no inconsistency in the possessive suffix (*taddhita*) in *agnīṣomīyam* or in its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "animal.

Consequently, just as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for the rice-grains and so forth is understood from the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) itself by implication, and thus the injunction for grinding and so forth is made with reference to them; [so it is here].

Similarly here as well, since the heart and other parts are understood to be the means of accomplishment by the word "animal" (paśu) itself, it is logical that the injunction for the purificatory rites such as the cutting off (avadāna) should be directed toward them; this is the intended meaning.

(An explanation establishing that the re-enactment of the cutting-off (*avadāna*), even though already obtained by extension (*atideśa*), is for the purpose of ensuring the cutting-off of each individual part:

Although the cutting-off—which brings about the middle and the fore-part—is already obtained by extension as a means of consecrating the heart and other organs, since they possess the status of sacrificial material (*havis*) characterized by being the means of sacrifice in the form of things to be offered (*pradeya*), this injunction would be redundant;
nevertheless, it is not untenable to enjoin again, for the purpose of consecrating the heart and other organs, that very same cutting-off which was obtained by extension.

And the purpose of that [injunction] is the establishment of each of those [limbs] as a sacrificial offering (*havis*) individually. Otherwise, although it is understood through the limbs that the animal is a means of accomplishment due to the injunction for its slaughter, since the individual status of the limbs as means of accomplishment is not understood— because it would be untenable for the whole (the animal) to be the means of accomplishment by virtue of residing collectively in all the limbs— [each limb must be established separately].

Since it is established that the members [of the sacrifice] function as means only when combined, and since that [procedure] which was formulated for the purpose of purifying the aggregate is extended by analogy (atideśa) even to the case where they are present individually,

yet it is enjoined here for the purpose of purifying each individual part such as the heart; therefore, just as in the case of the *pūtīka* plants, it is understood that the heart and other parts are each an oblation (*havis*) in their own right, and thus the cutting off of the middle and front portions is accomplished for each one individually.
And thus, by the word *paśu* (animal), which— assisted by the intentionality of being an oblation (*haviṣṭva*) residing solely in the eleven portions (*avadāna*) of the consecrated substance—

prescribes the animal as the source-material for that much alone, one obtains the result of excluding other parts from being the means of sacrifice (*haviṣṭva*), which consists in their exclusion from being the instrument of the sacrifice resulting from the enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*) of the portions. By this reasoning stated in the *Kaustubha*, he dispels the alleged redundancy of the injunction regarding the prescribed portions, [concluding] with "for this very reason."
(Regarding the phrase "The refutation of the *Nyāyasudhā* [on the grounds that] by the statement 'There are eleven portions' the exclusion of other parts is established":

by the word "etcetera" in the phrase "and so forth," the author refers to the fact that the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, having accepted the sentence "There are indeed eleven portions of the animal; one cuts off those twice each" as consisting of two separate sentences—specifically accepting "There are indeed eleven" as a distinct sentence—asserted that this very [sentence] serves the purpose of excluding other parts.)

Since the phrase "those [five]" (*tāni*)— which prescribes their duality by subverting the threefold number resulting from the accomplishment of the five offerings— is capable of establishing syntactic unity with the phrase "eleven indeed" (*ekādaśa vai*) precisely by providing a specific qualification, there is no evidence for treating them as separate sentences by accepting that the latter has exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) as its result;
for if one were to accept that very [phrase] as having exclusion as its result, the futility of the sentences concerning the heart and other parts would be difficult to avoid.
By the words "it is improper," it is indicated that other specific points mentioned by Kaustubha are included.

(Since it will be explained in the tenth book that the sequential combination of the heart and other organs is logically established, and since there is no remainder [of the animal] in the sentence concerning the animal sacrifice, this begins the formal statement of the Siddhānta regarding the sentence concerning Soma):

Therefore, because there is no pointlessness in the injunction for the portions (*avadāna*), even if the sacrifice itself is enjoined in the sentence concerning the animal, one understands from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the heart and other organs being the means of accomplishment that they must be combined as the means; thus, disregarding the fact that the observation of sequential combination will also be explained in the tenth book, [the conclusion follows].

Having considered that in the case of the animal-sentence, nothing remains to be established in the final conclusion (siddhānta), he states the conclusion regarding the Soma-sentence: "In the case of Soma as well."
The meaning is that this applies even in the case of the Soma sacrifice.
The term "burden" (gaurava) is also indicative of the undesirable consequence of resorting to metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).

(An exposition of the author of the *Prakāśa*’s view: that the statement of the Vārttikakāra—that there is either a restatement of the act of drawing [the soma] as already implied by its purpose followed by an injunction of the deities such as Indra-Vāyu alone, or an injunction of the act of drawing qualified by the deity—is merely a bold assertion.

This is the meaning: in the passages "He draws the Upāṃśu" and "He draws the Antaryāma," because the terms *Upāṃśu*, *Antaryāma*, and so forth are names (*nāmadheya*), and because it would be improper for them to be redundant due to the absence of any other thing to be enjoined, [they must be names].

Even in the sentences concerning the Aindravāyava and other cups, since there is an injunction of the connection with a deity by way of restating an already established act of drawing (*grahaṇa*), there arises the fault of sentence-split (*vākyabheda*) if one were to also enjoin a connection with a substance to be refined—namely, the juice qualified by the deity—as the object of the injunction.

If, on the other hand, the act of drawing alone were intended as the subject of the injunction, then that same injunction would apply even to the drawing of any random substance mentioned in the context.
Therefore, if it is qualified as being "Soma-juice," there results an injunction of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*), and thus the injunction of that [qualification] is indeed necessary.

Therefore, even though [the substances] may arise from other sources, by accepting their prior occurrence [in the ritual], these sentences— beginning with "for Indra-Vāyu"— perform the injunction of a qualified grasping for the purpose of consecrating the substance denoted by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Since the distinction between the substances denoted by the suffixes follows from the very principle of "different words" (*śabdāntara*) due to the difference in the meanings of the bases (*prakṛti*), it is not improper that in each respective sentence there is an injunction of that [substance] as qualified,
with reference to that specific substance.

And its purpose is the establishment of the unmanifest nature (*avyaktatva*) of this [sacrifice], for the sake of proving both the distinction between the substance and the meaning of the suffix in the portion pertaining to the deity, and its status as an auxiliary to the act of drawing (*grahaṇa*).

For in the absence of this injunction, since the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* mantras are recited, the deities—being merely auxiliaries to the sacrifice through the wording of their respective mantras, like the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*)—would have only the status of being helpful in the act of drawing.

However, when this direct injunction exists, because the status of being an auxiliary to the drawing is understood, and because the conclusion is reached that they are merely helpful in the sacrifice itself, the *yājyā* and other mantras do not constitute its constituent parts (*kalpaka*). Thus, the unmanifest nature of the sacrifice is established, and [the application of names such as] *Udbhid* and so forth [is secured].
Its status as a modification [of the original substance] is thus obtained.

Regarding the act of taking up (*grahaṇa*), although it is established by implication (*arthataḥ*) as a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭavidhayā*) through its function of purifying the substance, there is the attainment of an independent invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

When the injunctions for taking up require a purpose and no other purpose is possible, there is no fault even if one assumes it to be a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), like the *prayāja* offerings and others.

For this very reason, since there is a distinction based on the quality of the vessels being occupied by their respective deities, and because the injunction, by virtue of its restatement, accepts that the unseen (adṛṣṭa) alone is the motivator, one understands— following the requirement of that motivating unseen factor— that the offerings dedicated to those respective deities must be combined, just like the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings. Consequently, due to the force of the distinction between the substances belonging to different deities, there is also a combination of the materials to be taken.
Since the repetition of the sacrifice is established, the observation of both sequential order and simultaneous combination is also justified.

Nor should it be argued that—because the object of apprehension differs when it is grasped part by part—the practice of apprehension cannot logically occur through differentiation; and since the unification of what has been grasped as distinct does not establish the practice of sacrifice, the observation of the sequential performance and combination (*krama-samuccaya*) regarding that [sacrifice] would be untenable. This is because it is impossible to unify what has been grasped without distinction, and since it is understood that only that which remains in a state of distinction brings about the sacrifice, the practice of sacrifice is necessary, as there can be no means of accomplishing it through what has been grasped with distinction without such practice.
Because that is logically consistent.

(Refutation of the charge of violating the principle of single-syllable unity [ekaprasaratā] regarding the prescription of the qualified deity for the purpose of consecrating the Soma juice, and the establishment of the qualified injunction:

As for the objection that, in this view, the term *aindravāyava* would entail a violation of the principle of single-syllable unity because the substance intended by it lacks the status of being defined by the deity prescribed [in the same sentence]— as in the case of the statement, "He places the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks"— [the answer is as follows:]...

Since it has been admitted by [the opponent] himself that the injunction regarding the placement of bricks qualified by mantras is for the purpose of consecrating the bricks, it is clear from the Kaustubha that, by that same logic, there is no fault here either; thus, [the objection that] "it is improper" is incorrect.
By this, [it is shown that] because of the resulting complexity (gaurava) in a qualified injunction, only the act of taking up [the mantra] itself is enjoined.
Furthermore, the view that the terms *aindravāyava* and so forth are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of deities already established by the wording of the mantras is also refuted;

for, since it would otherwise result in the terms *aindravāyava* etc. being redundant, one must accept a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) whose purpose is to establish these terms as subsidiary elements of the act of drawing (*grahaṇa*).
Therefore, it is logical that the injunction prescribes the very act of drawing as qualified by the deity.
And the detailed account should be consulted in the Kaustubha.
(Refutation of the impossibility of the deity's connection with the act of drawing, and the rejection of the assumption of a sacrifice in the sentence concerning Indra and Vāyu):

He refutes the impossibility of the deity’s connection with the act of drawing [the soma] with the words "if it is possible" (*sambhavati*) and "having become the object of the action" (*karmībhūtā*).
And that word denoting the deity [is connected] by way of the relation of residing in it (tadvṛttitva); this is the meaning.
[The phrase is] "of that which depends on the deity."

The meaning is that since the Soma sacrifice requires a deity, and because the assistance required is obtained through incidental connection (*prasaṅga*) with the deities who are constituent parts of the *grahaṇa* (the act of drawing the soma), the [Soma sacrifice] itself serves as the fulfiller of that requirement.

By this, the following view is refuted: "When there is a requirement for a sacrifice—as in the case of the *Āgneya* injunction—it is logical to postulate a sacrifice only where such a requirement exists, not in another sentence; therefore, it is proper to enjoin the sacrifice within the *grahaṇa* sentences themselves."

In the case of the sentence concerning Agni, because it does not conclude by itself due to the non-mention of human activity, the postulation of a sacrifice there is indeed appropriate. However, in this case, since it concludes through the mention of human activity in the form of "taking" (grahaṇa), and since there is a need for only that which effects the relationship between the substance and the deity already expressed, it is improper to postulate the injunction of an unmentioned sacrifice; for the sacrifice enjoined by direct statement (śruti) in the Soma-sentence itself is capable of effecting that relationship.
"Otherwise than the prescribed method of ritual action."

(Since *soma* is already established either as that which is to be offered or as the material substance, the objection that the word *soma* in the injunction "one should sacrifice with *soma*" (*somena yajeta*) is a name is restated here:
This is the meaning— here, an injunction of *soma* as the object to be offered is not tenable,
because it would result in the futility of the injunction regarding the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
Nor [is it established] as being the material cause (*prakṛti*);
for that is established even by the fact that the injunction regarding the preparation (*saṃskāra*) would otherwise be inexplicable.

In the sentence concerning the drawing (*grahaṇa*), when there is a requirement for the application of the substance denoted by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), which has been prepared by the act of drawing, its status as the offering material (*pradeya*) in the various repetitions of the respective sacrifices—known through the fact that the connection with the deity would otherwise be inexplicable—is understood.
The postulation of a specific application (*viniyoga*) is not untenable.

Since a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix denoting the meaning of a general term requires something that determines its reference to a particular substance, it is established—by way of proximity—that its object is the liquid substances ascertained through the sentence.
In that context, there is an injunction regarding the mere pouring (*dhārā*), by way of restating the specific vessels obtained from their respective sentences.

If one were to pour [the liquid] with a thick stream into small vessels, it would spill even outside the vessel; therefore, because the quality of minuteness (*aṇutva*) would result, the injunction of minuteness is not established.

Furthermore, since the stream requires a correlate and the verb "to take" (*gṛhṇāti*) requires an object, it is impossible for them to imply an independent correlate such as water—as they might in the case of the "upper half" and so forth.

Consequently, it is established that the scope of the injunction concerns liquid substances derived from Soma, as determined by the sentence "He purifies the Soma" (*somaṃ pāvayati*) and others which have the Soma under discussion as their material cause.

In the purificatory statement (*pāvanavākya*), since it is impossible for the word *soma* to refer to the creeper itself, it refers—by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—to the juice associated with the creeper. And thus, because the injunction regarding the preparation (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) would otherwise be inexplicable, the attainment of the status of being the material source (*prakṛtitva*) for the *soma* is also not untenable.
By this [it is shown that] even though there is proximity, because the stream (*dhārā*) is common to all liquid substances, the restriction to the subject matter of *soma*-juice [is established].
The statement in the *Śāstradīpikā* that "in the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there is no attainment of Soma" is refuted. Thus [it is said].

(An explanation of how the injunction is established as having the result of excluding *saktu*, since even *saktu* would otherwise be obtained due to the impossibility of the performance-ritual being otherwise accomplished):
"In order to exclude *saktu*."

The meaning is as follows: since the injunction regarding the preparation (*saṃskāra*) would otherwise be inexplicable, one might assume that barley flour (*saktu*), like Soma, is also enjoined for use; thus, because both would apply as options, the injunction of Soma would serve the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) intended to exclude the barley flour that was only optionally available.

Consequently, because the Soma is enjoined from the very outset (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), it is impossible to assume a use for the barley flour there through the inexplicability of the preparation injunction; therefore, no contingency of optionality arises.
And this is how it is "in such a case."
"In the Siddhānta" means "given that there is oneness of the sacrifice";
[this is explained] in the Kaustubha itself.
This has been explained previously.
(Somavākyasiddhāntaprayojanam) [The purpose of the Soma-sentence doctrine]: "And in the case of the Soma [sacrifice]."

Furthermore, because the injunctions regarding the Aindravāyava cup would result in the verbal formulation "one should sacrifice with the Aindravāyava" (aindravāyavena yajeta) within the prescription of the sacrifice, the Jyotiṣṭoma itself possesses a "manifest injunction" (vyaktacodana) characterized by having its own specific substance and deity prescribed for its purpose; since it lacks the character of an "unmanifest injunction" (avyaktacodanā) found in the Ekāhas, Ahīnas, and Satras, there is no application of its procedural details (vidhyanta).

However, even though a substance is heard in the injunction of the sacrifice by means of the sentence regarding Soma, because the Jyotiṣṭoma lacks a deity prescribed for its own sake and is thus an "unmanifest" (avyakta) injunction, the extension of the Jyotiṣṭoma’s ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) to the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) and others occurs due to their similarity to it;
this is the purpose that will be stated in the eighth section (*adhikaraṇa*), beginning with the sūtra *avyaktastu somasya*. This is the meaning.

As for what is stated in the *Vārtika*: "When there is a difference of acts, [otherwise] there is an option regarding a single act; for there is no division because of the unity of the injunction"—according to the principle of the eighth section (*adhikaraṇa*), since the details of the procedure (*vidhyanta*) of a single sacrifice enjoined by the sentences concerning the Aindravāyava and other cups are extended by way of option to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the properties of one [set] should be performed optionally, and the sacrifices should be performed once; this is another purpose stated [by the author], namely that when the act is one, it should be as in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

And this is indicated by the word "eva" (only), as it is not tenable because there is no evidence for the application of either the *upāṃśuyāja*— by virtue of similarity in the specific feature of having an unmentioned deity in the scriptural statement— or the application of any one of the *aindravāyava* sacrifices in the *ekāha* and other rites; consequently, the undesired result would follow that the ritual properties (*dharma*) could not be applied through option.
For this very reason, in the Kaustubha, it is stated that in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) pertaining to the Upāṃśuyāja is the intended purpose.
Thus ends the sixth section concerning the Animal and Soma sacrifices.
(B1) (7. The Legal Topic //)
Because they reside separately.

In passages such as, “He offers three oblations with the mantra ‘O gods, honor him who honors’,” and “He performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings,” a number other than unity does not directly cause the cognition of a difference in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), because that number is pervaded by a difference residing in its own locus (the sacrifice) which has as its counter-correlate the same locus; for it is not perceived that the productive operation is the locus of that stated number.
Nor does it indicate a difference in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*);

because that [action] is already determined by the number one previously cognized, a connection with another number is untenable— just as in the cases of "he performs eleven *prayāja*s" and "he offers the *agnihotra* consisting of the *virāṭ*"— and thus, since this number is understood to refer to repetition (*abhyāsa*), there is no distinct action (*akarmāntaratva*).
When [the number] is obtained from the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), there is no exclusion of other numbers here.
For that [number] is not expressed by the *tiṅ* itself, since it resides in the agent (*kartṛ*).

Nor should it be argued that—because an unqualified [agent] cannot logically enter into syntactic relation (*anvaya*), and because there is no reason to bypass the first [option]—one must infer the number one in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
Since the absence of a cause is unestablished when the number [of recitations] is heard, inference does not apply.
For this very reason, in the case of the eleven *prayāja* offerings, wherever inference applies in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is the scope for repetition (*abhyāsa*).

Nor does it follow that, in this way, the inference of oneness would fail to apply even in the case of the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) regarding the attainment of the *virāj* and so forth.

In such cases, because it is impossible for an inference that has already functioned previously to be sublated by the subsequent hearing of a number—since this would result in the perception of that number as being the object of repetition (abhyāsa) for the sake of maintaining the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by its own source, the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*)—it is logical, in the present instance, that the inference occurring after the verbal cognition is obstructed, since the number is perceived even before the verbal cognition, just like the other constituent meanings. This is explained in detail in the *Kaustubha*.
Therefore, it is established that a number prescribed as coreferential with the action mentioned in the originative injunction serves to differentiate the actions.
The distinction in the mode of cultivation (bhāvanā), however, arises solely from the difference in words.

As for the purpose: just as with the mantra for sprinkling the altar (vediprokṣaṇa), according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) the mantra is recited once, whereas according to the established conclusion (siddhānta) it is repeated.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, has conducted an investigation into whether there is a difference or non-difference of sacrifices in the sentence, "One should sacrifice seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati.
In this regard, although the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) denotes a specific substance qualified by its deity-status,
and although the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation occurs within the word *prājāpatya* itself;

Nevertheless, it is undisputed that the number expressed by the subsequent case-ending (vibhakti) is construed with the qualificand (viśeṣya) alone within the meaning of the base (prakṛti), and not with the qualified entity (viśiṣṭa);
for such is the established linguistic usage (vyutpatti) in cases such as "two" or "three.
Furthermore, even that [construal] does not occur after the deity-hood (devatātva) has been construed with the substance (dravya).

That being the case, since the substance related to the deity-status is not understood as a collective whole, the relation to it is perceived only as residing in each individual animal, delimited by the property of "animal-ness" (paśutva). Consequently, because plurality is understood, there would arise the cumbersome assumption of multiple sacrifices due to the multiplicity of relations.
Therefore, for the sake of parsimony (lāghava), the connection with number occurs prior to the connection with deity-status.
For in that case, since there is a single connection with the deity-status delimited by plurality, there is parsimony through the assumption of only a single sacrifice.

Nor can the number [of animals] be construed after the deity has already been construed, on the grounds of conforming to the singularity of the group of eleven cuttings (avadāna) produced from a single animal as obtained in the archetype (prakṛti);

for the singularity residing in the animal is sublated by the directly stated number seventeen, and the singularity of the group of cuttings is not extended here because it was merely implied in the archetype.
Therefore, since there is no evidence for a difference in the connection with the deities, there is no difference in the sacrifice.

Or, even if there were a difference in the relationship due to the deity’s connection occurring prior to the connection with plurality—on account of the direct scriptural statement (śruti) of a common designation—nevertheless, for the sake of parsimony (lāghava), there is oneness of sacrifice.

For just as in the established conclusion (siddhānta) multiple sacrifices are accomplished by a single performance, so too in my view multiple connections with deities are accomplished by a single sacrifice. This being the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa): [the reply is] that because the status of being a deity is more internal (antaraṅga) due to the direct scriptural statement of a common designation, it is connected first, prior to the connection with number.

Furthermore, since each individual animal possesses its own locus of ownership (*svatva*), the status of being an oblation (*haviṣṭva*)— consisting of the performance of an act conducive to the destruction of that ownership—

is resident in each one individually; therefore, in accordance with the Smṛti rule beginning with "of the hymns and the oblations" (*sūktahaviṣoḥ*), it is appropriate that the connection with the deity occurs precisely as delimited by the nature of the animal (*paśutva*), which is the delimiting factor for the status of being an oblation.

And therefore, since the counter-correlate (pratisambandhin) is precisely that which is not delimited by plurality, the distinction between counter-correlates is perceived because the delimiter of the counter-correlate-ship resides in each individual instance. By means of that distinction, the distinction between the relations is established.
Nor does the unity of the sacrifice follow even when there is a distinction between the relations;

for while it is possible in both ways—whether the relations are one or many—the injunction regarding the acquisition of the singularity of the animal (*paśvekatāprāpti*) is stronger as a scriptural authority (*śāstra*), and thus serves as the restrictive factor on account of its parsimony (*lāghava*).
Therefore, it is established that in all cases, the distinction between sacrifices and the distinction between productive operations (bhāvanā) follow precisely from that [distinction].
The practical application is as follows: if there is unity of sacrifice, then even if one animal is forgotten, since the sacrifice has already been performed, there is no need to perform it again;
however, according to the final conclusion (siddhānta), such repetition is required. // 7 //
Thus ends the seventh section concerning the classification of actions performed according to number.

(B2) [The determination of the connection with the chapter, the connection as a counter-example with the section on repetition (*abhyāsa*), and the connection through the relationship of the dependent and the supported]: The connection with the chapter arises from the consideration of the differentiation of rituals (*karmabheda*) by means of number.

Likewise, regarding the principle established in the section on the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*), which proceeds for the purpose of refuting the differentiation of rituals already established in the section on repetition (*abhyāsādhikaraṇa*) through the fact of repetition; [the present section is connected to it].
When the [view that there is] a separate sacrifice (*upāṃśuyāja*) has been refuted by the first three sections— beginning with "It should be like the *paurṇamāsī* [sacrifice]"— then,

because the consideration regarding the restatement of a collection (*samudāyānuvāda*), which serves as a refutation of the distinction based on repetition, is brought to mind through the section on the *paurṇamāsī*, and because the consideration regarding repetition as a refutation of the restatement of a collection is thus present in the mind, it is logical that repetition possesses the power to differentiate [actions], since it is heard more than once.

In the present case, however, since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises from the fact that hearing [the injunction] only once does not constitute a differentiator of ritual acts, there is a connection by way of a counter-example with the section concerning repetition (*abhyāsādhikaraṇa*).

Likewise, just as the sequence and combination [of rites] are possible through repetition even when the *Soma* sacrifice is one, so too the number three and so forth can be accounted for by repetition and thus does not differentiate [the acts];
setting aside this immediate connection because it is obvious, the author proceeds by formulating the prima facie view based on the reliance upon the immediately preceding discussion of repetition.
He states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) itself, preceded by examples of the differentiation of ritual acts according to number, beginning with the words "Thou art the Āmana."
(The explanation of *āmanamasi*, and the explanation of the phrase *dvādaśa dvādaśāni juhoti* regarding the meaning of the word *ādi*):
This is recorded as having been taught following the introductory statement: “One desiring a village should offer the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice dedicated to the Viśvedevas.”
By the phrase "and so forth," there is an inclusion of such scriptural injunctions as, "He offers twelve by twelves," following the performance of the *vasordhārā* oblation into the fire.

Here, the meaning is that one offers twelve such sets of twelve oblations, each consisting of a single offering made with the twelve mantras beginning with "May strength be mine, may procreation be mine.
This will be examined in detail in the twelfth [chapter].
And thus, the sense is that he performs it in such a way that one hundred and forty-four oblations are accomplished.
(The number does not differentiate the bhāvanā that does not have it as its own substrate. With this in mind—

that although the number expressed by the word "three" (*tisraḥ*) is connected with the *bhāvanā* which serves as the primary qualificand, it cannot be understood as differentiating a *bhāvanā* that does not have it as its substrate because it is taken as referring to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)— given that the word "oblation" (*āhuti*) is seen to be in grammatical apposition with it, and because [the number] relies upon that [root-meaning] through the relation of having that [root-meaning] as its substrate— [the author] says:
Regarding the phrase "of that":
it refers to the unity previously cognized.

(Since it is impossible for the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) to appear without being delimited, and since the primary number one serves as its delimiter, there is no differentiation of the meaning of the verbal root.
Although the singularity expressed by the verb suffix in *juhoti* is understood as residing in the agent and not as residing in the meaning of the verbal root;

nevertheless, because it is untenable for the undelimited meaning of the verbal root to be connected with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), there arises a requirement for a number that serves as its delimiter.
The meaning is that, because there is no reason for skipping the first [instance], the evidence for the number one residing in the meaning of the verbal root is untenable;
thus [the conclusion is] "eleven."

The meaning is as follows: just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings, where the number five is already established, and in the *agnihotra*, where the number one is established, the mentioned numbers eleven and ten refer to the repetition of the performance and do not cause a division of the ritual act (*karmabheda*),
so it is here as well.

(The established conclusion is that because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of the verbal root—as in "three oblations" (*tisra āhutīḥ*)—there is the cognition that [the number] resides in that [root-meaning], and since the number one is not sublated, there is a difference of ritual acts.

Because of the coreferentiality in the phrase "three oblations," it is logical that [the number] resides in the meaning of the verbal root, and thus it serves precisely as a differentiator of the ritual acts.

In the case of the *prayāja* offerings, however, since their number is already determined at the time of their origin by their individual oneness or by the fivefold number qualified by accumulation, the heard number eleven cannot sublate the inferred number; for, being otherwise inexplicable, it lacks any other recourse.

In the case of the primary meaning, however, as soon as one begins to infer a number for the meaning of the verbal root, that inference has no scope, because the requirement is satisfied by a number directly heard in the text.

Furthermore, since there is no mention of a number [other than one], unity must be assumed. For when a plurality (three) is heard here, it is not the case that [unity] exists; rather, it is logical that the number explicitly heard is itself the delimiter of the root-meaning. Thus, intending to show that this is merely an obstruction to inference, he states the established conclusion:
"Not here."
When the number is heard in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is no inference of another number;
when it is not heard, there is such an inference.
Furthermore, even an inferred number is not sublated by a number taught in the originative injunction (*utpannaśiṣṭa*).
Such is the detailed examination of the Kaustubha; thus ends the section on the Kaustubha.

Where a number is heard in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), because the number heard there connects with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) even before the operation of inference, it necessarily requires a connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) to fulfill that requirement; thus, since the expectancy is satisfied by that very [number], there is no room for the subsequent inference of another number.
However, where that [number] is not heard in the originative statement (*utpattivākya*),

because the subsequent statement— functioning as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what has already been produced— prescribes the number and thus depends upon the former by virtue of its subsequent operation,
there is no defect whatsoever in the inference of the delimiting number at the time of determining the meaning of one's own sentence within that originative statement.

Precisely because it is that upon which others depend (*upajīvyatva*), there is no sublation (*bādha*) of what was previously cognized—even by a subsequent scriptural statement (*śruta*) that operates at a later time—despite the latter being weaker.
For there is no lack of recourse (*agatikātva*) for a rule taught [subsequently] once it has arisen;
this is because its validity is established even through the medium of repetition (*abhyāsa*).

In the present case, however, there is a disparity: since the number heard in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) is understood as connected to the injunction (*vidhi*) through its connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) even before the number [of the subsequent sentence] is inferred—and because there is no subsequent occurrence that would obstruct such inference—it is logical that it functions as a differentiator. For this very reason, even in cases where the number contained in the originative injunction does not connect with the injunction due to the resulting complexity of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), [the same principle applies].

In that context, since the singular number functions to indicate oneness through its connection with the occurrence of the sacrifice dedicated to the deity residing in itself—acting as a restatement of the deity obtained from the wording of the mantra—it connects precisely with the sacrifice dedicated to that deity indicated by the nominal stem. Thus, because the literal meaning (the singular number) lacks connection with the injunction, it does not differentiate the meaning of the verbal root, as in the case of "He sacrifices the *samidhs*" (*samidho yajati*) and so forth; this is the meaning, as explained in detail in the *Kaustubha*.

(An exposition on how the number of the predicate serves as a differentiator of the action when it is in grammatical apposition with the object, and does not so differentiate it in its absence): "In grammatical apposition with the object" (*karmasamānādhikaraṇa*).

For this very reason—namely, precisely because of the absence of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the object (*karman*)—in such cases as "he sprinkles the altar three times" (*na trir vediṃ prokṣati*), the word [three] functions as a differentiator of the action (*karmabheda*). The meaning is that the word *triḥ* ends in the suffix *suc*, which denotes a number pertaining to repetition (*abhyāsa*), and thus it expresses a number belonging to a repeated occurrence.

(Regarding the distinction between meditative cultivations (*bhāvanā*), it is the "differentiation by means of another word" (*śabdāntara*) as stated by the Venerable Pāda that is intended here, and not that mentioned in the root-text; furthermore,
in the case of the sentences concerning the *aindravāyava* offerings and so forth, there is another [type of differentiation] as explained in the Kaustubha— such is the analysis.)

Since it may be asked how there can be a difference in the efficient force (bhāvanā) even when the number serves to differentiate the meaning of the verbal root, he says: "But the difference in the efficient force... and so forth.

Although a difference in the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) cannot arise from the principle of "different words" (*śabdāntara*) as mixed with the principle of "subordinate elements" (*guṇanyāya*)— on the grounds that when the meaning of a verbal root expressed by the same word is already occupied, the meaning of a verbal root expressed by another word cannot serve as its qualifier—

nor can it arise from the nature of "different words" as stated in the root text (which defines it as a verbal form derived from non-synonymous roots), because a verbal form (*ākhyāta*) is produced from synonymous roots as well.

Nevertheless, because there is a distinction between each specific *homatva* (the nature of being a sacrifice) which delimits the effect, there is likewise a distinctness (*vaijātya*) even within the effort (*yatnatva*) that delimits the cause; this distinction is indicated by the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "only thus," as it is stated in our own text and in other passages such as the *Śabdāntara*.

Furthermore, although the various *bhāvanās* (efficient forces) are distinct, since they are perceived simultaneously through the employment of a single word, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because the definition of a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*)—which consists in the absence of multiple primary qualificands that would otherwise be objects of separate cognitions—is possible here.

By this [same reasoning]—just as there is oneness of the deity qualified by multiple Agni-Soma pairs conveyed by a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*), so too let there be oneness of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) qualified by multiple oblations conveyed by a single verbal root (*dhātu*). For where the instrumentality of actions produced independently is heard in the sentence stating the result, even if there is no evidence for a difference among those instrumentalities, the logic of "distinct words" (*śabdāntara-nyāya*) does not apply; because that logic—which holds that where actions are distinct at the very moment of their production, a difference in instrumentalities is impossible without a difference in the productive urge—is not operative here. Thus it is also [said].
This is rejected;
the sense is that the logic of the "other words" (*śabdāntara*) as stated by us remains entirely intact.
Although the logic of the "other words" as stated by the Venerable Master (*pūjyapāda*) is likewise non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*).

In cases such as *aindravāyava*, where a difference in the substance denoted by the suffix follows from a difference in the meaning of the stem—as established in various places in the Vārttikas and in the Kaustubha by the principle of "different words" (*śabdāntara*)—such [number] is impossible. For this very reason, when the meaning of the suffix is already occupied by the meaning of a single stem, it is illogical for another stem to enter therein; thus, it is precisely the "different word" (*śabdāntara*), conflated with the principle of form and quality, that serves as the differentiator. Nevertheless, since according to the aforementioned method number cannot function as a differentiator of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) in its own context, the "different word" as a cause for the differentiation of the *bhāvanā* must be understood exactly as stated by the venerable teacher (Pārthasārathi Miśra).
Let there be some other purpose for the distinction between [the suffixes] *devatātva* and so forth;
however, if one insists on their uniformity, then they are simply different words (*śabdāntara*) whose meanings consist in distinct bases (*prakṛti*).

It should be inferred that this [difference] makes known the distinction in the meaning of the suffix in some cases by making known a difference in the delimitors of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), and in other cases by making known a distinction created by its own internal restriction. Thus it should be understood.
(An examination of the distinction between number and quality, followed by an examination of the independent authority of number:

Nor should it be argued that "number is not an independent means of knowledge, because it is included within quality itself due to the commonality of being non-eternal in a single action. This must not be said.

Even though there is a commonality in the fact that [the number] does not enter into the production [of the action], the number belonging to the production serves only to indicate the distinction of that very action whose production is established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For in the case of "three oblations," the determination that the focus is on the production is made through "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*) and other such criteria;
the number has no operative function there.
However, it is merely a matter of understanding multiplicity.

Even though a quality mentioned in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*)—such as that belonging to the *Āgneya* sacrifice—is a differentiator, a quality mentioned in the injunction concerning the already-established form (*utpannavākya*) does not apply there; thus, there is a disparity, insofar as the former brings about the cognition of difference by way of producing an action qualified by itself.
Therefore, it is logical that number constitutes a distinct means of valid cognition.
(The purpose of the prima facie and final positions; the non-contradiction of the purpose stated by the author of the *Prakāśa*; and the refutation of his alternative views.)
It is like the mantra for sprinkling the altar.

Regarding the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) enjoined by the rule "he sprinkles the altar three times," although there is an injunction for the repetition of that single act three times, because the action itself is one, and since there is no contradiction in the time-limit of the mantra—beginning with the start of the action and ending with its completion—being recited only once, the mantra "Thou art the altar; for the sacrificial grass, Svāhā! should be employed only once; this will be explained in the final section of the eleventh book (*Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*).

Similarly here as well, because the ritual action (*karman*) is a single unit, even though it is performed three times, the mantra *āmanamasyāmanasya* is used only once according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

However, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since the three mantras are auxiliary to the three actions respectively, there is a repetition by reciting each individual mantra for each respective action.
Although this purpose was stated by the authors of the *Prakāśa*, it should be understood to apply only in cases where a single mantra is enjoined for such [repeated] actions.

In the context of the *āmana-homas*, where the injunction states, "He offers three oblations with the words ‘āmanamasyāmanasya devāḥ’," there is the application of the three mantras beginning with the pratīka "āmanamasyāmanasya": namely, "āmanamasyāmanasya devā ye sajātāssamanasaḥ," "āmanamasyāmanasya devā ye kumārāssamanasaḥ," and "āmanamasyāmanasya yāḥ striyaḥ samanasaḥ. In that case, regarding the subordinate elements (*guṇas*)...

And according to the maxim "and because it is for the sake of another," since there is no evidence for the view of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the mantra] is subordinate to the repetition (*abhyāsa*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) among the three mantras as being subordinate to a single ritual act;
whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the purpose stated is that the three mantras are subordinate to the three acts.

Nevertheless, even when there is an option (*vikalpa*), since only a single mantra is obtained, its application is indeed just once; thus, the accomplishment of the stated purpose is entirely complete.

As for their mention of an option, that is set aside by the Venerable Teacher (*pūjyapāda*) because, although the ritual action (*karman*) is one, the three mantras included within the *itikaraṇa* are understood to be used in conjunction (*samuccaya*). Thus, [the mention of an option] is deemed appropriate [only in that specific context].

(Regarding the application of the particle *iti*, even in the final conclusion [siddhānta], the determination that each of the three mantras is an auxiliary to one respective ritual act is as follows:
If it is asked, "How is it then that, according to the final conclusion, the entire [set of mantras] is not the means for accomplishing each individual ritual act?
it is replied:

For, in the view that there are three separate rites, since each of the three mantras is established as an individual mantra, and because of the statement, "The beginning of the rite should be joined with the end of the mantra," which is supported by the principle of equal number,
it follows that each mantra is an auxiliary to each respective rite. Nevertheless,
since the conjunction understood from the particle *iti* can also be explained as intending the conjunction of the three rites, there is no defect whatsoever.

For this very reason, the venerable teacher will explain in the eleventh [chapter] that the meaningfulness of the statement, "The beginning of the ritual act is with the end of the mantra," is for the sake of establishing repetition (*āvṛtti*) regarding precisely such a subject.
