Although in the *Saṃhitā* there is one mantra beginning with, "O gods who are of a pleasing mind, the youths who are of one mind, those who are great... and another beginning with, "O gods who are of a pleasing mind, the women who are of one mind... and so forth; [nevertheless, the rule applies].
Only two mantras are traditionally handed down;

nevertheless, by relying on the division of words in the phrase *sajātāḥ kumārāḥ*, one should understand there to be three mantras: by supplying *samanasaḥ* after *sajātāḥ* and by supplying *āmanamasyāmanasya* before *kumārāḥ*.
And another purpose should be sought in the Kaustubha.
(The author of the Bhāṣya’s presentation of a different example for the investigation into difference and non-difference, setting aside the example shown by the author of the Vṛtti:

The author of the Bhāṣya indicates with the word *tu* that this example, although presented by the author of the Vṛtti, is improper because the distinction of the action based on number through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the object is so evident that no prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) could arise; therefore, with that intention, he provides another example.
Difference and non-difference have been examined; he shows that examination with the words: "But by the author of the Bhāṣya..."
(Analysis of the base, suffix, and their respective meanings in the word *prājāpatyān*):

Regarding the word *prājāpatyān*, the actual state of affairs is as follows: by the nominal base (*prakṛti*) "Prajāpati" [is expressed]; by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), a substance qualified by that deity—namely, the animal—is expressed; by the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*), instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is indicated through indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and by the plural number (*bahuvacana*), plurality is expressed. This is the established reality.
And the word *paśu* serves to indicate the intended meaning of a specific substance (*dravya*).

In that case, although plurality (*bahutva*) is connected to both words in the pair by way of the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the instrumentality [of the sacrifice], its subsequent connection is only with the substance.

This being the case, since the formation of a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) is necessary for the connection of the plurality denoted by the plural suffix, why indeed would this *ekaśeṣa* be formed of those words ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*)?

Alternatively, does the application of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) occur after the formation of the *ekaśeṣa*? For the plurality of the meaning of the suffix is directly perceived, and since that plurality necessitates the *ekaśeṣa*, it would not apply to the base form (*prakṛti*). This is stated in the Vārttika in accordance with the connection of the plurality heard after the secondary suffix.

The author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, disregarding the view that the suffix alone (*pratyaya*) appears [in the compound], has rejected the possibility of a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of the suffixes alone because such usage is impossible; furthermore, since even a *taddhita* suffix denotes a substance qualified by a deity, if there were a *ekaśeṣa* of only that [suffix], then—even though it refers to the qualified entity—the plurality would have to attach to the meaning of the *taddhita* itself. Consequently, due to the difference in the connection between the substance and the deity, a difference in the sacrifices (*yāga*) would result, which would lead to the impossibility of the opponent's prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) arising. Therefore, he set aside the view of the suffix alone.

Because a pronoun functions to denote the meaning of all [the preceding nouns], and because a pronoun refers back to the animals mentioned in proximity, the pronoun itself—through the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder)—is understood as "of these" (*teṣām*) by conforming to the plural animal-word "of this one, of this one, of this one. Thus, Prajāpati is the deity of these [offerings] because the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) arises in the sense that "Prajāpati is the deity of these," which are delimited by the number of plurality; and since the subsequent plural ending is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), [it applies] to many.
The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) has been established that there is a unity of action based on the connection of the animals with a single deity; however, [the author],

indicating that this is untenable because there is no evidence for assuming an unmentioned *sarvanāma* (pronoun) or *ekaśeṣa* (grammatical retention), and because— even though the *taddhita* suffix denotes a qualified entity— the plurality can properly be construed with the substantive itself according to the method to be explained, thus making the emergence of the prima facie view possible, [proceeds as follows].

Accepting precisely that [explanation] of the *taddhita* suffix and the *ekaśeṣa* compound as shown by Pārthasārathi, he states the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa): "In that regard, even though... and so forth.
(An examination of the *ekaśeṣa* [retention of one] for all secondary suffixes):

Although it was stated that "even if... and so forth in order to avoid the impossibility of an *ekaśeṣa* of suffixes—since the employment of a suffix alone is impossible—the three occurrences of the suffix *yañ* would result from the rule "from *garga* and others, *yañ*" when the meaning is "the descendants of Garga. In that case, just as...
Just as Garga stated that because the aggregate "u ya ya" ends in a secondary derivative suffix (taddhita), it is a nominal stem (prātipadika), and thus when the first case ending follows it,

a single-remainder formation (ekaśeṣa) occurs— as taught in the Mahābhāṣya— so too here, in accordance with the plural number, there is a single-remainder formation of "Prajāpati u ya ya ya. Consequently, in the sense of "Prajāpati is the deity of these," the secondary derivative suffix is applied afterwards.
The meaning is that one should utter "prājāpatya" seventeen times, and then form a *taddhita* derivative followed by a *ekaśeṣa* compound.

(An exposition of the connection of substance and number prior to the connection with the deity, based on the contradiction with the logical rule that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base):

And thus, since it is possible both ways—either the connection of plurality with the substance denoted by the suffix through the *ekaśeṣa* [formation] occurs after the connection with the deity, or even before it—one must state the determining factor. To do so, he first establishes its connection with the bare substantive, [beginning] with the words "tathāpi" ("nevertheless").
It is exactly so because of the derivation [of the term].

Although, because suffixes denote their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the base, the connection of plurality would necessarily occur only with the substance—the meaning of the base—qualified by the status of being a deity residing in Prajāpati, making the resulting distinction between sacrifices (yāgabheda) introduced by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* unavoidable;
nevertheless, the meaning of the suffix, in the form of number, must indeed be connected with the qualificand (viśeṣya) which is the meaning of the base.
Otherwise, in cases such as "two" or "three," if the number were connected with that which is qualified by duality and so on, there would result the perception of four or nine [entities].

Therefore, just as in that case [of the nominal suffix] there is agreement with the qualificand alone, so too here, even though the meaning of the taddhita-suffix is the qualified entity, it is undisputed that number agrees with the qualificand alone; this is the meaning.
[The phrase] "because of the cognition of its relation" [is used].
(An examination of the sublation of the singularity of the original animal by the seventeen [animals] heard in the text, even under the view that number applies to the substance:

Now, even if there is simplicity [of the rule], if doubt remains, let the determination be made from the extended application (*atideśa*), which functions like a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*);
for that [extended application] brings forward from the archetype a single group of eleven cuttings produced from a single animal.

In the injunction "one should immolate the animal at the archetype sacrifice" (*prakṛti*), the singularity residing in the animal—which serves as the archetype for the heart and other organs—is also intended to be expressed. Consequently, because only a single set of cuttings (*avadāna-gaṇa*) constitutes a subordinate element, and because the unity of the sacrifice results in only one such set being obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) from the *savanīya* sacrifice, it would be impossible for seventeen animals to serve as the archetypes. As for the point raised in the *Śāstradīpikā*—where, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), although the unity of the eleven-fold set of cuttings is obtained by virtue of this being a modification (*vikāra*) of the *ekādaśinī* group, a conflict with the injunctive force (*codaka*) is pointed out in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that remains as stated.

The principle from the eighth [book], namely "its application would occur in groups," although it establishes that the *ekādaśinī* is a modification (*vikāra*) of the group-status when there is a plurality of sacrifices,

must be disregarded; for in the case of a single sacrifice, that principle does not apply, and the *Vārttika* has stated that, due to the commonality of the time of the *sutyā*, it is simply a modification of the *savanīya* like the *ekādaśinī*.

As for the argument supported by Somanātha—that because the similarity of being connected to a group of animals to be touched at a single time (*ekakālālambhanīyagaṇasaṃbandhitva*) outweighs the similarity of having the same time of slaughter (*sutyākālatvasāmya*), this [rite] is a modification of the *ekādaśinī*—that is incorrect.

Even in comparison with that, since the internal similarity consisting in being a single sacrifice (*ekayāgatva*), which presents itself more quickly, is greater, it follows that this is actually a modification of the *savanīya*.
Furthermore, since the *ekādaśinī* is not an independent rite but is connected to a group [of sacrifices], its status as a modification [of the *savanīya*] is established in the final Siddhānta.

Since this [the status of being a "group"] is not admitted even in the case of a single sacrifice included within that [set], it is improper—and thus to be disregarded—that the state of being a group exists through the relation of pervasion (*paryāpti*) despite the presence of a plurality of animals, because the connection with a "group of animals" would otherwise be untenable.

Furthermore, although the directly taught (*aupadeśikī*) number of animals might sublate the extended (*ātideśikī*) number, nevertheless, because the singularity of the heart and other organs pertains to a different domain, there is no sublation; thus, the impossibility of the singularity of the heart and other organs serving as the seventeen-fold archetype remains exactly as it was.

However, in the case of a distinction between sacrifices (*yāgabhed*), since there is a distinct extension (*atideśa*) for each sacrifice, that many groups [of animals] are obtained; thus, it is logical for that many to serve as the archetypes (*prakṛti*) for the animal offerings.

Therefore, since a definitive conclusion is possible through extension itself—which stands in the place of a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*)—the connection of the number "many" occurs only with the substance (*dravya*) in its qualified form after the connection with the deity has already taken place. With this in mind, having raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the ancient teachers, [the author proceeds].
He refutes [this] with the words "and not," meaning that [the word does not denote] the singularity residing in the animal.

(The determination is made by that [extended application] because there is no contradiction with it, as it stands in the place of a supplementary statement; this explains why the connection with the substance is impossible only after the connection with the deity has occurred):

For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), although it follows from the requirements of the scriptural injunctions regarding the animal—which have as their purport acts such as slaughter—that the animal is understood to be the means of accomplishment through all its limbs, nevertheless, by virtue of the scriptural injunctions concerning the heart and other organs, there is an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of the other limbs, and thus [the connection with the substance is restricted].

Since the animal-ritual scriptures (paśuśāstra) teach that the heart and other organs are the means [of sacrifice], and since the singularity of the heart and so forth is established by implication through the singularity of the animal itself, there is no need to postulate an injunction regarding the singular number of those organs either.

Even if one were to postulate an injunction for the heart and other organs as the means because of the otherwise inexplicability of the injunction for the "cutting-off" (avadāna), [the same logic applies].

Nevertheless, since the oneness residing in that [the animal] is already established by the requirements of the situation (*arthasiddha*), it is not at all necessary for it to be an object of injunction (*vidheya*). Consequently, just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the group consisting of the heart and other parts— which serves as the means of the sacrifice— possesses oneness in accordance with the oneness residing in the animal, so too,
because that oneness is sublated by the seventeenfoldness taught regarding those parts, there is a seventeenfoldness in the group of the heart and other parts in accordance with that [teaching].

The meaning is that even if the sacrifice were one, since there is no extension (atideśa) of what is merely implied and because the explicit number sublates it, there is no possibility of that [implied number] being a decisive factor, as it would not conflict with the extension.
(An exposition on the individual capacity for action in sentient beings) "Of sentient beings" (paśūnām).

For where the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of each individual [element] is understood through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in their respective originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*), there, when plurality is subsequently connected (*pārṣṭhika*) to those very bases of individual instrumentality, it is the instruments themselves that are combined (*samuccaya*), and not a single instrumentality belonging to them collectively.

However, where the distinction between those [factors] is not understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there, by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), one postulates only a single instrumentality; thus, the subsequent connection of that [instrumentality] rests solely upon a single substratum of instrumentality. Therefore, in that case, the instrumentality belongs to the factors taken collectively.
Consequently, where a single instrumentality is indeed perceived through another means of valid cognition, [the aforementioned principle applies].

In that very context, since it is established that [the animals] act as instruments when combined, and since in the present case the fitness of the animals to serve as the instrument of sacrifice is perceived only individually, the number "plurality" (bahutva) is construed with the substance that serves as the substratum for each individual instrumentality. Consequently, the status of being the deity's correlate belongs only to that which is delimited by the nature of a "sacrificial animal" (paśutva). Indeed, a single ownership (svatva) does not exist in the aggregate of the animals.
This is because there is no evidence for such a thing,
because the effects of ownership— such as the right to employ [property] as one desires— are observed in each individual member, and because a collective cannot be employed independently on its own.

Therefore, since each individual animal is the locus of ownership (*svatva*), the status of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*)—defined as the activity conducive to the destruction of that ownership—belongs to each one individually. Consequently, by means of the deity-designating *taddhita* suffix prescribed for that purpose, the connection with the deity-status is understood to belong to each one individually.
For this very reason, it is the word denoting the animal qualified by its status as an instrument that serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
But it does not apply to the plural number either;
the meaning is that the referent of that [number] does not serve as a delimiter for the status of being an oblation (*havis*).

And therefore, in its capacity as a means to the sacrifice, it is precisely that which is delimited by "cowness" (the generic property of being a cow)—which is itself delimited by plurality—that possesses the fitness [to be the offering].

He states "and therefore" (ataśca) because, due to its connection with the deity, that [sacrifice] is established as distinct by virtue of the differences between the counter-correlate, the capacity for fulfillment, and the substratum.

(An exposition on how, in the case of the number seventeen, the very connection with the substance—prior to the connection with the number—is the means of establishing a difference in sacrifice, because the divinityhood expressed by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) connects first with the number):
"Therefore, it is precisely in accordance with that [divinityhood]..."

As for the argument in the *Śāstradīpikā* regarding the establishment of a difference in sacrifices (*yāgabheda*) in such cases— based merely on the cognition of plurality in a substance denoted by a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) as something qualified— it is stated that in instances such as "one sacrifices *kapiñjala* birds to Spring," since there is no secondary derivative suffix, a difference in sacrifice would not arise even when the connection with the deity applies to those very things delimited by plurality; therefore, the status of being a deity (*devatātva*), which is conveyed by the secondary derivative suffix, must precede the connection with plurality.

It has been stated that while the co-occurrence (*anvaya*) in the substance establishes a difference in sacrifice (*yāgabhedasādhaka*), it is rather the favoring of the injunction (*codanā*) which brings about the unity of the group of eleven cuttings (*avadānagaṇa*) produced from a single animal; the word "only" (*eva*) is used to refute that [view].

Consequently, since the unity belonging to the group of cuttings is obtained as a matter of course (*arthika*) in the *Vasanta* sentence according to the previously mentioned method, and thus there is no extended application (*atideśa*), there is no difference in sacrifice (*yāgabhedah*) on that account.

However, since the deityhood (devatātva) denoted by the dative case— which consists in being the intended recipient of the substance being relinquished— is untenable without the status of an oblation (haviṣṭva), which consists in being the substance being relinquished, and since each individual *kapiñjala* bird possesses the status of an oblation in the sense of being a means of accomplishing the sacrifice, the meaning is that there is a distinct connection with the deity for each individual [bird] delimited by the property of being a *kapiñjala*, which serves as the delimitor of the correlate.

By this very same principle, in the case of the passage, "He procures seventeen three-year-old heifers for the Maruts; [he procures] seventeen bulls; having performed the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite on them, they immolate the others and release the rest," one should understand that because the procedure consisting of the subsidiary rites ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa* is enjoined, the establishment of distinct sacrifices is justified due to the absence of the attainment of the group of eleven portions (*ekādaśāvadānagaṇa*).
The word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) is used to indicate that this is not according to the method stated by the ancient authors.

As for the authors of the *Prakāśa*’s assertion regarding the unity of the sacrifice— which is based on the literal reading of the *Śāstradīpikā* passage in the ninth penultimate section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the *Paraskaravākya*—
that refutation is to be found in the *Kaustubha* itself.
Therefore, the intention is that in the statement of the opponent, it is precisely the distinction of sacrifices (*yāgabhedah*) as established by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* that is logical.
(An examination of the purpose of the preceding and subsequent sections:
"The purpose" means...

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), even though the sacrifice has been performed by means of sixteen [animals] due to the forgetfulness of one animal, the sacrifice is considered complete; therefore, there is no performance of the sacrifice again.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the meaning is that another sacrifice involving that specific animal substance must be performed.
Other purposes have been shown by the ancients and should be consulted in the *Kaustubha*.
Thus ends the seventh section concerning the distinction of actions based on number.
(B1) (8th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.2 Pā.2 Adhi.8) And [the word] *saṃjñā* [is a name].

With reference to the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the scripture states: "Now this is the *jyotis*, now this is the *viśvajyotis*, now this is the *sarvajyotis*; one should sacrifice with this [sacrifice] which has a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇa*).

Since the words *jyotis* and so forth have no established conventional meaning as specific ritual accessories (*guṇaviśeṣa*), and since establishing them through their etymological sense of "being luminous" would result in that same application to the primary action itself, and since enjoining them by means of the pronoun *etad* (in "with this") would result in the fallacy of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and other defects, [the conclusion follows regarding] those [words].
First, its status as a name is beyond dispute; however, that [name] does not belong to the sacrifice under discussion,
because it is already occupied by the name "Jyotiṣṭoma," since the practical function of a name is accomplished by one alone, rendering any other redundant.
Nor is there an option (vikalpa) due to a lack of a determining factor (vinigamaka),

because the word *atha*— which marks the termination of the qualification for previous ritual acts— is the determining factor. For this very reason, there is no suspicion that it is a modification of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta-vikāra), as in the case of the injunction "every spring, one should perform the Jyotiṣṭoma."
Because, while its qualification remains uninterrupted, it is accepted as such through traditional recitation (*samāmnāna*).

Nor should it be argued that, in the absence of an interruption in qualification, there would be no resulting distinction from names such as *udbhid*, since—given that the name *jyotiṣṭoma* is not taught as an original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*)—why could there not be an option between the two or even a reversal? [This is not so.]

In the Soma sacrifice, since the name *Jyotiṣṭoma*—whose application-condition (*pravṛttinimitta*) is already established—already occupies the ritual, it is impossible for the name *Udbhid* to be applied to it in any way; therefore, that [name] functions as a differentiator.
For this very reason, where there is no other restrictive factor, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*) between the two names in the preliminary resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth.
But in the present case, because of the interruption caused by the word *atha*, the name itself acts as a differentiator.

Since the injunction of a subsidiary quality (*guṇavidhi*) is possible by the mere statement "one should sacrifice with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee" (*sahasradakṣiṇena yajeta*) as a reference to the sacrifice under discussion (*prakṛtayāga*), it would follow that the sentences beginning with "Jyotis," which contain different words (*etacchabdānta*), would be rendered purposeless.

Therefore, three distinct rites named "Jyotis" and so forth—characterized by their connection with illumination (*dyotana*) and the like, having the Soma-sacrifice as their archetype (*prakṛti*), produced by their respective sentences, and involving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee—are enjoined for a result by the sentence "He who desires prosperity should sacrifice with this. Thus, there is a distinction of rites (*karmabheda*) based on name (*saṃjñā*). // 8 //
Thus ends the eighth section, concerning the distinction of actions performed through designations.

(B2) (An examination of the connection between the seeds for the commencement of the section concerning the differentiation of rituals based on names, prior to the section concerning the differentiation of rituals based on qualities; although six types of ritual differentiation will be discussed here—

namely, difference of words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṅkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*)— as seen in the order of enumeration in the introductory commentary to the chapter, and because number and quality share the commonality of being subordinate factors of the ritual, [the discussion of] quality follows immediately after number.)
An inquiry into qualities (*guṇa*) follows;

nevertheless, because the investigation of qualities and so forth must be accomplished through multiple topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*), it requires great effort. Since the investigation into whether a name (*saṃjñā*) functions as a differentiator—like number (*saṅkhyā*)—concludes within a single topical section, it is brief and does not distract the intellect; therefore, it is treated first.

Desiring to explain the investigation of names (*saṃjñāvicāra*) as it is composed in the *Sūtrakṛt*, [the author] establishes the connection between the chapter and the section through an investigation of distinctions;
likewise, he establishes the connection with the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) due to the similarity of the reason known as "residing in distinctness" (*pṛthaktvaniveśa*).

Alternatively, just like number (*saṅkhyā*), a name is pervaded by a distinction whose counter-positive is its own substratum and which is co-referential with itself—this being the nature of distinctness (*pṛthaktva*).

Having established that there is no differentiating factor because of the inherent nature [of the acts], and thus having set aside— without explicitly showing— the prior objection (pūrvapakṣa) and its immediate connection in the form of a counter-example, he states the final conclusion (siddhānta) according to the Sūtra, preceded by an illustration,
beginning with the words: "The Jyotiṣṭoma..."
Following the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Dakṣiṇā," it is also heard: "With this, one desiring prosperity should sacrifice.
This is an illustration that also includes other examples, such as "This is Jyotiḥ," "This is Gauḥ," and "This is Āyuḥ."

Since the differentiation of ritual acts (*karmabheda*) cannot be established here through other words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), accessory qualities (*guṇa*), or a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), it must be demonstrated by means of the name (*saṃjñā*) alone.
In this regard, even if one supplies the word "exists" (*asti*) in passages such as "This is Jyotis," there are three distinct sentences because they lack mutual expectancy when divided.
By the phrase "with this," there is a fourth sentence, just as in the case of "he should sit upon that."

Although, in this case, there is no possibility of a "different word" (*śabdāntara*)— which differentiates based solely on the distinction of the mental realization (*bhāvanā*)— because it does not delimit the meaning of the verbal root;
nor is there the possibility of "repetition" (*abhyāsa*), which consists in the repeated hearing of an injunction, because no injunction is heard here.

Even though that [Brahman] exists in sentences such as "He for whom a thousand is the sacrificial fee," it is not [the primary meaning] there because the sentence is intended for another purpose, namely to enjoin a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
Nor can it be the subordinate quality itself,
because words such as *jyotis* (light) are not well-known to have a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of a subordinate quality.

Nor does it belong to another context, because there is an absence of qualities that are to be adopted, and even though such qualities exist in the passage concerning supernatural power (ṛddhi), there is no proximity here due to the lack of reference to the previous ritual action by means of this word "this" (etad).

Nevertheless, in order to establish their distinction by means of another proof for the forms of their designations, he establishes their status as names with the words "of the terms beginning with *jyotis*."

(An explanation of how the quality of being luminous in nature, due to the word *jyotis* being derived from the verbal root *dyut*, is established as common to [all] objects of action): "By virtue of its being luminous in nature."

The meaning is that because the word *jyotis* (light) is derived from the verbal root *dyut* by applying the *uṇādi* suffix *isi*—whereby the initial *d* is replaced by *j*—it is well-known as being of the nature of splendor (*dyuti*). This applies even to its status as an object (*karman*).

The meaning is that, because the word *jyotis* [in the first sacrifice] functions as a means to its own specific fruit, while the terms *viśvajyotis* and *sarvajyotis* function as means to all fruits, it follows that even in the case of the ritual action, the term *udbhid* must likewise be taken in its primary sense.

(The establishment of the status of *jyotis* and other terms as names, based on the principles of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), the arising of a learned tradition (*śiṣṭa*), the presence of qualities such as light (*jyotis*), and the principle of being named after that [quality]— this is what is meant by "the injunction of that" [*tadvidhāna*].)

The meaning is that by this word, if one were to enjoin the previously mentioned qualities while referring to the archetypal Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there would result a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) in enjoining both the qualities such as "light" (*jyotis*) and so forth, and the quality of a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasra-dakṣiṇā*) and so forth; furthermore, it would entail the inclusion of the qualities such as "light" which are already established as being known from other sources (*utpanna-śiṣṭa*), as indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).
"Without dispute."

The meaning is that, in the same way, it should be understood without dispute that words such as "cow" (gavādi) are also names by virtue of the *tatprakhyanyāya*, because they are obtained as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and as fruits obtained through the *sārvakāmya* injunctions.

(An objection based on the principle that a name is denoted by a part of its name: [the doubt that names such as *jyotis* are not differentiators])— But even if they are names, since they occur within the context, just as in the case of "Bhāmā" for "Satyabhāmā," it is possible for the words *jyotis* and so forth found here to be the names of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, because they possess the property of being composed of words that denote their own referents, in relation to the Vasantavākya, just like the word *jyotis* in that context.

Furthermore, just as the name "Jyotiṣṭoma" applies because of its connection with the *jyotis*-stomas, so too these [other sacrifices] could have that same name due to their connection with such stomas;
therefore, how can a distinction be established even by that? To this, he says: "And that... (*tacceti*).

(An exposition on how the word *atha*—by rejecting its meanings of immediate succession, dependence on what was previously mentioned, or its function as a marker for a new topic (*adhikāra*)—does not apply the principle of "part standing for the whole" [nāmaikadeśanyāya]):
"Of the word *atha*" and so forth.

For here it is not possible to suspect that the word *atha* has the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*); because there is no other action [prior to this] to serve as the counter-correlative of such succession, its having that meaning is untenable, and furthermore, because the impossibility of a sequence will be stated in the fifth book, since optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) are not subsumed under a single performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*).

Furthermore, since the mere fact of occurring at a subsequent time is already established, it would follow that the word *atha* (then) is redundant; nor does it have the sense of depending on what was previously mentioned,
because [the two] do not combine to form a means to a single result, and there is no relationship of primary and subordinate member (*aṅga-aṅgin*), and thus there is no need for such dependence.

Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), just as in the case of the phrase "now, the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*) and others, this [term] serves solely to introduce another governing topic (*adhikāra*) after signaling the conclusion of the previous one.
Since that restrictive factor exists, it follows that the name (*sañjñā*) of the previously mentioned sacrifice cannot apply here even optionally; such is the meaning.
(An exposition on how the word *atha* functions to delimit the primary ritual action, rather than delimiting the performance itself:

By this [it is shown that]— since the word *atha* delimits the qualification (*adhikāra*) precisely for that performance which is delimited by the preceding designation, and since it is understood that the word *etat* refers back to that performance associated with another designation in accordance with that [delimitation], [the mention of the word *atha*] serves there to establish the rule regarding the thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇā*) and so forth.

The argument that "the purposefulness of the different designations" is also refuted; for since the action itself is primary and possesses a manifest presence, the word *atha* is understood to indicate the commencement of a new topic (*adhikāra*).
Therefore... [end of quote].
The meaning is that a name occurring within the context of the Soma sacrifice is immediately determined to refer to that [sacrifice],
and not to something whose context has been interrupted.
"In some way or another."
The meaning is that it is also according to the principle of the words *bhāmā* and *satyabhāmā*.

(An exposition establishing that the term *jyotiṣṭoma* functions as a differentiator precisely because it serves to bring about the application of its specific ritual procedure, thereby achieving its own meaningfulness): "Therefore, where... and so forth.
For example, in the sentence "The Vaiśvānara Jyotiṣṭoma becomes the Prāyaṇīya day," the words *vaiśvānara* and *prāyaṇīya* have no meaningful application whatsoever [as adjectives];

for since the cup (*graha*) dedicated to the deity Vaiśvānara is prescribed, the word *vaiśvānara* functions as a name because it provides assistance to the sacrifice by way of *prasaṅga* (incidental benefit) through that very deity Vaiśvānara,
while the word *prāyaṇīya* functions as a name due to its connection with the quality of being the first (*prāthamya*).

In that case, because there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary], an option (*vikalpa*) is indeed accepted regarding the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*), the verbal expression (*ullekha*), and so forth.

However, the word *jyotiṣṭoma*—functioning as the applicator of the *jyotiṣṭoma* procedure (which was previously set aside by the procedure of the *dvādaśāha* due to the commonality of being a "group sacrifice," *gaṇatva-sāmānya*)—is not purposeless; therefore, there is no option regarding the mental resolve, the verbal expression, and so forth.
This is the meaning.

Therefore, he states that where—even though a previous operation is already occupied by a single designation—the purposefulness of another designation is established through the assumption of a different operation; or where, due to a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanā*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) between both [designations]; or where, although the designation does not differentiate the operations, another designation would otherwise be redundant for the previous operation—in such cases, it is absolutely necessary to assume a different operation so that the [new] designation may achieve its own objective.
"But in the present case," however.

Therefore, in these three sentences beginning with "Then this [is] light" (*athaiṣa jyotiḥ*), three distinct rites are enjoined, each associated with its respective name. Their nature as sacrifices is determined either by the subsequent transfer (*atideśa*) based on the authority of similarity, or by the reference (*anuvāda*) to them via the verb *yajati* in the sentence concerning the accessory (*guṇavākya*).
Furthermore, in the two subsequent sentences, the accessories and results are enjoined through the reference to those rites by means of the word "this" (*etac-chabda*).

The singular number in the word *etena* ("by this") is employed with the intention of referring to a collective whole, just as in the case of the term *rājasūya*, which indicates a plurality of constituent acts.
(An explanation of the interruption of the qualification for performance in the *Viśvajyotis* and other passages):
In the passages concerning the *Viśvajyotis* and *Sarvajyotis*, the word "atha" (*then*) does not serve to interrupt the qualification for the preceding sacrifice;
for if it did, it would entail the necessity of postulating a separate result [for that interruption].

Furthermore, [the author] concludes the established doctrine with the words "therefore," meaning that the distinction is proven in every respect because it serves the purpose of introducing a subsequent application.
(Disparity between a name and other words denoting qualities, and an examination of the purpose of the preceding and succeeding alternatives:
Nor should it be suspected that, in this way, even a name is included within the category of quality alone;

Because there is no possibility of attaching a quality [to the action], even though the name serves as a differentiator, it differs from the previous action in that— due to the understanding that its own function is already satisfied by the rule— it would be redundant as a differentiator; thus,
although the name is indeed a distinct word, there is a disparity.

Nevertheless, even when the words are different, there is a distinction in the *bhāvanā* due to the difference in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which colors it, just as there is a distinction in negation (*abhāva*) due to the difference in its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

However, since a name (*saṃjñā*) is a separate word that denotes an already established form, it does not lead to the cognition of a distinct *bhāvanā* colored by that [name]; rather, it culminates merely in a distinction of the verbal root's meaning. And because of that distinction, according to the principle of "different words" (*śabdāntara-nyāya*), [there is a difference in the *apūrva*].
The distinction in cultivation (*bhāvanā*) should be understood as a point of difference.

This was stated by the Teacher at the conclusion of the section beginning with "But because of non-distinction in proximity" (*sannidhau tv avibhāgāt*): "Because it does not denote its own essential form, the name is distinct from other words;
and because of its inherence in a composite whole, number is distinct from other qualities."
The purpose [of the discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is an option with the thousand-fold sacrificial fee (sahasradakṣiṇā);
whereas according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), it is a distinct optional sacrifice characterized by the thousand-fold fee—this has not been stated because it is self-evident.
Thus ends the eighth section, concerning the distinction of actions produced by designation.
(B1) (9th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.2 Pā.2 Adhi.9) And [the word] is a subordinate element (*guṇa*).

Because of the connection with what precedes and the equality of the two sentences, in the case of "The *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas," once a sacrifice qualified by both substance and deity has been enjoined, the subsequent statement "The *vājina* for the Vājins" does not enjoin a mere accessory (*guṇa*). This is because enjoining multiple accessories while restating an already established action would result in the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Nor can it be argued that, based on the etymology "those who possess *vāja*—that is, food in the form of *āmikṣā*," one might refer to the Viśvedevas or the sacrifice qualified by them, and then enjoin the *vājina* alone, either optionally or as a combination.

It should not be said that "let there be an injunction," because the word *vājī* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) and thus cannot serve as a reference (*anuvāda*) to the Viśvedevas, and furthermore, because when a substance is already enjoined by the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), it is impossible for another substance to be introduced.

By this, the view that the word *vājina* is the name of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice—accepting it as such because of the attainment of a connection with the *vājina* produced as a by-product—and that there is an injunction of the deity Vāji with reference to that [sacrifice], is also refuted; for when a deity is already enjoined at the time of the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), it is impossible for another deity to be introduced.
Furthermore, the connection of the *āmikṣā* with the deity is established by direct word-hearing (*pada-śruti*).
However, the weakness [of the word *vājina*] lies in its being a syntactical statement (*vākya*).

For the ancients hold that the nominal suffix (*taddhita*) has its power (*śakti*) upon a specific substance qualified by divinity, and the word *āmikṣā* serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*).
In reality, with respect to substances such as *āmikṣā* and so forth, as well as the status of being a deity (*devatātva*), there is a distinct power (*śakti*).

Alternatively, the relation of "qualifier-ness" (*nirūpakatva*) is the connection; or rather, the power resides in the status of being a deity itself, while it is through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that it applies to the substance.

Alternatively, the potency (*śakti*) resides only in the specific substance, while there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding its being the deity; or else, the potency resides in the substance in general, while the determination of the specific [substance] is made by the word *āmikṣā*. These positions have been established in the Kaustubha itself. In any case, it is established that the connection between the *āmikṣā* substance and the deity occurs through direct word-hearing (*pada-śruti*).
Furthermore, the status of the Viśvedevas as deities is expressed by their name through the suffix *taddhita*;
whereas for the Vājins, it is expressed by the dative case— which denotes the status of being a recipient— through a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on contemporaneity (*sāmpratika*).

Since the nature of being a deity (*devatātva*) is but a part of the nature of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*)— which consists in being a recipient characterized by being the intended object of the substance being relinquished—

and since that [deity] lacks the status of being a recipient, [the term "deity"] would necessarily involve figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, if one were to accept an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) in the form of deityhood, which pervades the recipient-hood that is co-extensive with the aforementioned property, then figurative indication would be even more certain.
For this reason also, [the latter] is weak.

Therefore, even in the sentence concerning the whey (*vājina*), a distinct ritual action—characterized by both substance and deity—is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice for the purpose of consuming the whey.
And because the quality (*guṇa*) cannot be accommodated within the preceding [sacrifice], it functions as a differentiator (*bhedaka*).

And it should be understood that this [interruption] occurs in various ways: in some cases due to the consequence of splitting the sentence, in some cases due to the obstruction by a more powerful poetic quality (guṇa), and in some cases due to the violation of the principle of single semantic thrust (ekaprasaratā). // 9 //
Thus ends the ninth section, concerning the distinction of actions produced by qualities.
(B2) (An examination of the connection by way of occasion for the section on *guṇa* following the section on *saṃjñā*):

Because it shares the commonality of not being included in the preceding [section] and because it possesses a distinction whose counter-correlate is proximate, the author— commencing an inquiry into the distinction caused by *guṇas* immediately after the discussion of *saṃjñās* due to its more rapid presentation compared to the section on *prakaraṇāntara*— establishes the immediate connection known as "occasion" (*avasara*).

Likewise, having avoided explicitly presenting the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) because it is easily refuted and thus clear [by implication] under the guise of dispelling objections, he announces the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) itself by first presenting an illustrative example: "The *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas."

(Just as the sentence *vaiśvadevīmāmikṣām* [the curdled milk for the Viśvedevas] is an injunction of a sacrifice, so too is the sentence *vaiśvadevyāmikṣā* [the curdled milk belonging to the Viśvedevas]).

Although in the Taittirīya [Saṃhitā], following the sequence beginning with "He offers the eight-potherd cake for Agni" (*āgneyamaṣṭākapālaṃ nirvapati*), there is the reading "*vaiśvadevīmāmikṣām*," and since an injunction of a sacrifice occurs there through the secondary application (*lakṣaṇā*) of the previously mentioned word *nirvapati* by ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*), it is not by means of the phrase "*vaiśvadevyāmikṣā*" alone that [the sacrifice is enjoined].
It is the injunction of a sacrifice qualified by both a material (*dravya*) and a deity (*devatā*);

nevertheless, since the sentence "He pours curds into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas" has been cited by the Mīmāṃsakas, and it has likewise been quoted here by the Bhāṣyakāra and others, [the injunction] is understood according to their intention by supplying the word *yajeta* (he should sacrifice) and by changing the case-ending.

It should be understood that the qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhāna) based on the formulated rule, "One should sacrifice with the curdled milk [āmikṣā] dedicated to the Viśvedevas," is not untenable.

Although only the sentence concerning the whey (vājina) is cited as an example, this [sentence regarding the āmikṣā] is included here in order to make known the difference between the ritual acts as contrasted with its counterpart.
(The demonstration that a quality which causes a split in the sentence is a differentiator of ritual acts, along with an illustrative example):
"Because it would result in a split in the sentence."

The meaning is that, as established incidentally in the *Paurṇamāsī* section, since this would result in a distinct ritual action (*karmāntaratva*) due to a quality that causes syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), it cannot be a mere injunction of qualities consisting of substance and deity.

(This includes the demonstration that if the sacrifice qualified by the Viśvedevas were the object of the injunction, the syntactical split caused by such a qualified object would be avoided; and the determination that the referent of the word *vājī* is indeed the Viśvedevas, not Agni and others. [The sūtra says: "Or [it refers to] the sacrifice."
In the sentence "One should sacrifice to the Vājins with the vājina," which is established through a portion [of the text] that is both heard and inferred, because the sacrifice is mentioned therein,
and because the phrase "to the Vājins" serves as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) when the sacrifice to the Viśvedevas alone is the object of reference,
there is no resulting split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to a qualified reference; therefore, it is said that "one should [perform] that sacrifice qualified by that [reference]."

By demonstrating the etymological derivation of "yeṣām" (of whom), it is indicated that since pronouns can refer to what is proximate, it is impossible for them to refer to something not proximate; therefore, by virtue of the plural number, neither a single entity such as Agni nor the Maruts are to be understood by the term "vājinaḥ" (the winners of the prize).
Or by way of conjunction.

If, in the word *vājin* which conveys the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) in the form of *vājina* functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), then there is conjunction (*samuccaya*). If, however, it functions as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), then because they serve a single purpose (*ekārthatva*), there is an option (*vikalpa*); such is the meaning.

(On the establishment of a difference in rituals because *āmikṣā* is taught as part of the originative injunction, and on the justification of the difference in rituals so that the sentence concerning *vājina* may not be rendered meaningless: Now, one might object: since the prescription of *vājina* is made with reference to the sacrifice for which the *Viśvedevas* are the deity—just like the *āmikṣā*—and since it is accepted that the *vājina* belongs to that very same sacrifice, the *āmikṣā* possesses greater force by virtue of being taught as part of the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).
Thus he says: "Furthermore... (kiñca).

Since the connection between the substance and the deity for the sacrificial procedure (*yāgakalpaka*) is perceived through the mention of *āmikṣā* within a single word, it possesses greater force than the connection with a deity mentioned in a separate word.
Consequently, once the sacrifice has been rendered free of expectancy by that [connection] alone, there is no possibility for the *vājina* to be included in the sacrifice.
For in this case, if there were no restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice in the phrase "the *vājina* is in that same sacrifice," the statement would result in meaninglessness.
The sense is that its purpose is fulfilled even by the injunction of another action.

(The exposition of the ancient view that the meaning of a secondary derivative suffix [taddhita] is precisely a specific substance qualified by divinity: "For of the secondary derivative... and so forth.

Since the hearing of a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix necessarily entails the cognition of a substance qualified by the status of being a deity (*devatātva*), and because of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) "that is its deity" (*sāsya devatā*), the *taddhita* suffix has its denotative power (*śakti*) upon a substance qualified by the status of being a deity. Furthermore, in this rule, although the Viśvedevas are taught as the deity by the word "it" (*sā*), they are not the actual meaning of the *taddhita* suffix;
for the cognition of them is established from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) "Viśvedeva" itself.

Furthermore, if [the word *devatā*] were to denote deityhood alone, its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *āmikṣā* would be untenable; therefore, it is also necessary that it denotes a substance present in the intellect as the referent of the pronoun *asya*. For this very reason—the fact that the grammatical rule defining the meaning of the pronoun *asya* as "this is its deity" (*sāsya devatā*) would otherwise be rendered purposeless—it is also refuted that the primary denotative power (*śakti*) resides solely in deityhood (by the maxim of "not grasping the qualifier first"), while the substance is understood through the process of individualization (*vyaktinyāya*).

If that were the case, it would result in the undesirable consequence of applying the grammatical rule "the fourth case is used for the recipient" (*saṃpradāne caturthī*) instead of the rule "the secondary suffix [denotes] the deity" (*devatāyāṃ taddhitaḥ*).

For this very reason, the view that the nature of being a deity (*devatātva*) appears as a relation between the meaning of the base and the substance which is the meaning of the suffix is also refuted. Therefore, the primary denotative power (*śakti*) resides in the substance, which is the referent of the pronoun, as qualified by the nature of being a deity.

Although in the initial cognition, the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is related to the deityhood (devatātva) by the relation of being the locus (ādheyatā), and that [deityhood] is related to the referent of the pronoun (sarvanāman) by the relation of being the object of definition (nirūpyatva)— such that deityhood is indeed thus understood first— nevertheless, because the word *āmikṣā* functions to grasp the intended meaning of a specific substance, one accepts a subsequent cognition (*pāriṣṭhaka-bodha*) to the effect that "the referent of the pronoun is a substance distinct from *āmikṣā*. Consequently, the connection of *āmikṣā* with deityhood is established through the direct denotative power of the word (*pada-śruti*).
Although the meaning of the dative case might be "deity-hood" through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), nevertheless it denotes only that much,
and not by way of its connection with the whey (vājina).

The meaning is that because the word "vājina" [is connected] with the word "āmikṣā" through the sentence consisting of their co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), it is already satisfied by the *āmikṣā*—which is more swiftly presented as being related to the status of a deity—even prior to the other word "vājina"; therefore, the inclusion of the *vājina* is not possible.
(Refutation of the aforementioned ancient view on the grounds that it renders the established conclusion of the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa* untenable):

Furthermore, according to this ancient view, since the deityhood is understood as being qualified by the substance (*dravya-vaiśiṣṭya*), it would result in the inconsistency of the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*, wherein the injunction of the form (*rūpa*) in the *Āgneya* passage—made by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the rites prescribed in the *Vidvadvākya*—is refuted on the grounds of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) and other such faults. Thus, that [ancient] position becomes untenable.
The capacity of that [deity] exists separately both in its status as a deity and in the substance;
and since these two are factors of action (*kāraka*), their connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is direct.

However, intending that the subsequent connection of the deity-status with the substance and the substance with the sacrifice is logical, he states the alternative views in their abstracted forms, beginning with "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*).
(The demonstration that the sentence concerning the *vājina* is directed toward a sacrifice for the purpose of the disposal of the *vājina* produced as a by-product of the *āmikṣā*:
"For the purpose of the disposal of the *vājina*."

The meaning is that, because the whey (*vājina*)—which exists in the form of water produced as a by-product of the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*)—requires a disposal (*pratipatti*), and because it thereby attains the status of being enjoined by a requirement, another sacrifice is enjoined for the purpose of that disposal.

(The *Śāstradīpikā*’s statement that a quality (*guṇa*) functions as a differentiator because it cannot be accommodated in the preceding [sentence] and because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is intended as an illustration of the violation of the principle of "single thrust" [*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*]).

As for what was stated in the *Śāstradīpikā*—that there are two ways in which a quality acts as a differentiator: in some cases, by being excluded from its own placement due to being obstructed by a quality enjoined in the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇa*), and in other cases, by resulting in a syntactical split—that is merely an illustration.

To indicate that a third possibility also exists, he states the common form of the qualifier across all three types when it serves as a differentiator: "And of the qualifier... The phrase "in the case of a breach of single-directionality" (ekaprasaratābhaṅga) implies "in the sentence concerning the vaṣaṭ-maker" (vaṣaṭkartṛvākya).

(Indication of the refutation of the view of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* regarding [the passage] "He buys with cloth," etc., concerning the claim that there is no distinction in the act of purchase due to the presence of subordinate qualities): As for what was stated here by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*— namely, that because the sentence concerning the red cow (*aruṇā*) necessarily enacts a qualified injunction of purchase through the inclusion of multiple qualities,

once that purchase has been enjoined, even though it is already occupied by the quality of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) which is prescribed at the time of the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), the purchases enjoined by such statements as "He buys with cloth" (*vāsasā krīṇāti*), although prescribed after the fact (*utpanna-śiṣṭa*), [are nevertheless distinct].

It has been stated that because there is no possibility of establishing a distinction between the seller and the non-excessive form of the action regarding substances such as clothing, there is no injunction of a different action based on a quality in the sentences concerning clothing and so forth;
the refutation of that [position] is to be found in the Kaustubha.
This will also be discussed in the section concerning the Aruṇā; it is not stated here for fear of prolixity.
(The purpose of the preceding and following arguments:

The purpose is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the performance of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is carried out with both the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) and the whey (*vājina*), or alternatively with either one of them;
whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is performed with the curd-mixture alone.
And because it is clear that the performance of another sacrifice occurs by means of the *vājina* [offering], it has not been explicitly stated.
Thus ends the ninth section, concerning the distinction of actions produced by qualities.
But in the case of that which lacks a quality. (B1) (10th Topic / [a.2 pā.2 adhi.10]) But in the case of that which lacks a quality...
But where there is no mention of an accessory in the original injunction of origin—
such as "He offers the Agnihotra"—
there, one performs the offering with curd by way of a reference to that [original act].

By all [injunctions] such as "he offers with milk" (payasā juhoti), there is an injunction of qualities (guṇavidhāna) through option (vikalpa); therein, according to the maxim of the pigeons on a threshing floor (khale kapotanyāya), because all [qualities] apply simultaneously, there is no exclusion of one by another—this is merely a counter-example (pratyudāharaṇa). // 10 // 27 //
Thus ends the tenth section, concerning the refutation of the distinction between actions based on their qualities.
(B2) This is for the sake of clarity.
Thus ends the tenth section, concerning the refutation of the distinction between actions based on quality.
(B1) (11th Topic /) (A.2 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 11) Because of the mention of a fruit.
With reference to the *agnihotra*, there is the Vedic text: "One desiring sensory power should offer with curd.
In this case, that very same oblation, qualified by curd, is enjoined for the sake of a specific result.

Nor does this entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), consisting in the simultaneous connection of a quality and a result through a restatement of an already established action (*prāptakarmanuvāda*).

The first position is that even for rites already established, just as in the case of the *rājasūya* injunction where those performed by a king are enjoined with reference to a specific fruit, so too here it is appropriate to enjoin them with reference to a fruit.

The second position, however, is that the principle of the *rājasūya* does not apply here. For the agent is connected with the performance (*prayoga*), while the fruit is connected with the application (*viniyoga*). Thus, although the rite has already been produced, its connection with a specific fruit occurs during the injunction of performance, and likewise, the connection with the agent is established through the injunction of application. Therefore, the qualification of both the fruit and the agent is logically consistent.

In the present case, however, since *dadhi* (curd) is connected as the material for production, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the lack of a single integrated meaning, because it would involve both a restatement of the already established production and an injunction of a quality, as well as an injunction of application qualified by a result.
Therefore, there is a distinction of rites (*karmabheda*) based on the quality;
and that [rite] qualified by curd is enjoined with reference to the result.
It is not merely curd;
for that would result in a contradiction with the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha-adhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, even though it is a *darvihoma*, because of its similarity to a sacrifice where curd is the substance, the form [of the rite] is obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) of the *agnihotra* sacrifice.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: where there is the non-attainment of both the meaning of the verbal root and the accessory (*guṇa*), or their potential attainment, or their actual attainment, or the non-attainment of the meaning of the verbal root alone—

as in the cases of "one should sacrifice with Soma," "he spreads the sacrificial cake with [the mantra] 'O wide-expanding one, expand yourself wide,'" "one who desires that offspring may be produced in due order should take the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu," and "he offers the Agnihotra," and so forth.
In that regard, there is the principle of the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārthādhikaraṇa):
however, where a quality itself is not already established and thus must be enjoined, there that very quality is connected with the fruit.
Furthermore, the acquisition of curd is not mandatory,
but rather optional; therefore,
in order to avoid the charge of being a mere restatement of an alternative, it is that very [curd] which must be enjoined, and thus it is connected with the result.

Since the result can arise even without the verbal statement due to the existence of the quality that has become the instrument (*karaṇībhūtaguṇasattva*), there would follow the contingency of the statement being useless. Therefore,

when there is a requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*) connected to the quality in a perceptible manner (*dṛṣṭavidhayā*) for the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) to be accomplished by one's own effort (*svakṛtisādhya*), the root *juhoti* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutvārtha*), because the status of being the substratum is obtained for the oblation (*homa*) through the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Rather, a distinct *bhāvanā* (efficient force) having curd as its instrument (*karaṇa*) is enjoined with reference to the result; for if both [the result and the instrument] were enjoined by way of restating a *bhāvanā* already established, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Some, however, [hold that] it is curd qualified by the state of being an instrument...
Alternatively, it is argued that the status of curd as an instrument (karaṇatva), which is conveyed by the third case ending, is enjoined as the instrument for the result;

furthermore, the requirement for a substrate (āśraya) is simply the requirement for a relatum (nirūpaka) of the instrumentality expressed by the third case. This is not correct, because there is no evidence for such a disparity with the sacrifice (yāga).
In every respect, the connection between the quality and the fruit is established.
According to the final conclusion (siddhānta), neither a substitute nor a specific mention [of the substance] serves as the purpose for the curd; this is how it should be understood. 1.1.10.
Thus ends the eleventh section concerning those who desire specific qualities.

(B2) (An explanation of the *apavādikī* connection with the preceding section: Since it was stated in the preceding section that a quality which causes a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) is a differentiator, and since an exception (*apavāda*) is being made here, the *apavādikī* connection is not explicitly shown due to its obviousness; rather, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated by means of two positions, preceded by an example: "The Agnihotra... etc.

[This explains] the statement of the connection between the quality and the fruit, because even though curd is already obtained [by the rule "one offers with curd"], its acquisition is impossible as a matter of necessity in the performance for one desiring sense-power (*indriyakāma*).
Although this position was not stated by the predecessors, he establishes it through the power of reasoning: "That very same oblation [is intended]."
Anticipating the second alternative, he refutes it with the words "And not... (na ca).

Although the quality [of curd] is already established by the injunction "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), such that the word denoting it may be justified as either a restatement (*anuvāda*) or a name (*nāmadheya*), and thus there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) merely from establishing its connection with the result; nevertheless, since other substances are also prescribed for the performance of the *Agnihotra*, they are obtained [as options], and because there is no mandatory attainment [of curd] specifically for the performance aimed at the result of sense-power (*indriyakāma*), neither a partial restatement nor a name is possible. Therefore, because the injunction of that [curd] is necessary, the syntactical split is unavoidable.
Considering it difficult to avoid, he avoids it by another method, stating: "Even of those that have been attained."

Although a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result from enjoining both the connection of the *anumatī* and other sacrifices with the fruit, as well as their connection with the king as the performer— since the animal sacrifices such as those beginning with the day-sacrifices are already linked to the *rājasūya* injunction— nevertheless, because the agent is a subordinate factor of the performance, and since the performance is not enjoined by another sentence apart from the *rājasūya*,

and because the performance, like its origination, has action as its object, there is [the injunction] of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of the *rājasūya* performance, qualified by the agent, for the sake of the fruit.
Having accepted the principle demonstrated in the *Aveṣṭyadhikaraṇa* according to the method stated in the *Sudhā*, [the objection] is resolved;
the meaning is that, in this case as well, such a resolution is easily obtained.

(An alternative presentation of the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa], based on the argument that, as in the case of the *rājasūya* injunctions, there is no connection of the fruit with a qualified subsidiary action in the present context):

Because substances, deities, and so forth serve to define the origin [of the rite], they are connected to the origin; because fruits and so forth serve to define the status of the principal [action], they are connected to the principal; because the application-injunction (*viniyoga-vidhi*), which conveys the relationship between principal and subsidiary, is connected [to the origin]; and because the agent, place, time, and so forth serve to define the necessity of performance (*kartavyatā*).

Furthermore, since it will be stated in the eleventh book that [the injunction] must be connected with the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*) which conveys the sense of "what is to be done," even though the rites produced by the *rājasūya* sentence obtain their spatial and temporal performances through the respective injunctions of place and time, there is still the possibility of the connection of the performer with the performance-injunction— which concerns what was previously unobtained— in terms of the application (*viniyoga*) qualified by the result and the connection of the agent.

In the present case, however, since there is an absence of a quality (*guṇa*) that could be connected with the performance as qualified by the application (*viniyoga*), it is impossible for there to be either the performance of the ritual act as qualified by that [quality] or the application of such a performance.

Consequently, because another origination of the ritual act (*karmotpatti*) is necessary to conform to that [requirement], and otherwise— by way of restating the origination— the injunction of the application of the *dadhi* (curd) toward the *indriya* (sensual power) through the act of offering (*homa*) would result in an unavoidable syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), it must be a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).
Intending that this is logical, he states the second position: "But the second [position]..."
(The refutation of the final position [siddhānta] that there is a connection between curd and the fruit [of the action], on the grounds that it contradicts the logic of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*:
He refutes the acceptance, within the final position, of a connection between the fruit and the curd as something dependent upon the oblation (*homa*), stating: "Not mere curd."

The meaning is that because the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* establishes that the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is the instrument (*karaṇa*)—by refuting that the meaning of the accompanying word (*upapadārtha*) is the instrument for the efficient-force of the result (*phalabhāvanā*)—there would arise a contradiction with that [established conclusion].
He dispels the objection that a prescription of a separate action (*karmāntaravidhi*) is untenable due to the absence of a distinct form (*rūpa*), by stating: "Even though... (*satyapi*).
Even though they are *darvihoma*s, by virtue of the requirement [for a model], there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *agnihotra* rules due to the similarity of having curd as the substance;
for there is no royal decree that *darvihoma*s are entirely original (*apūrva*).
This will be explained in the eighth book: "Because the procedure is prescribed in its entirety, and because there is no determination of a specific archetype (*prakṛti*), such is the case."
And since neither of those two [conditions] exists here,
the meaning is that because its form (rūpa) has been acquired, it is logical that it constitutes a separate action.

(An exposition of the injunction of the substance *dadhi* as a quality, based on the non-application of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* principle to the sentence "for one desiring sense-power, [he should sacrifice] with *dadhi*," preceded by an analysis of the scope of that section. Regarding the phrase *yatra*:
In the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), there is no prior application (*aprāpti*) of either [the substance or the action].

In the sentence "he should spread wide" (*uru prathasva*), however, because the spreading is otherwise impossible without the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and because the mantra is applicable to that object by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*), both have a possible application (*saṃbhavat-prāpti*).
In the sentence regarding the Aindravāyava cup, there is a fixed application (*niyatā prāpti*) of both.
In the Agnihotra passage, there is no prior establishment of the root-meaning itself;

therefore, according to the principle of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, it is the root-meaning alone that is enjoined. However, where the root-meaning is already established, enjoining the root-meaning as well would result in prolixity (*gaurava*); thus, since only the accessory (*guṇa*) is unestablished, it is that which is enjoined.

In that context, because that very [substance] is the object to be enjoined and is indicated by a word ending in the third case, it possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) with respect to the efficient-force of the result (*phalabhāvanā*), consisting in its being directed toward the result that defines it. Nor can *dadhi* (curd) and *payas* (milk) be considered names (*nāman*) by the principle of "being known from that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*), such that the enjoining of the meaning of the accompanying word (*upapada*) would not be possible.

The meaning is that since it is possible to interpret [the passage] as an injunction regarding qualities (guṇavidhi) with respect to the fruit, it is improper to assume that it is a name (nāmadheya) which is largely devoid of purpose.
Regarding the status as a partial restatement (pākṣikānuvādatva).
(An explanation that, although the phrase "beginning with the Aindravāyava" is a partial restatement (*pākṣikānuvāda*) in one instance, such a status is not possible in the sentence concerning curd.

Nor is there any fault in accepting that [status] here as well, on the grounds that the term "beginning with the Aindravāyava" is a partial restatement due to its optionality with respect to "beginning with the Śukra";

for even though the similarity of being partial restatements exists, when the "beginning with the Aindravāyava" is connected to a result, it becomes optional (*kāmya*), and thus, in the case of the *Bṛhat*-sāman alternative—

The meaning is that there is a disparity: whereas in the case of the sentence "if it has the *rathantara-sāman*," one might accept the status of the term *aindravāyavāgratā* as a partial restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the words *yadi* and *rathantarasāman*, here—in the case of the word *dadhi*—there is no such authority for accepting that status; furthermore, because one wishes to avoid the complexity of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), it is more appropriate to enjoin only the accessory (*guṇa*). Thus, the cases are not analogous.

(An exposition establishing that the sentence concerning the desire for sensory power (*indriyakāma*) has as its primary purport a distinct efficient force (*bhāvanā*) based on curd as a substrate for an oblation, even though the curd is already established. In that context, although the genus "curd-ness" (*dadhitva-jāti*) or the individual instance characterized by it might be enjoined for the sake of the result, it is first of all impossible for it to produce the result— being an accomplished entity like a sacrifice (*yāga*), etc.— without depending upon another action.

If that were the case, since the result would be produced simply through the existence of the instrument when there is a desire for the result— even without an injunction— the injunction regarding the instrument would become redundant;
for the causal relationship is not created by an injunction, but rather made known by it.
Moreover, there is no fruit for the cognition of that [injunction] as there is for the sacrifice and so forth;
for even in its absence, the fruit is established by the existence of the cause.
For this very reason, let only the injunctions regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) be of primary utility.
Nor, however, is there an injunction regarding the curd as the instrumental cause (*upakāraṇa*).

Therefore, for the injunction to be purposeful, when there is a requirement for a connection with a substratum (*āśraya*) in the form of a specific verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) that is to be accomplished by human effort (*kṛtisādhya*)— and when, by the force of compatibility (*yogyatā*), multiple root-meanings such as eating or offering oblations (*homa*) which are themselves to be accomplished by it are suggested— the [specific meaning] is determined by the context (*prakaraṇa*), known as the qualification (*adhikāra*).
Since the oblation itself is brought forward by means of the postulation of an injunction, there is no possibility of those [other elements] being its substratum.

For this very reason, even by means of a postulated injunction, the relationship of subordinate and principal between the curd and the oblation is not understood; for that would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava) and because [the curd] already possesses an established purpose.

Moreover, it is merely the restriction of the relationship between cause and effect as established in the world—that the oblation (homa) must be performed with curd (dadhi). Nor should it be argued that the sentence concerning the desire for sensory power (*indriyakāma*) is redundant because the obligation to perform the oblation produced by curd is already established by the injunction "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*); for in the absence of that [specific] injunction, the performance of the oblation qualified by curd would not be established as having the attainment of sensory power as its intended fruit. Therefore, since that [sentence] serves the purpose of making known that the desire for sensory power is a qualification of the eligible performer (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), it is not redundant.

And therefore, although the pure curd is understood to be an auxiliary (*kratvaṅga*) of the sacrifice by means of its own injunction, since it is here enjoined for the sake of a result, a distinct productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is enjoined which has as its locus the curd that serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The verbal root (*dhātu*), however, merely restates the connection with the locus already established by the context (*prakaraṇa*); it is used solely for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). With this in mind, he says: "having become the instrument" (*karaṇībhūta*).
(An exposition on the determination of the relationship as the substratum for [injunctions] such as "one desiring cattle should take the Ukthya [cup] at the Jyotiṣṭoma"):
