In this context, it should be understood as a general principle that the connection of the sacrifice (*homa*) with a quality (*guṇa*)—which is established in its own nature—is established by way of being the substratum (*āśraya*), because it is projected by the meaning of the verbal root which is to be accomplished through effort (*kṛti-sādhya*).

However, in cases such as "one desiring cattle should take the Ukthya," since the quality consisting of the *saṃsthā* (the completion of the rite) is itself directly to be accomplished through effort, it is untenable for the sacrifice to serve as its substratum, given that the sacrifice requires an object (*viṣaya*) rather than a substratum (*āśraya*).
Therefore, it should be understood that because completion (*samāpti*) is inherently relational, the *jyotiṣṭoma* serves as its substratum (*āśraya*) precisely through that dependence.

And thus, although curd (*dadhi*) is already connected to the requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*) within the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), its status as an instrument is not established until it is connected to a substratum; in this way, the substratum is grasped by the very requirement for an instrument, and not by a separate "requirement for a substratum" (*āśrayākāṅkṣā*). This is the intended meaning.

(In order to establish that the fruit is produced by a distinct effort of a different class, and because its connection [to the sacrifice] is also necessary, the difference in the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is stated through a split of the sentence:

As for what Bhavadeva said here—that since the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the efficient force is equal to that of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), there is no proof for a difference in the efficient force;

and that a difference in the efficient force arises from the accessory (*guṇa*) itself, because otherwise, if one were to enjoin both the connection with an accessory and the connection with a fruit while restating an already established efficient force, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)—[that is incorrect].

It was stated that the connection with the fruit is not something to be enjoined because it is already established through desire; that [objection] is now refuted by the phrase "the already-established bhāvanā."

Although it is understood from the world that the fruit called "the sense-organ" (indriya) is produced by some mere operation because it is something produced, its being produced by a distinct effort is not understood from common experience; furthermore,
since the effort conducive to the Agnihotra oblation is specifically understood to be the generator of heaven, and since it must necessarily be enjoined by the sentence itself,
the distinction [of the sacrifice] from the accessory— which would result in a split of the sentence— is necessary.

For this very reason, even though another *bhāvanā* (efficient force) requires a specific meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) to serve as its delimiting factor, and although the *homa* (oblation)— obtained through proximity— is connected as that delimiting factor, it does not possess the status of being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) in that respect,

because it is already established by another source. Rather, the meaning is that what is enjoined is simply another *bhāvanā* denoted by the suffix, which is delimited by the *homa* and has curd (*dadhi*) as its substratum (*karaṇa*).

(The determination of Pārthasārathi’s view: that the *bhāvanā* is connected [to the sacrifice] through the instrumentality of either the state of being the locus of curd or the curd itself which has become the instrument.

Thus, first of all, the instrumentality residing in the curd is defined in relation to the sense-faculty; and since that quality, consisting of the curd and so forth, requires a specific verbal root-meaning achievable by human effort (*kṛti*) in order to bring about its own instrumental status, [it connects with the sacrifice].
Having stated his own view— that this very [requirement] is the expectation for a substratum (*āśraya*),

and that through it there is the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the oblation (*homa*)— Pārthasārathi and others maintain that the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) conveyed by the third case-ending connects with the efficient-force of the sense-organ (*indriya-bhāvanā*) by way of the relation of instrumentality; thus, because the curd (*dadhi*) possesses primacy as the substantive (*dharmin*), the instrumentality belongs to the curd which possesses the power of instrumentality (*karaṇatā-śaktimat*).

Alternatively, because the meaning of the suffix (pratyayārtha) is predominant with respect to the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha), the very locus-hood (*karaṇatva*) of the curd is itself the instrumentality. As for the second instrumentality, since it is understood through co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*), its appearance is accepted as occurring via the sphere of relation (*saṃsargamaryādā*). Then, when there is a requirement for a relatum (*nirūpaka*) for the locus-hood expressed by the third case-ending, it is stated that the contextual substratum (*āśraya*) is obtained precisely in the manner of a counter-correlative (*pratisambandhin*).
He refutes that [position] by first providing its justification, beginning with the words: "But some, however..."

"Just as the sacrifice possesses the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*), but the status of being an instrument does not belong to the "instrumentality of the sacrifice," so it is also in the present case; thus is the refutation of the previous view.
This is [the meaning of] "the dissimilarity with the sacrifice" (*yāgavaiṣamya*).

Since the grammatical rule states, "The stem and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together," and since it has been established in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* that even the objecthood and instrumentality residing in the sacrifice appear as word-meanings (*padārtha*),
there is no evidence for a discrepancy [between the two cases], because in that instance too, it follows that the instrumentality of the sacrifice itself is what constitutes its instrumentality.

In this case as well, the avoidance [of the objection] is untenable because the relation of instrumentality (*karaṇatā*) is more cumbersome than the relation of being a qualifier (*nirūpakatā*). Even though the oblation itself is brought forth by the word as the qualifier of the substratum-ness of the curd, nevertheless, since the word "sense-faculty" (*indriya*) cannot be rendered meaningless, there is no fault in accepting that [the curd's instrumentality] is mediated by the oblation and is thus defined by the sense-faculty through a traditional succession. This is the meaning.

Having first refuted Pārthasārathi’s definition of "substratum" (*āśrayatva*), [the authors] establish that the common definition of a substratum— applicable to both the *manthyagrata* and the *grahaṇa*— is "the state of being delimited by a specific quality through a relationship that does not involve an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*).

Furthermore, based on the natural sense of the *Śāstradīpikā* passage in the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*, which states, "In this context, that wherein the enjoined quality becomes a factor of action (*kāraka*) is the substratum," they define the characteristic of a substratum as "being produced by the enjoined quality."

In the injunction regarding the fruit of a quality, such as "one desiring [success] should have the *tanmanthi* first," it is incorrect [to claim that the cups are the substratum] because the cups are not seen to be produced by the state of having the *tanmanthi* first;

rather, as should be seen in the *Kaustubha*, being a substratum consists simply in being delimited by a specific quality through a relationship that does not operate via an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*).
(An examination of the purpose of the former and latter views, preceded by the refutation of the purpose of the Siddhānta favored by the ancients.)
The purpose is as follows.
In the first case, once the rite has begun, if the curd is lost, a substitute must be employed in accordance with the principle of completing what has been commenced;
however, prior to that, in the absence of curd, there is no undertaking of the rite at all.

In the second case, although it is said: "That part of the sacrifice is severed which occurs when the ritual framework (*tantra*) of one [deity] is already extended while the ritual framework of another is being performed..."

Because of the prohibition, "it is extended," it is impossible to perform another optional rite within the same single performance [of the Agnihotra]. Therefore, the ancients stated the purpose [of this discussion] as follows: outside of the Agnihotra, the curd-oblation (dadhi-homa), which has no fixed time, should be performed once only because it is a *darvihoma* and thus a new (*apūrva*) rite. Nevertheless, even though it is a *darvihoma*, since the extension of the ritual properties (*dharmātideśa*) of the Agnihotra was established in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the time for it is determined by] the time of the Agnihotra.
Since the performance [of the two rites] would be obtained through *tantra* (simultaneous performance), there is no possibility of performing them outside of their respective ritual procedures;

therefore, the purpose of the mention "I shall perform both actions by way of *tantra* for the sake of each respective fruit" at the beginning of the *saṃkalpa* (resolution) must be understood as stated in the *Kaustubha*. This is indicated by the use of the terms "special" (*viśeṣa*) and "established conclusion" (*siddhāntapada*), which imply a distinction [from the general case].

(In this context, the determination that when the substratum in a rule concerning a quality and its fruit has an unseen purpose, there is a distinction between *apūrva*s, whereas otherwise there is unity:
Here, because of the difference in the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—which has curd as its locus and the sense organ as its object—there is one *apūrva* produced by the quality.

Since the oblation itself, prompted by heaven, serves as the substratum, there is another *apūrva* conducive to the heaven produced by the oblation; thus, there is indeed a distinction between the *apūrva*s.

However, where the act of carrying [the fire] and so forth serves its own purpose—namely, the reaching of a northern location—by way of a visible result, there the *apūrva* is produced solely by the subordinate factor (*guṇa*).

Therefore, since even the *homa* (oblation) merely effects the status of curd as an instrument (*karaṇatā*) and is not itself produced by a further *apūrva*, it should be understood that there is no other *apūrva* produced by the *homa* that is conducive to the [attainment of] sensory power (*indriya*).

(An exposition on how the requirement for the *itikartavyatā* [procedure] of another *bhāvanā* is satisfied through the extension (*atideśa*) of the properties of its substratum (*āśraya*), even in the absence of similarity):
Even if there is a requirement for the *itikartavyatā* of another *bhāvanā*, it is not possible to grasp the *itikartavyatā* of the substratum itself by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*),
because a *homa* connected with [results such as] heaven does not fall within the scope of that context.

Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*), since the substrate (*āśraya*) exists, its requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is satisfied by incidental extension (*prasaṅga*), and thus there is no need for a separate requirement for the procedure. This is because the substrate, by virtue of effecting the realization of the instrument (*karaṇatā*), is included within the category of the instrument; therefore, the procedure that assists it must be required as something distinct.
Nevertheless, the requirement is satisfied through the extension of properties (*dharmātideśa*) from the substrate.
Since there is an absence of similarity (*sādṛśya*), how can there be an extended application (*atideśa*) of a conceptual statement?
For the effect of similarity—namely, the presentation of a specific prototype (*prakṛti*)—is already established by the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself, and thus it is not required here.
Therefore, the extended application of ritual properties (*dharma*) is logical.
In this regard, the distinction as to why that [reasoning] applies to some dharmas but not to others should be examined in the *Kaustubha*.
Thus ends the eleventh section concerning those who desire specific qualities.
(B1) (12th Adhikaraṇa /) (A.2 Pāda 2 Adhi.12) When [the qualities] are equal.

Regarding the Agniṣṭut sacrifice enjoined by the rule “The Agniṣṭut is a Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma,” once its connection with a fruit has been established by the statement “Desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcas), one should sacrifice with this, having made the Vāyavyā verses the twenty-one-fold Agniṣṭoma-sāman,” there is subsequently recited:
“Desiring cattle, one should sacrifice with this very same [sacrifice], having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman upon the Revatī verses.”

In this regard as well, the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as before: according to the principle of the *rājasūya*, since there exists a quality connected to the counter-correlative—namely, the time, agent, and so forth, which constitute the meaning of the suffix *-ktvā* and are qualified by the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* bhāvanā characterized by its own factors—it is possible for an injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) qualified by application (*viniyoga*). And this very method is accepted even by the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) in the case of the *vāyavya* sentence.
But the second [position] is not correct here, because the logic of the *rājasūya* does not apply;

since both the performance and the fact that it occurs after the *agniṣṭoma* stotra are already established by the sentence concerning the *vāyavya* verses alone, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) if one were to enjoin the *revatī* verses by way of restatement and simultaneously enjoin the application of the *agniṣṭut* for the sake of the result.

For in the case of the *vāyavya* injunction, properties such as the sequence following the *agniṣṭoma* stotra—which could have been obtained through extension (*atideśa*)—are set aside by being treated as qualifiers of the performance (*prayoga*), on the grounds that [the *vāyavya* injunction] is accepted as applying first.
But this is not the case here; since the *vāyavya* injunction itself is already established (*klpta*), it is untenable to accept its prior application.
Nor is there a lack of a decisive factor (*vinigamanāviraha*).

Because primacy alone is the determining factor, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is the quality (*guṇa*) itself—either that which is called the *vāravantīya* having the *revatī* verses as its locus, or that which is called *revatī* itself—that is enjoined with reference to the fruit, since it has not [otherwise] been established.
This is because the *vāravantīya* is already established by the contextual sentence: "The *vāravantīya* should be performed as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*."
Nor, in the final position, is there an impossibility of indicating the *revatī* verses alone by means of this word ending in the third case, because it possesses different genders and numbers;

for even if there is an indication of the *vāravantīya* chant as qualified by the *revatī* verses, it is logical that the connection with the fruit belongs to the *revatī* verses alone—which were not previously established—according to the principle of the *dākṣāyaṇayajña*.
Therefore, the connection between the accessory (*guṇa*) and the fruit is indeed proper, according to the analogy of the curd (*dadhi*).
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that it is not possible to assert the attainment of a substratum (*āśraya*) here.

For although the sacrifice (*yāga*) is indeed the subject under discussion, it cannot serve as the direct substratum because the reference (*anuvāda*) to the "Agniṣṭoma-sāman" would otherwise be untenable.

Furthermore, the possibility of that very sacrifice serving as the substratum through the medium of the Agniṣṭoma-stotra is not to be suspected, since the Agniṣṭoma-stotra is already present by way of extension (*atideśa*) as being common to other stotras.
Nor is there a specific presentation of that [sāman] as being directly taught (aupadeśika) by the sentence concerning the Vāyu-vessel;

for when it is possible for an extended application (ātideśika) to sublate [a rule], it is improper to sublate what is directly taught, and thus a specific presentation cannot establish its status as a substrate. Nor can it be argued that there is no harm even if a substrate is not obtained—on the grounds that the sāman is of the nature of an action since it is denoted by the verbal root *gāyati*—because...

Since *sāman*— which is well-known from supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) and the like as being a collection of tones consisting of sound— is an established entity, its being denoted by a verbal root is not a determining factor; otherwise, it would be impossible for the *saubhara* to have the *stotra* as its substratum,
and the descriptive reference (*anuvāda*) "the *agniṣṭomasāman*" and so forth would be untenable if the *vāravantīya-sāman* did not require a substratum.

Therefore, since the *sāman* requires a substratum (*āśraya*), its substratum cannot first be obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*). Nor should it be argued that the substratum is provided by the very sentence within the context stating "the *vāravantīya* should be performed as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*," because—out of fear of prolixity—that sentence does not enjoin the *vāravantīya* as a subordinate element (*aṅga*). While it might be possible to obtain the substratum if the *sāman* were the subordinate element, such a connection is impossible when only the *revatī* verses are the subordinate element.
However, the quality-status (*guṇatva*) of the *sāman* is impossible because the injunction would apply only to those *revatī* verses that have not already been obtained [by another rule].

For in the absence of a word denoting a fruit, the injunction—operating toward whatever object it has not previously obtained—becomes connected with a fruit due to that object's requirement for a purpose, as is the case with the *godohana* vessel and so forth.

Therefore, in this instance, since the *vāravantīya* is already established by the contextual statement itself, the injunction results in applying only to the *revatī* verses that were not previously obtained; thus, it is that [injunction] alone which is connected with the fruit.
It must be stated that its substratum cannot be obtained by any means whatsoever.

Nor can its attainment be justified by this very sentence through the injunction of a quality qualified by a substratum, or through the injunction of an efficient force (*bhāvanā*) qualified by both the substratum and the quality, simply because it is not obtained by any other way.

It should not be argued that because the purpose [of the action] has already been established and for the sake of parsimony, one accepts the qualification [of the substrate] solely through the relation of "substratum-ness" (āśrayatā), and thus there is no resulting status of being a subordinate factor (guṇāṅgatā) [of the substrate];
for there is no grammatical derivation (avyutpatti) of the substrate's connection with the quality,

and because "substratum-ness" is difficult to define as something distinct from "object-ness" (karmatva), if one were to accept that the productive operation (bhāvanā) has two objects consisting of both the fruit and the substrate, it would result in the collapse of its status as having a single object.

And it is not the case that— having [performed] what is expressed by the word *kṛtvā*— since the substrate, namely the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*, is the object (*karman*), the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) which serves as the delimitant for a single *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) denoted by the verb suffix and qualified by the subsequent time, must have the sacrifice as its delimitant; for if the *revatī* verses were to become the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the sacrifice, they could not possibly be the instrument with respect to the *stotra*.

If, however, one accepts that the *stotra* (laudatory hymn) itself is the delimiter [of the action], then because there would be no two distinct efficient forces (*bhāvanā*) delimited by two distinct verbal root meanings, the suffix *-tva* (forming the word *revatītva*) would be untenable.

Nor should it be argued: "Let the very efficient force which has as its substratum a sacrifice performed with the *revatī* verses—characterized by a time subsequent to the efficient force of the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* qualified by the *revatī* verses—be enjoined with reference to the fruit. For in that case, the flaw remains: the efficient force denoted by the verb would incur the status of having two objects (*dvikarmakatva*).
Nor is it the case that because the sacrifice (*yāga*) can be established as the substratum through context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, the verb does not have two objects;

for even if that were so, since the pronoun *etad* ending in the third case would—out of fear of making the verbal root subordinate (*pārārthya*)—necessarily refer back to the sacrifice, there would be no evidence that it refers instead to the *revatī* verses and so on.
Therefore, rather than that, it is better to assume the injunction of a different, simpler action (*karmāntara*).

For instance: because this [rite] is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Agniṣṭut sacrifice by virtue of belonging to the same class (*nikāya*), the *Vāravantīya* chant is merely restated as something already established.
Only the production (*bhāvanā*) of another sacrifice—characterized by the subsequent time of the *stotra* (chant) qualified by the *Revatī* verses—is enjoined with reference to the fruit.
The word "this" (*etad*) in the genitive case serves to restate the relationship between the original form (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*).

The word *etat* (this) in the third case-ending, denoting the ritual action about to be introduced, is not defective. Furthermore, although the quality characterized by the subsequent time— because it is connected with the performance— might, like the *Aveṣṭi*, bring about a distinction [in the ritual], nevertheless,

since the time here has a possibility of being obtained [from elsewhere], even though it is prescribed for the sake of avoiding a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), it is understood through the intended meaning (*tātparya*) as follows:

In the sacrifice, because the enjoined accessory named Revatī is connected to the origination [of the rite] through a traditional relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*), there is no obstruction to its being understood as indicating a difference in the ritual action. // 1.2 //
Thus ends the twelfth section concerning Revatī.

(B2) [The distinction of the extracted meaning according to the established doctrine regarding the two statements concerning Vāyu and Revatī, and the connection by way of exception with the preceding section.
He cites the scriptural passage that constitutes the subject matter of the section: "trivṛt... etc.

And this has been cited merely for the purpose of demonstrating the counter-positive of the distinction, because only the *Revatī* passage itself is the subject of investigation. In the *Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa*, it is stated at the outset: "He who is as if impure should sacrifice with the *Agniṣṭut*; by means of Agni alone, he strikes away his evil."

Having prescribed one *agniṣṭut* sacrifice characterized by the *trivṛt* [stoma] with the words, "The *trivṛt* bestows splendor and Vedic luster," and having there proclaimed the defect in being *trivṛt*, [the text] prescribes another *agniṣṭut* sacrifice characterized by the *catuṣṭoma* with the words, "The *agniṣṭut* is the *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma*; for it,
[the verses] addressed to Vāyu [are used]," and then records, "For this very same [sacrifice], [the verses] addressed to Revatī [are used]."
In this regard, although the first three words ending in the nominative case are unfit for syntactic connection with the verb *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice"),
nevertheless, by supplying the word *kartavyaḥ* ("should be performed"), there is an injunction of a sacrifice named Agniṣṭut, characterized by two qualities, namely the *trivṛt* and so forth.
This is because these six Agniṣṭuts are recorded as being grouped together (*nikāya*) according to the commentary in the *Parimala* on the section concerning deities.

And since it has been established in the eighth [chapter] that there is an extension (*atideśa*) of those [details] from the former to the latter, the injunction that the *trivṛt* state applies to all the hymns (*stotra*s) by subverting the previously obtained fourfold nature of the *catuṣṭoma*— consisting of the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, *saptadaśa*, and *ekaviṃśa*— is made. For this very reason, it cannot be said that the word "Agniṣṭoma" is an injunction for the *agniṣṭoma* form [of the sacrifice].

Nevertheless, it should be understood that this [text] is intended to enjoin the *agniṣṭoma* arrangement (*saṃsthā*), with the result of excluding the *atyagniṣṭoma* status—which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *agniṣṭoma* arrangement caused by the presence of a Kṣatriya sacrificer.

As for what is stated in the *Kaustubha*: since the sacrifice preceding this one has the *ukthya* arrangement and is determined to be the archetype (*prakṛti*) of this sacrifice due to belonging to the same ritual group (*nikāya*), the *ukthya* arrangement alone would otherwise be obtained; therefore, this text is intended as an injunction for the purpose of restoring (*pratiprasava*) the *agniṣṭoma* arrangement.
An alternative view has been stated by Pūjyapāda:

although the *catuṣṭoma-agniṣṭut* sacrifice is enjoined earlier in the *Tāṇḍya*, it must be considered what its basis is, since it is not recorded as having the *ukthya* as its concluding form (*saṃsthā*).

Alternatively, the term *agniṣṭut* is a name based on the rule of "designation by that which is well-known" (*tatprakhyanyāya*), because of the recording of a hymn (*stotra*) to be accomplished by mantras dedicated to the deity Agni.

By the sentence “*tasya vāyavyāsvi*,” there is an injunction for the performance of the sacrifice— characterized by the time subsequent to the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* which is qualified by being the locus of the *vāyavya* verses beginning with “*upatvā jāmayo giraḥ*” and by having the twenty-one-fold hymn (*ekaviṃśastoma*)—
for the sake of the fruit.

In that context, regarding the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*, there is a reinstatement (*pratiprasava*) of the twenty-fold hymn (*viṃśastoma*) which had been previously obtained through extension (*atideśa*) but was sublated by the threefold hymn (*trivṛt*).

Thus, there is an injunction of the Vāyavya mantras by way of setting aside the mantras "yajñā yajñāvo" which would otherwise apply through extended application (*atideśa*). In the sentence concerning the *Revatīs*, there is an injunction regarding the fruit of the production (*bhāvanā*) of a sacrifice characterized by a time subsequent to the production of the *Agniṣṭoma* stotra—which has the *Vāravantīya* Sāman as its substrate and the *Revatī* Ṛk (beginning with "revatīr naḥ sadhamāda")—as its locus; consequently, there is a setting aside of the original source (*yoni*), namely "aśvaṃ natvā vāravantaṃ vandadhyai," as well as the two verses following it, because the *Revatīs* serve as the substratum for the *Vāravantīya*.

Although it is possible for the mental realization (*bhāvanā*) of the *agniṣṭoma* chant to precede the performance of the sacrifice— given that the *agniṣṭoma* is the very last [chant]— nevertheless, for the sake of facilitating the performance of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), such a determination is made from the beginning.

Since the verb *karoti* (he does) is used even in the sense of "determination" (*adhyavasāna*)— as in the expressions "he does with speech" and "he does with the mind"— it follows that [the action] is preceded by "comprehension" (*pratipatti*), which is another synonym for determination (*adhyavasāna*).

Alternatively, as in the case of "he sleeps with his mouth open" (*mukhaṃ vyādāya svapiti*), it should be understood that the application of the suffix *ktvā* is possible through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by virtue of simultaneity; this is the distinction.

In this regard, since the present section serves as a refutation (*apavāda*) of precisely those two points—the connection between a quality and a fruit and the non-difference of the verbal root's meaning—which were established in the preceding section, the author does not explicitly state the immediate transition (*anantara-saṅgati*) as a refutation, but rather states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) immediately:
"In that case also... (*tatrāpi*).

(An explanation that there is no difference in the ritual action [karmabheda] in the Revatī-vākya, because only the application and performance are enjoined according to the principle of the Rājasūya):

First of all, this is not a separate ritual action, because of the recognition of the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛta-pratyabhijñāna*), the hearing of the word "this" (*etac-chabda-śruti*), and the absence of any evidence [to the contrary].

Furthermore, it cannot be a connection between a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and a result (*phala*), because—as will be explained in the final position (*siddhānta*)—there is no basis (*āśraya*) for such a connection.

Therefore, the meaning of the first position is that, just as in the case of the Vāyavya passage, there is an injunction regarding the performance of that very same ritual action— characterized by a time subsequent to the *revatī*-based *agniṣṭoma* stotra— for the sake of the fruit. For here, unlike a quality such as curd (*dadhi*), which is connected to the originative injunction (*utpatti*), it is not possible for this [injunction] to bring about a different originative act.

It is intended to be stated that this is because you yourself must also assert that the agent, time, and so forth, function as qualifiers of the usage (*prayoga*), since they are connected with that usage by virtue of being its form. Thus it was said: "and it is desired to be indicated."

(The demonstration that Revatī is not enjoined as a subsidiary to the Sāman out of fear of postulating an unestablished function, but rather as a subsidiary to the Stotra, by means of the phrase "by way of reference to that":
*tadanuvādena*.)
The meaning is "by way of restating the Agniṣṭoma-stotra.

Although it is understood from the co-occurrence with the term *agniṣṭomasāman* that the Revatī verses serve as the substratum for the Sāman, nevertheless, because it would lead to the assumption of an unestablished function, the injunction of the Revatīs is not as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the Sāman.

However, the intention is that, having restated the connection with the *sāman* which is obtained through the sequence of the context (*pārṣṭhika-anvaya*), and having accepted the word *agniṣṭoma* as being dominated by its qualifier, the statement of the injunction for the mantra is made precisely as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *stotra*. Since it would be impossible to refer to the mere quality named *revatī* by means of this pronoun (*etac-chabda*) whose gender does not match, he speaks of the quality of the *vāravantīya* as qualified by that [quality], namely: "having the *revatīs* as its substratum" (*revaty-adhikaraṇaka*).
Because it has not been attained.
He establishes this very point with the words: "The Vāravantīya."

(Regarding the distinction [of the *vāravantīya*] through its understanding as a *pārṣṭhika* [subsequent] [rite] in the case of the *revatī* and *vāravantīya* [sāmans]: even though the meaning of the verbal root—the *vāravantīya* qualified by the *revatīs*—is not of the nature of an action (*akriyārūpa*), it has a connection with the result by being based on the sacrifice or based on the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*).
And here, in the first position, although this word is justified, there is no connection of the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*—which has the *revatīs* as its constituent part—with the result.
Because if the word "agniṣṭomasāman" were to have its qualifier as the primary meaning, it would result in the fault of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā);
rather, it refers specifically to the Vāravantīya sāman which has the Revatī verses as its locus.

Although there is no possibility of mutual qualification between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant because they function as distinct causal factors (*kāraka*), nevertheless, by accepting that both first enter into the *bhāvanā* expressed by the word *kṛtvā*, there is no obstacle to the subsequent cognition (*pārṣṭhika-bodha*) wherein the *revatī* verses are qualified by the *vāravantīya*. Thus, there is no inconsistency in the meaning: "Having performed the *vāravantīya* upon the *revatī* verses, one should bring about the result by means of it."

And since that [sāman], which consists of the natural collection [of sounds], exists as an established entity in the form of words such as *dhvanyādi*—just like the *saubhara* chant—it requires a substratum (*āśraya*). In this regard, it is logical that the very *agniṣṭut* sacrifice under discussion serves as its substratum; thus, the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that sacrifice. Nor does the *sāman* possess the nature of an action simply because it is denoted by the verbal root *gā* (to sing);
for even though cheeks and other parts are denoted by roots such as *gaḍi* (in the sense of a part of the face), they are not of the nature of an action because they exist as established entities.

Regarding the word *sāman*, since the Veda states that its meaning is a certain secondary tone (*svara*) which is a means [to the rite], and because the word *svara* denotes a collection of tones such as *ṣaḍja* and so forth;

and because, upon examining the treatises on music (*saṅgītaśāstra*)—such as the passage "The wind moving in the chest produces the deep tone (*mandra*)"—it is understood that the word refers to a specific sound consisting of resonance (*dhvani*) produced by the conjunction and disjunction of the established forms of the *vāravantīya* and other [chants]; and because it is thereby understood that the *vāravantīya* and so forth are already established entities.
Therefore, since there is a requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*) for that [Sāman], its status as a substratum is entirely logical.
For it is possible for the sacrifice to accomplish the stotra by means of the manifestation of the syllables of the *ṛc* verses through the Sāman, just as a stotra accomplishes the sacrifice.

Consequently, just as the Saubhara Sāman is based on the stotra, the Vāravantīya’s being based on the sacrifice is not contradictory; this is because it serves as the substratum for its own mantras, such as the *yājyā*, just like the quality of being recited loudly (*uccaiṣṭva*) and so forth.
For this very reason, it should also be inferred that even the *revatī* verses are to be employed in functions such as the *yājyā*.

Furthermore, although the general rule regarding monotonous chanting (*ekaśruti*) and so forth—obtained through a general injunction—is set aside by the optional *vāravantīya* chant, there is no fault in this.

If, however, one should suspect that the descriptive reference (*anuvāda*) "the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*" would be untenable [if the *vāravantīya* were merely optional], [that objection is addressed as follows].

In that case, since the *vāyavyā* verses are specifically presented as belonging to the *agniṣṭoma* stotra itself, that [stotra] alone serves as the substratum (*āśraya*). Furthermore, because that [stotra] is already established through its connection with the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice, the genitive ending in *yajñaḥ*, the word *etad* (this), and the suffix *-tva* are merely restatements (*anuvāda*); thus, there is no defect whatsoever.

(Although both the connection of the *revatī* verses with the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice and their connection with the fruit are being enjoined, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because another *bhāvanā* is accepted as subordinate to the primary *bhāvanā*.

In the second alternative, even if the fact that the *revatī* verses reside solely in the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* were obtained from another source—by which their attainment as a substratum would allow for the statement "the *agniṣṭoma-soma*" to be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*); [this is not the case].
Nevertheless, there is no defect whatsoever in this very injunction regarding the connection of the *revatī* verses with their substratum, the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*;

nor is there a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because such a split does not arise since it is accepted that the *revatī* verses, expressed by the word "having performed" (*kṛtvā*), connect with the subsequent productive urge (*bhāvanā*) through the sequence: "having performed the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* upon the *revatī* verses."

Therefore, the sense is that there is no harm even if, according to our own established doctrine (siddhānta), one accepts an injunction for the efficient-force of a quality (*guṇabhāvanā*) qualified by the efficient-force of a sacrifice, which is itself qualified by the efficient-force of a stotra characterized by [the asterism] Revatī and so forth.

(Since the second alternative of the first prima facie view has already been refuted, this section establishes the impossibility of either the sacrifice or the stotra being the substratum [āśraya] by way of the stotra; it does so by setting aside that refutation and addressing the second alternative, raising the question of how the substratum is obtained from the context: is the sacrifice the direct substratum, or is it so through the Agniṣṭoma-stotra? With the intention of refuting this by means of such alternatives, the author states the established conclusion [siddhānta]: "But the established conclusion... etc. Since the second alternative of the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has already been refuted, the author sets aside that refutation and, in order to establish the attainment of a substratum (*āśraya*) for the second alternative through the context (*prakaraṇa*), proceeds to refute it by posing the following dilemma: Is the sacrifice the direct substratum, or is it so by way of the Agniṣṭoma-stotra? With this intention, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The state of being a basis.

The word "tu" (but) indicates that it is impossible for the Agniṣṭoma stotra to serve as the substratum (*āśraya*) of the sacrifice by way of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭavidhayā*), since it is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice only through that [unseen potency].
For, by way of a seen potency (*dṛṣṭavidhayā*), a quality requires a connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which is to be accomplished by human effort (*kṛtisādhya*).

If it were to depend on that [sacrifice] by way of an unseen potency, then even without a substratum, the status of the quality as an instrument for the result could be established through an unseen potency; consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence that there is no requirement for a substratum at all.

Therefore, in the definition of the substratum (*āśraya*), the qualification of being delimited by a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣāvacchinnatva*) was introduced through a relation that does not involve the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) in the preceding section.
Thus, the meaning is that [the *agniṣṭoma*] is not a substratum by way of that [unseen force].
He states another objection as well: "of the *agniṣṭoma* chant" (*agniṣṭomastotrasya*).
(The demonstration that it is logical for the *atideśika* [extended application] of the Revatī verses to be sublated, resulting in their becoming the substratum for all the *stotras*:
"The term *ātideśika*... [is used].

The meaning is as follows: since the presence of the *agniṣṭoma* stotra as the locus for the *vāyavya* verses is indeed based on direct injunction (*aupadeśika*), there arises the contingency of subverting the directly enjoined *vāyavya* verses by means of the *revatī* verses; therefore, by accepting that all stotras—obtained through extension (*atideśa*)—serve as its locus, it is logical that the verses obtained through that same extension of the [original] *agniṣṭoma* stotra be subverted, resulting in the conclusion that all stotras indeed serve as the locus.
Nor should it be argued that the sublation of the obligatory (*nitya*) by the optional (*kāmya*) is established by logic alone;
for even in the view where the *vāravantīya* sāman is subordinate (*guṇa*) in the *Revatī-adhikaraṇa*, although the sāman is optional, the *revatī* verses themselves lack that status.

Furthermore, even in the view where the *revatī* verses are subordinate, the sublation of the archetypal (*ātideśika*) ṛg-verses by them is possible only to the extent that they [the *revatī*s] are employed.
The meaning is that, for the time being, it is not appropriate to object on the basis of the scriptural injunction regarding the Vāyavya sacrifice.
(Critique of the Vārtika on the view that *sāman* is of the nature of an action):
As for what is stated in the Vārtika—"For an action is supported by qualities that are themselves non-actional in nature;
but what purpose would there be for the action consisting of the singing of the *vāravantīya*?"—[that is refuted as follows].

By the words beginning with "ityādinā," it was stated that because *sāman* has the nature of an action (*kriyārūpa*), there is no requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*), and thus no connection between a quality (*guṇa*) and a fruit (*phala*).
This is restated in order to refute it by means of a bold argument (*prauḍhi*), and then refuted with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
This has been explained previously:

[it concerns] the demonstration that the statement "the Vāravantīya should be performed as the Agniṣṭoma-sāman" (which occurs in the section on the Catuṣṭoma) actually belongs to the section on the Agniṣṭut,
by means of the contextual factor (*prākaraṇika*).
Although this statement is recorded in the *Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa* within the context of the *Catuṣṭoma-Agniṣṭut* prior to the *Agniṣṭut* sacrifice itself— and not within the context of the *Agniṣṭut*—

nevertheless, because the *Catuṣṭoma* belongs to the same class (*nikāyin*) and thus has the subsequent *Agniṣṭut* as its archetype, it is stated that [the injunction] is by means of a contextual sentence (*prākaraṇika-vākya*) through the extension of an extended statement (*atideśaprāptavacanātideśatvena*).

Therefore, the *Vārttika* explains that the statement from the *Bhāṣya*, "But when a specific sacrifice is being undertaken, how then does the Vāravantīya Sāman come to be upon the Revatī verses?"— which is intended as a response to an objection— should be understood as a statement based on extended application (*atideśika*).

(Refutation of the view that the *vāravantīya* sentence within the context serves as the provider of the substratum, on the grounds that it possesses the quality of being [merely] a reference to Revatī:
"For fear of prolixity."

The meaning is that, in comparison with being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) characterized by being the agent of an action initiated for the sake of another (*paroddeśapravṛttakṛtikārakatva*), the status of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) characterized by being the object (*karmatva*) is simpler (*laghubhūta*).
Nor is it a defect in this view that the sublation of the original (upadeśika) ṛks would entail the sublation of the extended (ātideśika) ṛks;

for, since other stotras would have to serve as the substrata, there would result the sublation of both their respective ṛks and the sāmans. Compared to the sublation of both, the sublation of the original Vāyavya [ṛk] is more appropriate, and thus it is fitting that the Agniṣṭoma stotra serves as the substratum—this is the underlying sense.

Having thus considered the first position—stated by the ancients as being untenable because the substratum (āśraya) is obtained through the possibility of [the sacrifice's] acquisition—to explain its untenability on the grounds that the quality of the *vāravantīya* is already established here and thus lacks the status of being something to be enjoined, [the author] says: "Of the *sāman*... (*sāmna iti*).

In reality, however, there would arise the fault of inconsistency (*vairūpya*): this sentence, though belonging to the present context and though the *catuṣṭoma-vāravantīya-sāman* is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), would have to convey both the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* and, in this instance, the relationship with its substratum (*āśraya*).

Otherwise, since it would not even be possible for the *vāravantīya* to be obtained as a subordinate element of the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* by virtue of the *vāyavyādhikaraṇa* principle, it could not possibly convey a relationship with a substratum; thus, even if its attainment were otherwise established...
This is also indicated by the word "api" (even/also).

(The refutation [of the injunction of a quality qualified by a substratum in the form of the *agniṣṭoma* stotra], on the grounds that the nature of being a substratum—since it consists in being an object of action—makes qualification impossible, etc., and because its purpose is already established.
"Because its purpose is already established."
The meaning is that, because its purpose is already established by the extension (*atideśa*) of the substratum consisting of the *agniṣṭoma* stotra as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of this sacrifice.

He states—"of the substratum"—because even if the Revatī verses, as qualified by their substratum which is the Agniṣṭoma stotra, were enjoined for the sake of the fruit, a relation of qualification (vaiśiṣṭya) would still be impossible, since both [the stotra and the verses] are equally causal factors (kāraka).

[Objection: But surely, just as in the case of *soma* and other [substances], by accepting that both are initially construed as subordinate (*guṇa*) to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), their mutual qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) can indeed be established subsequently (*pārṣṭhika*). To this, he says: "other than being an object" (*karmatvātirikteti*). Their construction with the productive urge is not first of all as an instrument (*karaṇatvena*);
for if that were the case, the logic of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* would apply, resulting in that [instrument] itself becoming connected to the fruit.
Furthermore, because that which is presented as an instrument cannot be connected with a quality,
nor can it be [connected] as a procedure (*itikartavyatā*),
since its purpose is already established.
And because it would result in the qualities becoming subordinate members;
therefore, by process of elimination, [the object] is understood as the primary object (karma),
and when that is resorted to, it is understood as the desired object (īpsita-karma).
In that case, because there would be multiple intended objects, there would be the consequence of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*),
as well as the consequence that the accessory (*guṇa*) would become a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the substratum (*āśraya*).
However, if [the action] were considered an unintended object (*anīpsitakarman*), [this fault would not arise].

The meaning is that even then, because the fruit would also be construed as an object (*karman*), or because the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) would possess two objects, there would result the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
[This applies] only to the hymn (*stotra*).

Furthermore, the impossibility of the injunction "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) being a mere restatement (anuvāda) if one accepts the hymn as the limiting factor has been indicated by the word "but" (tu).
(Regarding the doubt concerning a difference in meditative cultivation:
[The objection] "by means of the suffix -ktvā" [is raised].

The meaning is that the suffix *ktvā*, which is prescribed after a verbal root denoting an action occurring at an earlier time between two actions having the same agent, would be untenable if there were no distinction between the two actions.
(The justification for the understanding of the bhāvanā as having the *revatī*-based sacrifice as its locus. The phrase "and not" (*na ca*) means:

although the word *revatīṣu* is connected with the *bhāvanā* of the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*, and thus an understanding of a *bhāvanā* having a sacrifice based on the *revatī* verses as its locus is not possible;

nevertheless, since the word *etena*—even though it denotes the *vāravantīya*—can, like the word *dākṣāyaṇa*, refer to the quality of the *revatī* verses, the understanding of a *bhāvanā* having a sacrifice based on the *revatī* verses as its locus is indeed possible. This is the intended meaning.
He establishes the very state of being light [in weight] with the words "for instance" (*tathāhi*);
this is the justification for [the statement] that it is a restatement of the *vāravantīya* verse,
because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice.

The phrase "the *trivṛt* *agniṣṭut* *agniṣṭoma*" refers to the previously mentioned *agniṣṭut* enjoined by that sentence; because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the earlier fourfold-stoma (*catuṣṭoma*) *agniṣṭut*, the term *vāravantīya* is a restatement (*anuvāda*), as it is obtained through a series of extensions (*atideśa*). Although, since both the *agniṣṭoma* stotra and the *vāravantīya* melody are obtained through extension, a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) would result from enjoining them with reference to one another due to the impossibility of their mutual qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*); nevertheless, in order to achieve such qualification, the extension operates according to the principle of the "qualified injunction" (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), which states: "That which is already obtained is enjoined in conjunction with a qualified injunction. Thus, the extension proceeds by way of this principle of qualified injunction.

Alternatively, it has been stated that even though it is an injunction, it is restated because it is already established, on the assumption that it was previously in operation, just as in the case of the Vāyavya passage.
(The genitive form *etasyaiva* indicates the relationship between the original material and its modification.

Now, one might object: since the force of the genitive-ending pronoun *etad* suggests that this [act] is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the preceding act—even though it is a distinct ritual act—how can it be enjoined with reference to a fruit? To this, he says: "The genitive-ending *etad*...
For if this word *etat* were also to provide the objective referent (*uddeśya*), there would arise the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by the multiplicity of objectives.
However, if it were merely a restatement of the relationship consisting in having the preceding sacrifice as its archetype, that [result] would not follow.
(The justification for the word *tena* [by him] is that pronouns refer to what is about to be introduced);
[this refers to] "ending in the third case."
Although pronouns generally refer back to what has preceded,

nevertheless, since it is observed that the word *etad* (this) in the sentence "Now this [is] Jyotis" refers even to a rite that is about to be introduced, pronouns may— by setting aside the rule of referring only to what precedes— function as common to both what has been introduced and what is about to be introduced.
The meaning is that there is no contradiction here either, because it is accepted that [the term] denotes merely that which is proximate.

(An objection is raised: "Just as in the case of the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice, since the intention is solely to enjoin the agent who performs the ritual procedure, there is merely a difference in the performance; so too in the present case, because such a time is enjoined, it must be that very same [act]. This is the doubt expressed by the phrase "like the *aveṣṭi*").

In the Rājasūya sacrifice, there are five distinct performances known as the Aveṣṭi offerings, which are traditionally taught; however, because the scriptural injunctions such as "if a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice" prescribe a Brāhmaṇa as the performer, and because the performer must be connected to the performance, it is impossible for these to be included in the previous performance performed by a king. Therefore, regarding the Aveṣṭi:
It will be explained later that a distinct performance (prayoga) is indeed enjoined;

likewise here as well, because the quality characterized by the subsequent time is connected to the performance, a distinct performance results from the performance enjoined by the Vāyavya passage belonging to the previous sacrifice, and not a separate ritual action (karmāntara)— this is the meaning of the phrase "of that which has attained possibility."

If the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) of the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* were not enjoined because it is already established [by another injunction], then, since it would be impossible to enjoin the *revatī* verses as qualifiers of an unenjoined action, they would have to be enjoined by the very injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) which is heard in the text; in that case, the previously mentioned syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would occur.
Therefore, even though that [stotra-bhāvanā] is already established, when it is enjoined, it connects with the subsequent *bhāvanā* through its relation to being posterior in time.

The meaning is as follows: although that which occurs at a subsequent time—which was not previously established by the *vāyavya* sentence—is to be enjoined, this is done by accepting its connection with the verbal root (*bhāva*) expressed by the word *kṛtvā*, in order to avoid the fault of *vākya-bheda* (splitting of the sentence) caused by enjoining both the connection with the quality of the *revatī* verses and the connection with the fruit.
(The fact that the quality of *revatī*, when enjoined through its intended meaning (*tātparyagati*), brings about a distinction between ritual acts,
and the refutation of the doubt that it merely distinguishes the hymns.
[The term in the sūtra is] "non-obstruction" (*avighāta*).

For in all cases, even a quality associated with a number serves as a differentiator only when it is itself the object of an injunction; and here, according to the previously stated reasoning, since it is impossible to enjoin the *revatī* verses as a result, and because they cannot be included in the previous sacrifice due to being precluded by the *vāyavya* verses,

one must— in the injunction of the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) of a sacrifice qualified by the *revatī* verses— take recourse to the sacrifice through the medium of the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*, [the *vāravantīya* being the *agniṣṭoma*...].

The meaning is as follows: since it is accepted that the restatement "having performed the *sāman*" serves merely to indicate the intended purport (*tātparya*), the quality of the *revatī* verses, being enjoined through that intended purport, brings about the status of a distinct rite because it necessitates another production of the action by virtue of its connection with the original production.

Now, one might object: "In that case, since the quality of the *revatī* verses is connected to the *agniṣṭoma* stotra, it would only differentiate that stotra and not differentiate the sacrifice. This doubt is refuted by the word "without obstacle" (*avighāta*).

The meaning is that, since it would follow that another performance must necessarily be enjoined—just as a sacrifice is enjoined with reference to a specific result under such circumstances—it is more appropriate, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), to regard [the difference in words] as a differentiator of the action itself alone.
(The purpose of the prima facie and final positions:

The purpose of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because the optional qualities (*kāmyaguṇa`) are performed just as in the original *agniṣṭut*, [the result follows]. In the final position (*siddhānta*), however, according to the principle of the eighth book (*āṣṭamikanyāya*), there would be the application of the preceding [archetype] to the subsequent [ectypes], because another sacrifice—possessing the characteristics of the previously enjoined *agniṣṭut*—is performed through extension (*atideśa*).
It was not stated explicitly.
Thus ends the twelfth section concerning Revatī.
(B1) (Thirteenth Topic:
[The Saubhara Hymn]) (A.2 Pāda 2 Adhikaraṇa 13) Regarding the Saubhara.

With reference to the hymn known as the *brahmasāman*, the *saubhara* chant— resting upon that hymn— is enjoined for the sake of three results by these sentences: "He who desires rain, he who desires food, and he who desires heaven, should praise with the *saubhara*."
Because there are multiple objects to be enjoined, the sentence-split (*vākya-bheda*) is perceived through the syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*) with the word "one should praise" (*stuvīta*).

Furthermore, in the *saubhara* chant, according to different Vedic branches, syllables such as *hīṣ*, *ū*, and *ūrj* are recited as being based upon the final constituent part of the chant called the *nidhana*.
Thus, with reference to that very *saubhara*, [the text states]: "One desiring rain should employ *hīṣ* as the *nidhana*."
It is heard in scripture: "‘Ū’ for one desiring heaven; ‘Ūrk’ for one desiring food.

In that context, since words such as "one desiring rain" refer to the fruit, the qualities such as *hīṣ* and so forth are enjoined specifically with reference to those fruits. And the *saubhara* chant, being the subject under discussion, serves as the substratum (*āśraya*), just like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and other such entities.

Since the recitation of *hīṣ* and so forth is restricted solely by its status as being based on the *nidhana*, and because it would otherwise entail the sublation of other syllables such as *stobha* in other sections, it cannot follow that the portion beyond the *nidhana* serves as its locus.

Nor should it be suspected—on the grounds of parsimony—that the purpose is merely to establish a restriction for *hīṣ* and so forth, which are obtained without restriction in the *nidhana* of the *saubhara* used as a means to rain;

for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*lakṣaṇā*) of the words "desirous of rain" and so forth indicating the *saubhara* itself as the specific means to those respective results.
Furthermore, if that [term *nidhana*] were a qualifier of the [sacrifice], it would result in the fallacy of enjoining a qualified object (*viśiṣṭoddeśāpatti*).

Therefore, since the *hīṣ* and other syllables serve to produce a different fruit than the fruit of the *saubhara*, this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). However, in accordance with the principle of parsimony regarding restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhilāghava*), one must accept that the terms "one desiring rain" (*vṛṣṭikāma*) and so forth indirectly indicate (*lakṣaṇā*) the *saubhara* as the means to rain;
thus, only a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) concerning the *hīṣ* and other syllables is adopted.

Furthermore, since the attainment of the *pakṣa* (the alternative) occurs only at the position of the *nidhana* due to the textual recitation (*pāṭha*), the rule (*niyama*) also acquires that very position.

In reality, however, in accordance with the parsimony of the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi-lāghava*), it is accepted that *hīṣ* and the others serve the purpose of rain and so forth through their relationship as being the substratum of the *saubhara* which is their own means; thus, there is not even a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And the *saubhara* that constitutes the connector of the relationship is not [the *saubhara*] as delimited by the property of being *saubhara* (*saubharatva-avacchinna*).
Rather, it is specifically a particular *saubhara* chant;
for, according to different Vedic recensions (*śākhā*), various distinct *saubhara*s are recorded in some instances as being joined with other *nidhana*s.
In that case, since the *hīṣ* sound is not even optionally established for that *saubhara*, it cannot serve as a factor constituting a relationship with it.

Moreover, since *hīṣ* and other such elements are prescribed without restriction for a particular class of *saubhara*, they apply only to that specific class. Consequently, by establishing the restriction that *hīṣ* alone is used for the purpose of rain through its specific connection, just as other *nidhanas* are excluded from the *saubhara* that constitutes that connection,
so too is the exclusion of other *saubharas* of a different class from having rain and other purposes established.
Therefore, the distinction is that this [practice] results in being exclusively the domain of constant application. // 1.3 //
Thus ends the thirteenth section concerning Saubhara.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the Bhāṭṭadīpikā composed by the venerable Khaṇḍadeva.

(B2) (The determination that this very passage, which is recited in proximity to a permanent injunction and serves as an applicatory statement for a desired purpose, constitutes the subject matter of this section:
In the *Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa*, within the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the *Ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, it is stated: "The *saubhara* becomes the *brahmasāman* of the *ukthya*s.

By this, the *saubhara*—which is understood from the scriptural recitation to be intended for the *brahmasāman* chant that is a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the *ṣoḍaśin*—is enjoined as a permanent (*nitya*) requirement.

Similarly, within the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the *Atirātra* sacrifice, it is also prescribed as a contingent rule (*naimittika*) with reference to three specific *ukthya* chants, by means of the two statements: "If the *Atirātra* should have the *Bṛhat* as its *sāman*, the *Saubhara* should be performed as the *sāman* for the *ukthya*s; likewise, if the *Rathantara* is the *sāman*, one should perform the *Saubhara* among the *ukthya*s. Thus, it is enjoined sequentially with reference to each of the three *ukthya*s.

Thus, even though it is recited within the context of an obligatory injunction (*nityavidhi*), that which is read there serves merely as an applicatory statement (*viniyojakavākya*) for its fulfillment through desire; therefore, he cites it as an example relevant to the discussion in the present section:
"That which is called the *Brahmasāman*."

(Justification for the injunction of the Saubhara chant as based on the Stotra, with reference to the three fruits): Since it was established in the preceding section that the Saubhara Sāman is of an accomplished nature—consisting of sounds such as "dhvani" and being composed of a collection of notes beginning with Ṣaḍja—it requires a substratum (*āśraya*) when its connection to a fruit is to be established; therefore, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), [it is connected] to the *brahmasāma* stotra.

In order to indicate that it is the substratum (*āśraya*), the term "resorted to" (*āśrita*) was used. Consequently, since the *saubhara* chant is also already established as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), both the meaning of the verbal root and the meaning of the nominal suffix would be established; thus, although it might seem—as in the case of the rule "the cups for Indra and Vāyu come first"—that only the meaning of the verbal root is enjoined, nevertheless, if the hymn (*stotra*) itself were connected to the result, it would follow that it must be performed outside the sacrifice. Since enjoining the *saubhara* in that context—where it is not otherwise established—would entail the fault of a complex injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi-gaurava*), that [interpretation] is not adopted.
This is the state of affairs.

By this [argument], having raised the objection that because *saubhara* denotes an action in the form of singing, it does not require a substratum—just like the *vāravantīya*—and thus the explanatory reference (*anuvāda*) "he should praise" (*stuvīta*) would be untenable;

[the author replies] that because it forms a single syntactical unit with the word "he should praise," the very fact that such an explanatory reference is otherwise impossible necessitates that the word *saubhara*, ending in the third case, [denote the means].

Since it is precisely the state of being a qualified instrument (*viśiṣṭakaraṇatva*) of the *Saubhara* that is enjoined through the relation of instrumentality, and since, upon its requirement for a defining correlate (*nirūpaka*), the *stotra* (hymn) is construed as its substratum (*āśraya*), the justification for the restatement (*anuvāda*) of that [hymn] is established.

However, because the *Vāravantīya* ends in the accusative case, it lacks the status of an instrument; rather, it serves as the object (*karman*) with respect to the meaning of the word *kṛtvā*. Therefore, it has no requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*). Thus, the effort made in the *Śāstradīpikā* regarding this point is as follows: [the passage from the Śāstradīpikā is omitted per instructions].

Because the *vāravantīya* is also referred to by this [word] ending in the third case (*etena*), its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is established, and there is no evidence for any disparity [between it and the other elements].
Regarding what was stated—that "by these sentences"—he provides the justification: "because of the multiplicity of the subjects.

Since the three occurrences of the word *yaḥ* (e.g., "one who desires rain") require three corresponding instances of the word *saḥ*, they must each be construed individually through ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) with the phrase "he should praise with the *saubhara*"; thus, the intended meaning is that there is indeed a distinctness of sentences (*bhinnavākyatā*).
It is called "Nidhana."
For the Sāman has five divisions known as the Prastāva, Udgītha, Pratīhāra, Upadrava, and Nidhana;
the meaning is that [the meditation is on the syllable Om] by virtue of its being the substratum for that which is the final constituent part of the Sāman called the Nidhana.

(Since the distinction of *bhāvanā* is incidental, and because of the exception [to the previous rule], there is a determination of the two types of connection and a description of the form of the doubt.

In this regard, just as with number (*saṅkhyā*), a quality (*guṇa*) cannot directly differentiate the *bhāvanā*. Therefore, since it is the differentiation or non-differentiation of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) that is to be investigated here in the section on qualities (*guṇaprakaraṇa*), both ways [of differentiation] result in a lack of connection to the context due to the differentiation of the verbal root's meaning; nevertheless, starting from the section on "desiring the sense-organ" (*indriyakāmādhikaraṇa*)...

Since the distinctions among incidental meditations (*prāsaṅgika-bhāvanā*) must also be examined, there is a topical connection (*saṅgati*) with that; likewise, there is an immediate connection of exception (*āpavādikī-anantara-saṅgati*) because both the section on those desiring sense organs (*indriyakāmādhikaraṇa*) and the section on the *revatī* verses constitute exceptions. Furthermore, [the question arises]: are the stobha-syllables such as *hīṣ* and so forth, which depend upon the *saubhara* chant under discussion, enjoined for the purpose of rain and other results?

Without explicitly showing the doubt—namely, whether for the sake of rain and other results, those [melodies] which are obtained without restriction in the Saubhara itself are being restricted—he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) directly with the words "In that case" (tatra).
(The prima facie view is that the injunctions for the *hīṣ* and other [syllables] are intended solely for the purpose of attaining the *saubhara* melody as their own inherent goal.
This is because they are directed toward a result.

The meaning is that, by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), it has the result as its primary purpose, according to the principle of the section concerning those desiring heaven (svargakāmādhikaraṇa).
"Precisely with reference to that" means...

For, by means of the dative case denoting purpose (*tādarthya-caturthī*), there is the cognition that *hīṣ* and the others possess the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*)—which is synonymous with "being for the sake of"—and that rain and the others possess the status of being the primary object (*uddeśyatva*)—which is synonymous with "being the principal. The fact that they are enjoined with reference to those [results] is indicated by the particle *eva* as the very reason [for their use]. Thus, it is not the case that this [particle] refers to the *bhara*.

The syllables such as *hīṣ* and so forth, being established forms, take the *sāman* known as *saubhara*—which is under discussion—as their substrate because they are suitable for completing the portions of the *sāman*.

For it is logical that, since the *sāman* serves as the substratum for the *stobha* syllables through its own constituent parts, it stands in a relationship with *hīṣ* and the others by way of a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭavidhayā*).
The meaning is that the *sāman* functions as the substrate because it is accomplished by the *stobha* syllables through its own constituent parts.

In order to avoid the objection that *sāman* cannot function as a substratum because, being an already established entity, it lacks the quality of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the phrase "like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)" was stated. The point is this: just as the *khadira* wood serves as the substratum for the sacrificial post by virtue of being the object of the act of production, so too does sound—consisting of articulated phonemes—function as a substratum; for it is accomplished through effort by virtue of being the object of the act of utterance, and its eternality is not admitted [in this context]. Thus, its status as a substratum is logically consistent.

(Refutation of the suspicion that *hīṣ* and so forth are enjoined as being located in the *nidhana* by way of restating the *nidhana* word): Now, it might be argued that enjoining both the location of *hīṣ* and so forth in the *nidhana* and their connection with the result would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). To this, he says: "By virtue of being the substratum for the *nidhana*."

And for this reason, since the word *nidhana* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) and thus lacks the capacity to present something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), there is no resulting application [of that rule]; such is the meaning.

(The resolution by demonstrating that, since the status of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is impossible according to the Siddhānta, it is more appropriate that it be an original injunction [*apūrvavidhi*]:

As for the claim made in the Siddhānta—that because [the injunction] would result in being an original injunction under the Pūrvapakṣa, one must accept it as a restrictive injunction and therefore there can be no connection between the accessory and the fruit—this is restated with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
Does the word *kiṃnidhana* serve to designate [the sacrifice], or does the word *vṛṣṭikāma* do so?

Not the first, because since that [designation] is already established by the mere recitation [of the text], it would be redundant; furthermore, if it were qualified by the word *vṛṣṭikāma*, there would be the consequence of designating a qualified object (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*).
Furthermore, there would be the contingency of [the word *hiṣ*] being a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the *saubhara* chant within the context of the desire for rain.

For this very reason, the second alternative is not tenable; because even with respect to the *nidhana* occurring in the *saubhara* that serves as the means for rain and so forth, the *hiṣ* and other syllables are already established by the text, and thus their injunction is impossible.

If, however, it is argued that—just as in the case of the *saubhara* chant used for achieving rain and other results—a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) serves to exclude the possibility of *hīṣ* and so forth occurring even in the *nidhana* of a *saubhara* that is not a means to those results (since such occurrence is theoretically possible)—then, because the *stobha* syllables serving as the basis for the *nidhana* would be absent in the performance of the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) *saubhara*, the injunction would result in being dependent on something else (*sāpekṣatva*).
Therefore, with the intention that even a simpler restrictive injunction is impossible, he refutes [the position] by saying: "In that case... (*tathātve*).

Therefore, he concludes the preceding prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), demonstrating its purpose: that there are two rains resulting from the *saubhara* chant and the *hīṣ* etc. *nidhana*, and through the combination of both, a "great rain" occurs—this is what is indicated by the words "ataḥ" (therefore).

(An exposition establishing that even though there is an injunction of a quality with respect to its substratum, it is more appropriate for it to function as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) by following the principle of parsimony [of injunctions]): Although the ancient teachers rejected the injunction of the connection between a quality and a fruit because a substratum was not obtained, [the author] considers that rejection to be untenable since a substratum can be obtained through the manner previously described; thus, he states the final conclusion based solely on the parsimony of restrictive injunctions: "In the case of a restrictive injunction," etc.
(An analysis showing that even resorting to figurative indication [lakṣaṇā] elsewhere is not a defect due to the simplicity of an injunction of restriction):

Even for the sake of three results, the *saubhara*—by the logic of the *yogasiddhi* section—accomplishes only one result in a single performance when uttered once, and not the others; because they share a single purpose as subsidiaries of the *saubhara*, all three would otherwise be obtained as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*).

And thus, just as there is the application of *hīṣ* in the ritual performance of Saubhara for the sake of the fruit of rain, so too other [syllables] would be obtained as alternatives; therefore, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is appropriate for *hīṣ*, which is already optionally obtained.

Furthermore, since it is improper to accept a result residing in the object of reference (*uddeśya*) when a result residing in the enjoined *hīṣ* etc. is possible, this is indeed a restriction of the subsidiary element (*śeṣaniyama*).

Even though the explicit text (*pāṭha*) is directly perceived, because it would require the assumption of an injunction and would apply to the performance for one desiring rain only by way of a general rule, its operation is slow; therefore, since we accept that [the application] occurs prior to that, *hīṣ* alone is what is to be enjoined here.

Consequently, since the fruit belongs precisely to the restriction (*niyama*) inherent in that [word], and there is no restriction on the subordinate element (*śeṣin*), there is no obstruction to the application of *hīṣ* and so forth in the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) performances of the *saubhara*. Thus, the phrase "precisely" (*eva*) indicates that this is indeed an injunction of a restriction regarding *hīṣ* and the rest.
This has been indicated.

By following the principle of parsimony regarding restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*), one accepts the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the *ājyabhāga* offerings related to the primary *paurṇamāsī* sacrifice in the terms *vārtraghnī* and *paurṇamāsī*, as well as the indication of the two case-endings in the sentence concerning the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings; by the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that such [indication] is not defective here either.
"From the recitation," it says.

If, however, it were argued that because the recitation has already fulfilled its purpose through its connection with the door known as the *nidhana*, it cannot serve as the basis for inferring a scriptural injunction (*śruti*) for the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) performances—and thus the application of *hīṣ* and so on would remain unestablished in those performances—then [we reply]:

even when there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the *saubhara* alone as the means for rain, the status of being located in the *nidhana* is obtained precisely for the sake of securing the result of a lighter restriction (*niyama*).
For in the absence of this rule, by virtue of the mere textual recitation (*pāṭha*), *hīṣ* and so on would be applied without restriction to the *nidhana* itself.
And therefore, the attainment of the status of being the final cadence (*nidhana*) arises solely from the power of the injunction and its fruit,

not from the mere recitation [of the text]. For this very reason, it is logical that even an inferred scriptural statement (*śruti*), postulated for the sake of establishing the optionality required by the restrictive rule (*niyama*), is inferred only as a connection with some *saubhari* cadence occurring in any performance whatsoever in a general sense.

By this [principle], it should be understood from the Kaustubha that the *hīṣ* and other [syllables] pertain to the performance of obligatory and occasional rites, and that the *saubhara* chant for the sake of rain has its place in the *nidhana*.

(Proving the previously stated point even without resorting to *lakṣaṇā*): Just as in the case of the rule "for the Vāsiṣṭhas, the Nārāśaṃsa is the second *prayāja*," [the injunction] serves the purpose of the Vāsiṣṭhas by way of the second *prayāja*, which is an auxiliary of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices that produce the results desired by the Vāsiṣṭhas—even so here, since the restrictive injunctions regarding *hīṣ* and other syllables for the sake of rain are justified through an indirect relationship (*paraṃparā-sambandha*), there is no need for *lakṣaṇā*. Thus, he states another position: "In reality, however... (*vastutastu*).
It is indeed a specific variety of the Saubhara.
The meaning is that it is specifically a particular form of the Saubhara chant, composed with the *hīṣ* and other *nidhana*s.
And for this reason...

When the meaning of the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*)— that one should perform [the rite] for rain by means of the *saubhara* of a different class through the insertion of *hīṣ*— has been established, then even within the injunction for the *saubhara* intended for rain,

another restriction is also established as a result: that among the various *saubharas* of a different class which have obtained as optional alternatives for the purpose of rain, only that specific *saubhara* which has *hīṣ* as its finale (*nidhana*) is the means for achieving rain, and not the others.

For it is not possible in any way to establish the restriction that "hīṣ" must be used for rain in the case of the *saubhara* chant when its endings (*nidhana*) are different, provided there is no such other restrictive rule;
this is because the *saubhara*, even when joined with a different ending, is performed for that same purpose [of obtaining rain].
(The nature of the analogy of the one who eats from a bronze vessel, the determination of the subject matter by means of it, and the purpose of the preceding and succeeding methods.)

And therefore, just as it will be stated in the twelfth section (*adhikaraṇa*) regarding the "rule of eating from bronze" (*kāṃsyabhojinnyāya*)— wherein it is observed in the world that when a teacher and a pupil are to eat together, the teacher, though permitted to eat from any vessel, conforms to the pupil’s rule of eating only from bronze— by that same principle, it is established that even though the injunction for the *saubhara* chant intended for rain may be taken in its unrestricted form, it nevertheless conforms to the second restrictive rule and takes up only that specific *saubhara* which is composed with the *hīṣ* and other *nidhana*s.
The meaning is that this is another restrictive rule (*niyamāntara*).
In response to the inquiry, "Where, then, is there an application for the *saubhara* found in other recensional branches (*śākhāntara*)?", he says: "And therefore... (*ataśca*).

In the Siddhānta, since there is no fruit of rain and so forth distinct from the fruit of the Saubhara itself, it is possible to understand through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone that the fruits such as rain do not arise from the *hīṣ* and other syllables; therefore, this was not explicitly stated.
Thus ends the thirteenth section concerning Saubhara.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the *Prabhāvalī*, a commentary on the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*, composed by Śambhubhaṭṭa, disciple of Khaṇḍadeva, the ornament of poets.
